items.title: Java4Shell Vulnerability: How Should Security Teams Identify and Reduce Exposure?
items.summary: TL;DR: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a high severity vulnerability affecting the OpenJDK HotSpot compiler, with a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1. The published advisory identifies Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 release lines as affected, although exact vulnerable versions vary by distributor. Security teams should identify affected Java installations, prioritize production workloads and apply available security &mldr

items.title: Introducing simplified onboarding for AWS WAF Bot Control at the targeted inspection level
items.summary: Today, we’re announcing simplified onboarding and bot confidence levels for AWS WAF Bot Control at the targeted inspection level, which we refer to as Targeted bot control in this post, matching the console. Bot confidence levels and the new LATEST rule group version are available for the resource types that AWS WAF protects: you act on advanced bot detections by confidence level instead of writing label rules, and you stay on the newest detections without manual upgrades, helping you respond to automated traffic, including traffic from AI-powered bots. For the websites and applications that you deliver through Amazon CloudFront , simplified onboarding goes further: you turn on Targeted bot control from a single console setting, and automatic SDK integration , which launched last month , removes the need for application code changes in many cases. In this post, we explain what the simplified onboarding experience looks like and how to get started when protecting CloudFront-delivered applications. Granular control takes effort to configure Targeted bot control uses advanced behavioral analysis designed to help identify sophisticated bots that attempt to evade traditional detection mechanisms. It uses machine learning and client-side signals to help detect sophisticated AI-based bots. It’s also deliberately granular: it surfaces each detection as its own label, so you can build rules around specific behaviors. The number of choices (which labels, which combinations, and which order) is a lot to evaluate and implement when your immediate goal is to implement the first round of protections. To get the full value of Targeted bot control, and to help reduce false positives by grouping its signals into confidence levels, you typically do the following: Add the AWS WAF Bot Control managed rule group to your protection pack, set the inspection level to Targeted , and choose a rule group version. Integrate the AWS WAF JavaScript SDK into your application. This is an application code change, often owned by a different team at your company and tied to a different release cycle. Learn which AWS WAF labels the rules emit and what they mean, and decide which combinations indicate a bot with high confidence. Write label-match rules that group those labels into bot confidence levels, place them in the right order, and keep them current as new rule group versions add labels. We’ve published guidance on grouping targeted bot labels into confidence tiers . For teams without dedicated security engineers, the path to implement the solution can be long. Completing every step can take time, especially when the SDK integration depends on another team’s release cycle, so rules can remain in Count mode longer than intended. What’s new You can now turn on Targeted bot control with a single toggle. AWS WAF sets up the recommended configuration for you and keeps it on the latest detections, and you don’t need to change your application code to integrate AWS WAF JavaScript SDK for CloudFront-delivered applications in many cases. When you use this toggle, AWS WAF configures the following for you: Targeted inspection level – The AWS WAF Bot Control rule group is added (or configured) with the inspection level set to Targeted and machine learning turned on. Actions for each bot confidence level – Each confidence level (High, Medium, or Low) gets an AWS-recommended action, which you can change. Rule group version – The rule group is set to the LATEST version, which points to the most recent AWS WAF Bot Control release, so you get new detections without upgrading manually. Rule order – A newly added AWS WAF Bot Control rule group is placed after the existing rules. Automatic SDK integration – This option is available for protection packs with the CloudFront scope and is turned on by default, so the targeted detections receive browser signals from the start. If you want, you can use this feature stand-alone. Bot confidence With bot confidence, AWS WAF Bot Control now adds a High, Medium, or Low bot confidence level to each request that it evaluates at the targeted inspection level. The confidence level reflects how likely it is that the request comes from an automated client that exhibits behaviors that you might not want. Several AWS WAF Bot Control rules already report their own confidence levels with AWS WAF labels , for example TGT_ML_CoordinatedActivityLow/Medium/High and TGT_TokenReuseIpLow/Medium/High rules, and the TGT_VolumetricSession rule emits labels ending in volumetric:session:low , volumetric:session:medium , and volumetric:session:high . Each of those describes the strength of one detection. Bot confidence combines the targeted detections into one High, Medium, or Low level for each request, so you choose one action per level instead of writing rules across many labels. Bot confidence also emits three labels ending in targeted:signal:bot_signal:low , targeted:signal:bot_signal:medium and targeted:signal:bot_signal:high . The confidence levels and their default actions reflect AWS recommendations to AWS WAF Bot Control customers. Confidence level What it indicates Default action High A signal that by itself strongly indicates automation, or two or more signals that corroborate each other CAPTCHA Medium A signal that indicates automation, but no other signal corroborates it; the request might still come from a person CAPTCHA Low Only weak signals of automation Challenge The defaults are chosen to help keep false positives low. High-confidence and Medium-confidence bot traffic receives a CAPTCHA puzzle rather than a block, so a misclassified user can still get through. Low-confidence bot traffic receives a silent Challenge, which is designed to complete in the browser without requiring user interaction. You can change any of these actions to Allow, Block, CAPTCHA, Challenge, Count, or Monetize. The confidence levels are added alongside the existing AWS WAF Bot Control labels. The existing detection labels that AWS WAF Bot Control emits are still attached to the request, so you can inspect any request and see which signals contributed to its confidence level. Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront The AWS WAF JavaScript SDK runs in the viewer’s browser, where it can see signals the server doesn’t normally receive, such as mouse movements, key presses, form interactions, and device characteristics. These client-side signals help improve the accuracy of the targeted detections in distinguishing between a person and an automated client. The SDK silently acquires and refreshes an AWS WAF token as the page loads, without the extra charges or interruptions of Challenge and CAPTCHA rule actions. That token travels with each request and is used by AWS WAF Bot Control at the targeted inspection level, AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention , and AWS WAF Fraud Control account creation fraud prevention . Until now, integrating the SDK meant adding a script tag to your pages yourself. With automatic SDK integration for CloudFront, you don’t add the script tag yourself. When the setting is on, CloudFront inserts the same script tag that a manual integration uses, pointing to your protection pack’s integration URL. AWS WAF evaluation, token acquisition, and token refresh work the same way as they do with a manual integration. Automatic SDK integration is available for any protection pack with the CloudFront scope that contains one of the following managed rule groups: AWS WAF Bot Control with targeted inspection level AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention AWS WAF Fraud Control account creation fraud prevention For the up-to-date list of managed rule groups supporting this feature, see Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront distributions . A rule group also qualifies when its actions are overridden to Count, so you can add the SDK while you evaluate the rule group. When you create a new protection pack with the CloudFront scope in the console, automatic SDK integration is turned on by default. Protection packs created before the feature launched aren’t changed. You can also turn the setting off with a single toggle if you prefer to integrate the SDK yourself. The SDK collects client-side signals and stores the AWS WAF token in a cookie named aws-waf-token . The token contains information collected from your visitors’ browsers. As described in AWS WAF token characteristics , the information gathered is non-unique and can’t be mapped to an individual human being. Before you turn on automatic SDK integration, review your privacy notice and any cookie consent obligations that apply to your sites, for example under GDPR and the ePrivacy Directive. Walkthrough In this section, we show you how to enable Targeted bot control with bot confidence and automatic SDK integration for CloudFront. Prerequisites To follow this walkthrough, you need the following: A CloudFront distribution that serves HTML pages. The CloudFront distribution uses pay-as-you-go pricing, because distributions on a CloudFront flat-rate pricing plan don’t support AWS WAF Bot Control at the targeted inspection level. Enable Targeted bot control on a new protection pack When you create a new protection pack, you can turn on Targeted bot control together with automatic SDK integration. Open the AWS Management Console for AWS WAF & Shield and choose Protection packs (web ACLs) , then Create protection pack (web ACL) . Under App category , select the category that describes your application. Under Add resources , select your CloudFront distribution. Select one of the predefined protection pack options. The Targeted bot control section isn’t available when you choose Build your own . In the Targeted bot control section, choose Enable Targeted bot control . Figure 1: The Targeted bot control section during protection pack creation Review the action for each confidence level. The defaults are CAPTCHA for High, CAPTCHA for Medium, and Challenge for Low. To observe the effect before you enforce, select Set all actions to Count . Confirm that Enable automatic SDK integration is selected. Choose Create protection pack (web ACL) . Enable Targeted bot control on an existing protection pack These steps work whether your protection pack doesn’t yet have AWS WAF Bot Control, uses AWS WAF Bot Control at the common level, or uses an older AWS WAF Bot Control version. In the AWS WAF & Shield console , open Protection packs (web ACLs) and select a protection pack with the CloudFront scope. Figure 2: Choosing an existing protection pack In the side pane, choose Configure Targeted bot control . Choose Enable Targeted bot control . Figure 3: The Configure Targeted bot control page Review the actions for each confidence level and the automatic SDK integration setting. Choose Save . If the change upgrades the AWS WAF Bot Control rule group to LATEST , a confirmation dialog shows the current and target versions. Review it and confirm. Configuring through the API If you manage AWS WAF as code, you can configure the same pieces directly. For automatic SDK integration, add the ChallengeJavascriptSdkInjection setting to the AssociationConfig of the web ACL in a CreateWebACL or UpdateWebACL request, using the CLOUDFRONT key with an empty configuration object: "AssociationConfig": { "ChallengeJavascriptSdkInjection": { "CLOUDFRONT": {} } } Through the API, the setting is off by default. An UpdateWebACL request that omits the setting turns it off, even if you turned it on in the console. For the rule group, set the inspection level to TARGETED with machine learning enabled in the AWSManagedRulesBotControlRuleSet configuration, and use RuleActionOverrides to set the actions for TGT_SignalBotHigh , TGT_SignalBotMedium , and TGT_SignalBotLow . For the API specifications, see AssociationConfig and ManagedRuleGroupStatement in the AWS WAF API Reference . Considerations Considerations when using bot confidence and automatic SDK integration for CloudFront: Bot confidence Review the following when you use bot confidence. Exclude known automation from bot inspection. If you find known clients that are being flagged, add a scope-down statement to the AWS WAF Bot Control rule group that excludes them, for example by path, header, or IP set. This also keeps you from paying to inspect traffic you already trust. Stay on the LATEST version. Bot confidence requires version 8.0 or later. LATEST keeps you on the newest release automatically; if you pin a static version for change control, choose 8.0 or later and review new versions as they’re released. For the full list of considerations about bot confidence, see Bot confidence levels in the AWS WAF Developer Guide. Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront Review the following before you turn on automatic SDK integration. Confirm that the SDK reaches the pages that matter. After you turn the setting on, view the source of your key pages, such as the home page, sign-in, checkout, and search, to confirm the script tag is present. If your distribution caches HTML, invalidate the cached HTML paths so viewers get the updated pages right away. Do the same when you turn the setting off. Update your content security policy. If your pages set a content security policy, allowlist https://*.awswaf.com in the directives shown in Using the JavaScript API with content security policies . Use Cache-Control: no-transform to keep the tag off specific pages. The setting applies to the whole protection pack, and scope-down statements don’t limit where the tag is inserted. Keep your existing integration where your application relies on the SDK directly. Single-page applications that attach tokens to their own API calls, and applications that use the CAPTCHA JavaScript API or the mobile SDKs, should continue to integrate the SDK as they do today. For the full list of considerations and edge cases, see Considerations and limitations and When pages don’t receive the tag in the AWS WAF Developer Guide. Availability and pricing Simplified onboarding to Targeted bot control is available for protection packs with the CloudFront scope. Bot confidence levels and the new LATEST rule group version are available for the resource types that AWS WAF protects, in the AWS Regions where AWS WAF Bot Control is available. Automatic SDK integration is available for protection packs with the CloudFront scope. This post focuses on CloudFront because you get both features there. Standard AWS WAF Bot Control charges for the targeted inspection level apply. Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront is available at no additional cost. For details, see AWS WAF pricing . Conclusion Simplified onboarding for Targeted bot control takes care of most of the configuration work. You enable Targeted bot control and choose one action for each of three bot confidence levels, or keep the defaults, and enable automatic SDK integration for CloudFront. Your protection pack starts with the configuration we recommend, stays on the latest detections, and doesn’t require you to integrate the JavaScript SDK manually with your CloudFront-delivered applications. If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . Pengfei Shao Pengfei is a Senior Technical Account Manager at AWS based in Stockholm, and has more than 20 years of experience in Telecom and IT industry. His main focus is to help AWS Enterprise Support customers remain operationally healthy, secure, and cost efficient in AWS. He is also focused on AWS Edge Services and loves to work with customers to solve their technical challenges. Amitai Rottem Amitai is a Principal Product Manager at AWS on the AWS WAF team, focused on bot detection and threat intelligence. He brings over 20 years of experience in enterprise security across product management, software development, and startups, including prior roles at large technology companies.

In this post, we explain what the simplified onboarding experience looks like and how to get started when protecting CloudFront-delivered applications.

Granular control takes effort to configure

It uses machine learning and client-side signals to help detect sophisticated AI-based bots. It’s also deliberately granular: it surfaces each detection as its own label, so you can build rules around specific behaviors.   1. Add the AWS WAF Bot Control managed rule group to your protection pack, set the inspection level to Targeted, and choose a rule group version.
  2. Integrate the AWS WAF JavaScript SDK into your application. This is an application code change, often owned by a different team at your company and tied to a different release cycle.
  3. Learn which AWS WAF labels the rules emit and what they mean, and decide which combinations indicate a bot with high confidence.
  4. Write label-match rules that group those labels into bot confidence levels, place them in the right order, and keep them current as new rule group versions add labels.

We’ve published guidance on grouping targeted bot labels into confidence tiers. For teams without dedicated security engineers, the path to implement the solution can be long. Completing every step can take time, especially when the SDK integration depends on another team’s release cycle, so rules can remain in Count mode longer than intended.

What’s new

You can now turn on Targeted bot control with a single toggle. AWS WAF sets up the recommended configuration for you and keeps it on the latest detections, and you don’t need to change your application code to integrate AWS WAF JavaScript SDK for CloudFront-delivered applications in many cases. When you use this toggle, AWS WAF configures the following for you:

  • Targeted inspection level – The AWS WAF Bot Control rule group is added (or configured) with the inspection level set to Targeted and machine learning turned on.
  • Actions for each bot confidence level – Each confidence level (High, Medium, or Low) gets an AWS-recommended action, which you can change.
  • Rule group version – The rule group is set to the LATEST version, which points to the most recent AWS WAF Bot Control release, so you get new detections without upgrading manually.
  • Rule order – A newly added AWS WAF Bot Control rule group is placed after the existing rules.
  • Automatic SDK integration – This option is available for protection packs with the CloudFront scope and is turned on by default, so the targeted detections receive browser signals from the start. If you want, you can use this feature stand-alone.
Bot confidence

With bot confidence, AWS WAF Bot Control now adds a High, Medium, or Low bot confidence level to each request that it evaluates at the targeted inspection level. The confidence level reflects how likely it is that the request comes from an automated client that exhibits behaviors that you might not want.

Several AWS WAF Bot Control rules already report their own confidence levels with AWS WAF labels, for example TGT_ML_CoordinatedActivityLow/Medium/High and TGT_TokenReuseIpLow/Medium/High rules, and the TGT_VolumetricSession rule emits labels ending in volumetric:session:low, volumetric:session:medium, and volumetric:session:high. Each of those describes the strength of one detection. Bot confidence combines the targeted detections into one High, Medium, or Low level for each request, so you choose one action per level instead of writing rules across many labels. Bot confidence also emits three labels ending in targeted:signal:bot_signal:low, targeted:signal:bot_signal:medium and targeted:signal:bot_signal:high.

The confidence levels and their default actions reflect AWS recommendations to AWS WAF Bot Control customers.

Confidence level What it indicates Default action High A signal that by itself strongly indicates automation, or two or more signals that corroborate each other CAPTCHA Medium A signal that indicates automation, but no other signal corroborates it; the request might still come from a person CAPTCHA Low Only weak signals of automation Challenge

The defaults are chosen to help keep false positives low. High-confidence and Medium-confidence bot traffic receives a CAPTCHA puzzle rather than a block, so a misclassified user can still get through. Low-confidence bot traffic receives a silent Challenge, which is designed to complete in the browser without requiring user interaction. You can change any of these actions to Allow, Block, CAPTCHA, Challenge, Count, or Monetize.

The confidence levels are added alongside the existing AWS WAF Bot Control labels. The existing detection labels that AWS WAF Bot Control emits are still attached to the request, so you can inspect any request and see which signals contributed to its confidence level.

Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront

The AWS WAF JavaScript SDK runs in the viewer’s browser, where it can see signals the server doesn’t normally receive, such as mouse movements, key presses, form interactions, and device characteristics. These client-side signals help improve the accuracy of the targeted detections in distinguishing between a person and an automated client. The SDK silently acquires and refreshes an AWS WAF token as the page loads, without the extra charges or interruptions of Challenge and CAPTCHA rule actions.

That token travels with each request and is used by AWS WAF Bot Control at the targeted inspection level, AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention, and AWS WAF Fraud Control account creation fraud prevention. Until now, integrating the SDK meant adding a script tag to your pages yourself.

With automatic SDK integration for CloudFront, you don’t add the script tag yourself. When the setting is on, CloudFront inserts the same script tag that a manual integration uses, pointing to your protection pack’s integration URL. AWS WAF evaluation, token acquisition, and token refresh work the same way as they do with a manual integration.

Automatic SDK integration is available for any protection pack with the CloudFront scope that contains one of the following managed rule groups:

  • AWS WAF Bot Control with targeted inspection level
  • AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention
  • AWS WAF Fraud Control account creation fraud prevention

For the up-to-date list of managed rule groups supporting this feature, see Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront distributions.

A rule group also qualifies when its actions are overridden to Count, so you can add the SDK while you evaluate the rule group. When you create a new protection pack with the CloudFront scope in the console, automatic SDK integration is turned on by default. Protection packs created before the feature launched aren’t changed. You can also turn the setting off with a single toggle if you prefer to integrate the SDK yourself. The SDK collects client-side signals and stores the AWS WAF token in a cookie named aws-waf-token. The token contains information collected from your visitors’ browsers. As described in AWS WAF token characteristics, the information gathered is non-unique and can’t be mapped to an individual human being. Before you turn on automatic SDK integration, review your privacy notice and any cookie consent obligations that apply to your sites, for example under GDPR and the ePrivacy Directive.

Walkthrough

In this section, we show you how to enable Targeted bot control with bot confidence and automatic SDK integration for CloudFront.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need the following:

  • A CloudFront distribution that serves HTML pages.
  • The CloudFront distribution uses pay-as-you-go pricing, because distributions on a CloudFront flat-rate pricing plan don’t support AWS WAF Bot Control at the targeted inspection level.
Enable Targeted bot control on a new protection pack

When you create a new protection pack, you can turn on Targeted bot control together with automatic SDK integration.

  1. Open the AWS Management Console for AWS WAF & Shield and choose Protection packs (web ACLs), then Create protection pack (web ACL).
  2. Under App category, select the category that describes your application. Under Add resources, select your CloudFront distribution.
  3. Select one of the predefined protection pack options. The Targeted bot control section isn’t available when you choose Build your own.
  4. In the Targeted bot control section, choose Enable Targeted bot control.

    Figure 1: The Targeted bot control section during protection pack creation

  5. Review the action for each confidence level. The defaults are CAPTCHA for High, CAPTCHA for Medium, and Challenge for Low. To observe the effect before you enforce, select Set all actions to Count.
  6. Confirm that Enable automatic SDK integration is selected.
  7. Choose Create protection pack (web ACL).
Enable Targeted bot control on an existing protection pack

These steps work whether your protection pack doesn’t yet have AWS WAF Bot Control, uses AWS WAF Bot Control at the common level, or uses an older AWS WAF Bot Control version.

  1. In the AWS WAF & Shield console, open Protection packs (web ACLs) and select a protection pack with the CloudFront scope.

    Figure 2: Choosing an existing protection pack

  2. In the side pane, choose Configure Targeted bot control.
  3. Choose Enable Targeted bot control.

    Figure 3: The Configure Targeted bot control page

  4. Review the actions for each confidence level and the automatic SDK integration setting.
  5. Choose Save. If the change upgrades the AWS WAF Bot Control rule group to LATEST, a confirmation dialog shows the current and target versions. Review it and confirm.
Configuring through the API

If you manage AWS WAF as code, you can configure the same pieces directly. For automatic SDK integration, add the ChallengeJavascriptSdkInjection setting to the AssociationConfig of the web ACL in a CreateWebACL or UpdateWebACL request, using the CLOUDFRONT key with an empty configuration object:

"AssociationConfig": {
  "ChallengeJavascriptSdkInjection": {
    "CLOUDFRONT": {}
  }
}

Through the API, the setting is off by default. An UpdateWebACL request that omits the setting turns it off, even if you turned it on in the console. For the rule group, set the inspection level to TARGETED with machine learning enabled in the AWSManagedRulesBotControlRuleSet configuration, and use RuleActionOverrides to set the actions for TGT_SignalBotHigh, TGT_SignalBotMedium, and TGT_SignalBotLow.

For the API specifications, see AssociationConfig and ManagedRuleGroupStatement in the AWS WAF API Reference.

Considerations

Considerations when using bot confidence and automatic SDK integration for CloudFront:

Bot confidence

Review the following when you use bot confidence.

  • Exclude known automation from bot inspection. If you find known clients that are being flagged, add a scope-down statement to the AWS WAF Bot Control rule group that excludes them, for example by path, header, or IP set. This also keeps you from paying to inspect traffic you already trust.
  • Stay on the LATEST version. Bot confidence requires version 8.0 or later. LATEST keeps you on the newest release automatically; if you pin a static version for change control, choose 8.0 or later and review new versions as they’re released.

For the full list of considerations about bot confidence, see Bot confidence levels in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront

Review the following before you turn on automatic SDK integration.

  • Confirm that the SDK reaches the pages that matter. After you turn the setting on, view the source of your key pages, such as the home page, sign-in, checkout, and search, to confirm the script tag is present. If your distribution caches HTML, invalidate the cached HTML paths so viewers get the updated pages right away. Do the same when you turn the setting off.
  • Update your content security policy. If your pages set a content security policy, allowlist https://*.awswaf.com in the directives shown in Using the JavaScript API with content security policies.
  • Use Cache-Control: no-transform to keep the tag off specific pages. The setting applies to the whole protection pack, and scope-down statements don’t limit where the tag is inserted.
  • Keep your existing integration where your application relies on the SDK directly. Single-page applications that attach tokens to their own API calls, and applications that use the CAPTCHA JavaScript API or the mobile SDKs, should continue to integrate the SDK as they do today.

For the full list of considerations and edge cases, see Considerations and limitations and When pages don’t receive the tag in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Availability and pricing

Simplified onboarding to Targeted bot control is available for protection packs with the CloudFront scope. Bot confidence levels and the new LATEST rule group version are available for the resource types that AWS WAF protects, in the AWS Regions where AWS WAF Bot Control is available. Automatic SDK integration is available for protection packs with the CloudFront scope. This post focuses on CloudFront because you get both features there.

Standard AWS WAF Bot Control charges for the targeted inspection level apply. Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront is available at no additional cost. For details, see AWS WAF pricing.

Conclusion

Simplified onboarding for Targeted bot control takes care of most of the configuration work. You enable Targeted bot control and choose one action for each of three bot confidence levels, or keep the defaults, and enable automatic SDK integration for CloudFront. Your protection pack starts with the configuration we recommend, stays on the latest detections, and doesn’t require you to integrate the JavaScript SDK manually with your CloudFront-delivered applications.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

items.title: How to Find, Mitigate, and Patch the Critical Java4Shell Flaw (CVE-2026-114938) Now
items.summary: Executive Summary Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. The researchers who found it rate it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, and Oracle rates it 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can corrupt Java heap memory, read secrets from it, and reach remote code execution. Researchers demonstrated pre-authentication RCE on default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Unpatched OpenJDK builds from 17.0.6 onward, from any vendor, are affected when they run on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI, which includes Intel Xeon from Ice Lake through Granite Rapids and AMD EPYC from Zen 4 onward. Oracle released fixes on November 17, 2026, and a single JVM flag closes the exposure where patching has to wait. CISA has issued an alert urging organizations to patch immediately. Start with internet-facing identity, CI/CD, and collaboration systems, and assign an owner and a deadline to every system still unpatched. What’s at Risk A Critical Java Flaw Could Hand Attackers Your Identity and Build Servers. Java4Shell is in the Java runtime itself, so no application or library has to be at fault for a service to be exposed. The flaw sits in handwritten assembly that speeds up Base64 decoding with AVX-512 instructions. A short malformed input makes that code write 62 bytes past the end of a buffer before Java rejects the input. Base64 carries login headers, tokens, and file uploads, so the vulnerable code often runs before a user has authenticated. Calif , the firm that discovered the flaw, demonstrated remote code execution against the following products in their default configurations: Access required Products None (pre-authentication) Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, PingFederate Authenticated user Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, Netflix Spinnaker The researchers say these lists are not exhaustive. They also reached RCE in sample applications built on Apache Struts and Spring Boot. The pre-authentication list is where the business risk concentrates. Identity providers issue the tokens every other system trusts, and build and artifact servers sign and ship your software. A compromise of either can expose downstream systems that trust its identities, tokens, or software artifacts. Code execution is not the only outcome. A successful exploit chain can read Java heap memory before it runs any attacker code. That memory can hold private keys, tokens, and personal data. CISA also warns that crafted input can crash the JVM, so availability is at risk too. Java clients are exposed as well. The researchers report a client-side exploit in which a Java program is compromised simply by connecting over TLS to a malicious server. Are You Affected? A system is in scope only when both conditions are true. For an attack to work, attacker-controlled data must also reach the vulnerable Base64 decoding path in the application. Condition Affected Not affected Java runtime Unpatched OpenJDK-based builds from 17.0.6 onward, including 21, 25, and 27. Also Oracle Java SE 8 Enterprise Performance Pack 8u511b33-perf Releases before 17.0.6, including standard OpenJDK 8 and 11. Also any vendor build that contains the fix Processor x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids), AMD EPYC and Ryzen (Zen 4 and newer) ARM64, and x86-64 without AVX-512 VBMI The runtime condition covers every OpenJDK-based distribution: Oracle Java SE, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, and Red Hat OpenJDK. items.summary_html:
Executive Summary

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. The researchers who found it rate it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, and Oracle rates it 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can corrupt Java heap memory, read secrets from it, and reach remote code execution. Researchers demonstrated pre-authentication RCE on default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Unpatched OpenJDK builds from 17.0.6 onward, from any vendor, are affected when they run on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI, which includes Intel Xeon from Ice Lake through Granite Rapids and AMD EPYC from Zen 4 onward. Oracle released fixes on November 17, 2026, and a single JVM flag closes the exposure where patching has to wait. CISA has issued an alert urging organizations to patch immediately. Start with internet-facing identity, CI/CD, and collaboration systems, and assign an owner and a deadline to every system still unpatched.

What’s at Risk

A Critical Java Flaw Could Hand Attackers Your Identity and Build Servers.

Java4Shell is in the Java runtime itself, so no application or library has to be at fault for a service to be exposed. The flaw sits in handwritten assembly that speeds up Base64 decoding with AVX-512 instructions. A short malformed input makes that code write 62 bytes past the end of a buffer before Java rejects the input.

Base64 carries login headers, tokens, and file uploads, so the vulnerable code often runs before a user has authenticated. Calif, the firm that discovered the flaw, demonstrated remote code execution against the following products in their default configurations:

Access requiredProductsNone (pre-authentication)Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, PingFederateAuthenticated userApache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, Netflix Spinnaker

The researchers say these lists are not exhaustive. They also reached RCE in sample applications built on Apache Struts and Spring Boot.

The pre-authentication list is where the business risk concentrates. Identity providers issue the tokens every other system trusts, and build and artifact servers sign and ship your software. A compromise of either can expose downstream systems that trust its identities, tokens, or software artifacts.

Code execution is not the only outcome. A successful exploit chain can read Java heap memory before it runs any attacker code. That memory can hold private keys, tokens, and personal data. CISA also warns that crafted input can crash the JVM, so availability is at risk too. Java clients are exposed as well. The researchers report a client-side exploit in which a Java program is compromised simply by connecting over TLS to a malicious server.

Are You Affected?

A system is in scope only when both conditions are true. For an attack to work, attacker-controlled data must also reach the vulnerable Base64 decoding path in the application.

ConditionAffectedNot affectedJava runtimeUnpatched OpenJDK-based builds from 17.0.6 onward, including 21, 25, and 27. Also Oracle Java SE 8 Enterprise Performance Pack 8u511b33-perfReleases before 17.0.6, including standard OpenJDK 8 and 11. Also any vendor build that contains the fixProcessorx86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids), AMD EPYC and Ryzen (Zen 4 and newer)ARM64, and x86-64 without AVX-512 VBMI

The runtime condition covers every OpenJDK-based distribution: Oracle Java SE, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, and Red Hat OpenJDK. There is one exception on Java 8. Oracle lists the 8u511b33-perf build of Java SE 8 as vulnerable.

On Linux, run this command to check the processor. The host meets the hardware condition only if all four flags appear.

grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’

Two cautions when scoping:

  • Check the runtime each application actually runs. Many products and container images bundle their own JDK, which operating system updates do not touch. CISA notes that bundled runtimes, including those in appliances, may not appear as separate entries in a software inventory.
  • Use the processor condition to order the work, not to close findings. A workload on an unaffected CPU today can land on an affected one after an instance resize or a move to newer hardware.
Exploitation Status

As of November 17, 2026, we have not seen public confirmation of exploitation in the wild. Do not plan around that. The trigger is a short malformed Base64 string; the root cause and exploitation technique are public, and the researchers have said details of the bug leaked before the patch.

The researchers are holding back their product-specific exploits until organizations have had time to upgrade, and plan to publish them later. They report finding the bug with AI assistance in about an hour and having a first working exploit two hours after that, for under $200 in AI token costs. Expect others to repeat that work.

There is one limit worth knowing. No universal exploit exists: each product needs its own chain, and the technique is sensitive to network conditions. That slows mass exploitation. It does not protect a specific target such as your identity provider.

What to Do Now

Updating the Java runtime is the only complete fix. Oracle released fixed builds on November 17, 2026.

Oracle Java SEFixed build8 Enterprise Performance Pack8u513-perf1717.0.21.12121.0.13.12525.0.5.12727.0.1.1

Other OpenJDK vendors publish on their own schedules. As of November 17, 2026, Amazon had released Corretto 17.0.21.1.2 with the fix. Use your vendor’s advisory to identify the fixed build and confirm it addresses CVE-2026-114938.

If you cannot patch today, there is a temporary workaround. It is a startup setting for Java, applied by the team that runs the application, and it takes effect after a restart. You need only one of the two options below.

  • Preferred: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. This turns off the fast Base64 decoder where the bug lives. Java falls back to its standard decoder, and everything else runs as before. Applications that decode large amounts of Base64 may run slower, so test first.
  • Alternative: -XX:UseAVX=2. This turns off a wider set of processor optimizations, including the vulnerable one, so the performance cost is broader. Use it only on Intel and AMD servers. Java on ARM does not accept this setting and will not start.

Neither option replaces the patch.

Either way, restart every Java process. A patch or a flag takes effect only when the JVM restarts, so verify the running process and not only the installed package. Do not rely on a reverse proxy as a control. Request buffering breaks some exploit chains but is not a general mitigation.

Reduce exposure while you wait for a patch. Take identity, build, and collaboration consoles off the open internet, or put them behind a VPN, until they are patched. CISA also suggests validating Base64 input and enforcing input-size limits at the application boundary. Size limits alone will not stop this bug, because the malformed input is very short. The JVM flag above is the more direct stopgap because it removes the vulnerable code.

Work in this order:

  1. Internet-facing identity providers such as Keycloak and PingFederate.
  2. Internet-facing Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, and Artifactory.
  3. Other internet-facing Java services that handle logins, tokens, or file uploads.
  4. Internal Java systems, starting with Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker.

Assign an owner and a remediation deadline to every system that is waiting on a vendor build.

What to Watch For

CISA advises monitoring for rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. Qualys TRU suggests starting with these checks:

  • Unexpected JVM crashes or restarts on internet-facing Java services.
  • Java processes that start a shell or open outbound connections they have not made before.
  • Java runtimes on a host that your inventory does not account for.
How Qualys Can Help

Qualys helps you respond to Java4Shell: discover and assess exposure using Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM). It inventories Java installations across your assets and helps put internet-facing ones first.

Use the following CSAM query to identify potentially affected OpenJDK installations across Java 17, 21, 25, and 27 for further assessment.

(version>=21 AND version<21.0.13.1) OR
(version>=25 AND version<25.0.5.1) OR
(version>=27 AND version<27.0.1.1)
))

As distributions publish their own advisories, InstaScan turns them into findings without waiting for the next scheduled scan.

Detection QIDs

Qualys is releasing the following detection QIDs. We will add distribution-specific detection QIDs to this blog as they are released.

items.title: WhatDR Meets AI: Is “AIDR” the Next EDR, or Three Racoons in a Trench Coat?
items.summary: Warning : this blog is another experiment. The idea for a blog came from a thought that has been bugging me for months. The content is researched, debated, refined, “hardened” by a Gemini skill I created (using Gemini 4 Argon). Then Claude Fable 5.2 performed a peer review, and refined the text. I then reviewed it and utterly hated it! It went into the trash. I refined the idea seed that I feed into my Gemini skill and tried again. The whole process ran better this time. And then I lightly edited it, and tuned a few jokes. I replaced 3 kids with 3 racoons (racoons are funnier!). Let me know if this sucks, and I will stop. Promise! Back in March 2024, in WhatDR or What Detection Domain Needs Its Own Tools? , I begged the universe: “And, gods, please, no AIDR…” Naturally, cybersecurity marketing gods did not listen. I suspect they read my plea as a product spec. (Reminder: I have been out of the acronym-crafting business since 2019 , so do not blame me for this one.) By late 2026 the pitch is everywhere: agents are the new endpoint, this is “ the EDR moment for AI”, and you need a dedicated AI Detection and Response (AIDR) product. Right? This is no longer only crazy startup talk. CrowdStrike says it is defining the AIDR category and draws the EDR comparison itself. Meanwhile, the grumpy minimalist in the back row mutters: “Relax, AI is just JSON over HTTPS. Ship the logs to SIEM and go home.” Both camps are half-wrong. Well, more like two-thirds wrong, but anyhow. My short version: AI agents need runtime detection and response, and my own 2024 “WhatDR” test says so. What they do not need is one more new console , because what is sold as “AIDR” today is three different jobs inside one trench coat. One is new, one is not detection and response at all, and one already belongs to your SIEM. Three Raccoons in the AIDR Trench Coat When I named EDR in 2013 , it earned its seat in the SOC because the endpoint is a coherent boundary. Endpoint threats detection could not be reduced to OS logs (“Sysmon into SIEM” was always a sad, poor person’s EDR, or a decent “second EDR”), and one local sensor could watch memory, process trees, DLLs and kernel activity, then isolate the host within seconds. It can both sense and act. Now look at typical 2026 “AIDR” pitch. I see 3 raccoons in a trenchcoat model here. a 3 racoon model of AIDR There are three jobs, and the easiest way to tell them apart is to ask what each one watches: Top raccoon watches the agents you run: the inline agent and model gate. Inspecting prompts, retrieved context and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool calls mid-flight, and blocking an injected instruction or an unauthorized tool call before it executes. As I argued recently, the model has preferences, but the harness got controls . Architecturally this is close to RASP (now dead and forgotten) plus an API gateway: heavy on prevention, light on investigation. This is the new job. IMHO, very real. Middle raccoon watches humans using AI: workforce AI control. Catching the seven shades of Shadow AI : unsanctioned browser extensions, local coding agents, employees pasting M&A spreadsheets into public models. This is useful, but it is not detection and response, in my book. Most of the time there is no attacker and no incident, only a policy to enforce. It is a hall monitor in a detective’s coat, and your DLP, CASB and EDR budgets already pay for it. (In that WhatDR post I said DDR probably should not exist because data is not a technology domain. Same logic, new sticker.) Bottom raccoon watches an agent’s trail across your other systems: cross-domain correlation. Catching an agent whose OAuth token reads a Jira ticket, queries a customer table and posts a summary to an external Slack channel. That is application visibility from the SOC Visibility Quad joined with identity and data logs. This one is real detection and response, and it already has an owner: SIEM. (Some decks also file “catching AI-generated phishing” under AIDR. Yuck! That belongs in the same hall of shame as “VMDR.”) Running AI Through the WhatDR Test The original post had seven decision dimensions for when a domain needs its own “?DR” or “*DR” tool versus just using a broad tool like SIEM. BTW, there and here as well, this was a lot more about D, detection, than about R, response. Here are the seven, scored for AI agents, with the raccoon each row belongs to. AI scored vs WhatDR critia + racoons Read the “2024 verdict” column honestly: rows 2, 3, 5 and 6 point to a dedicated tool, and all four belong to the top raccoon. So by my own 2024 test, the top raccoon passes and this means that AIDR should exist. Agent runtime detection and response is a real domain with its own telemetry, its own context and its own response actions . Somebody has to build that capability. The middle raccoon shows up only in row 4, and it should not be taking this test at all. WhatDR was a test for detection domains, and policy enforcement on employee AI use is not one. The bottom raccoon is row 7, which was always SIEM. So why not hand the top raccoon a console and call it the next EDR? I made two arguments (and then got tired of it, but I think there are more): Inherent broad needs. EDR got its console in an era when the SOC had nowhere else to investigate an endpoint. An agent incident is cross-domain from the first minute, because the question that matters is what the agent’s identity touched in other systems. “AIDR console” would be too narrow to be useful, or will have to become SIEM to work . RASP history. I compared the gate to RASP on purpose. RASP had to live inside somebody else’s application, and that is a big part of why it ended up as a feature and then a bad memory. The agent gate has the same dependency on the harness, so I expect it to ship with the harness, the AI gateway or the platform. You do not own most harnesses. The agents inside your SaaS suites run in the vendor’s harness, and you cannot put a sensor there. You get whatever audit logs and admin controls the vendor exposes, and those go to SIEM. For many lean teams this is the majority of their agents. My verdict: separate sensor — yes, separate control point — maybe, separate console — likely no. Note that I have changed my mind on this kind of thing before. In 2022, I leaned toward CDR deserving its own category . By WhatDR time (2024) it sat in my gray zone, and my read is that much of it has since ended up as a capability inside CNAPP and SIEM. In 2026, there are not many CDR vendors left, if any. I expect AIDR to take the same road, but faster (because AI). When would I be wrong? If you build and run many of your own agents, own every harness, and have a dedicated AI security team, a separate console for that team can be justified. That describes a small number of AI-heavy companies, and they know who they are. Why “Just Ship It to SIEM” Fails Saying “AI is just another log source” in 2026 is as naive as saying “Sysmon into SIEM is as good as EDR” was in 2014. (I am a constructive cynic, not a full-on SIEM museum curator .) I see four reasons, but, come on, this is kinda obvious: Data becomes control flow. Application logs assume deterministic code paths. When an agent reads an untrusted email or a poisoned wiki page, the content can redirect what the agent does next. AgentDojo built a benchmark of 97 tasks and 629 security test cases around exactly this. A log line written after the tool call cannot make the allow-or-block decision. It has to be made at the harness, before the call runs. A key argument for “?DR” is a need for control on the spot. Timing. A SIEM rule that runs every few minutes will notice that an agent read an untrusted document and then called an export API. By then the export has happened. Detection after the fact is still worth having, but it does not help much for rapid sequence of automated actions. Response granularity. If the only lever your SOC has is revoking the shared service-account token, containment means an outage for every legitimate user of that application. You need to be able to end one agent session or block one tool call. Sensitivity, then volume. An illustrative example with round numbers (yours will differ): 500 agents running 200 tasks a day is 100,000 runs. If each run has 10 steps carrying about 50 KB of prompt history, retrieved documents and tool output, that is 500 KB per run, or about 50 GB a day of unstructured text. This is fine, for now. Still, having the harness evaluate locally and emit only structured and useful logs, analyzed on the spot is better AND cheaper. Potentially Useful Actions Based on This This was fun — we concluded the world does need AIDR, but it may not be what people call that name. To reduce confusion, do these: Open the trench coat on every “AIDR” pitch. Ask which raccoon the vendor builds. Score the gate against the seven rows above. Judge workforce AI control as a policy tool against the DLP and CASB you already own (this isn’t AIDR). Evaluate cross-domain correlation against your SIEM collect and detect capabilities. Inventory the agents whose harness you do not own. For each SaaS agent, find out which audit logs and kill switches the vendor exposes, and get those logs into SIEM. Here you do need SIEM, not AIDR. Add an AI-telemetry question to your next MDR or SIEM review. Ask whether their detection content uses gen_ai tool-call telemetry and correlates it with identity and data-access logs. No tool removes the learning cost of knowing which data an agent is allowed to touch. Keep raw prompts out of SIEM by default. Follow an Output-Driven SIEM approach: have gateways and harnesses emit structured OpenTelemetry spans with a conversation ID, tool names and guardrail verdicts, and keep redacted payloads in local trace storage for on-demand retrieval. As much harder extra credit: Test your “R” at the session level. Run an API or Die audit on your agent orchestrators and codify Context as Code for agent identities. If your SOC or MDR cannot end a single agent session, remove a single tool permission, or quarantine a poisoned document without revoking the application’s master key, you have no usable response. So, Is AIDR the Next EDR? One raccoon of three is, and what it gives you is “the next EDR”, perhaps. That is also the math behind “two-thirds wrong.” Some of the AIDR fans are wrong about two raccoons of three. Every new computing substrate replays the same sequence. First we pretend the old log pipelines are enough. Then somebody sells a new console for the new domain. Then operations forces a settlement: sensors and inline controls live in the new runtime, and cross-domain detection and investigation stay in SIEM. AI is running that sequence faster than cloud did. Just do not give the trench coat its own island in your SOC. Agree? Disagree? [A.C. — note to self: this is v7.5 Gemini skill using 4 Argon, take 2] Related blogs: WhatDR or What Detection Domain Needs Its Own Tools? The Model Has Preferences, but the Harness Got Controls (Part 1) How to Solve the Mystery of AI Defense in Depth WhatDR Meets AI: Is “AIDR” the Next EDR, or Three Racoons in a Trench Coat? was originally published in Anton on Security on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Read the “2024 verdict” column honestly: rows 2, 3, 5 and 6 point to a dedicated tool, and all four belong to the top raccoon. So by my own 2024 test, the top raccoon passes and this means that AIDR should exist. Agent runtime detection and response is a real domain with its own telemetry, its own context and its own response actions. Somebody has to build that capability.

The middle raccoon shows up only in row 4, and it should not be taking this test at all. WhatDR was a test for detection domains, and policy enforcement on employee AI use is not one. The bottom raccoon is row 7, which was always SIEM.

So why not hand the top raccoon a console and call it the next EDR?

I made two arguments (and then got tired of it, but I think there are more):

  • Inherent broad needs. EDR got its console in an era when the SOC had nowhere else to investigate an endpoint. An agent incident is cross-domain from the first minute, because the question that matters is what the agent’s identity touched in other systems. “AIDR console” would be too narrow to be useful, or will have to become SIEM to work.
  • RASP history. I compared the gate to RASP on purpose. RASP had to live inside somebody else’s application, and that is a big part of why it ended up as a feature and then a bad memory. The agent gate has the same dependency on the harness, so I expect it to ship with the harness, the AI gateway or the platform.
  • You do not own most harnesses. The agents inside your SaaS suites run in the vendor’s harness, and you cannot put a sensor there. You get whatever audit logs and admin controls the vendor exposes, and those go to SIEM. For many lean teams this is the majority of their agents.

My verdict: separate sensor — yes, separate control point — maybe, separate console — likely no. Note that I have changed my mind on this kind of thing before. In 2022, I leaned toward CDR deserving its own category. By WhatDR time (2024) it sat in my gray zone, and my read is that much of it has since ended up as a capability inside CNAPP and SIEM. In 2026, there are not many CDR vendors left, if any. I expect AIDR to take the same road, but faster (because AI).

When would I be wrong? If you build and run many of your own agents, own every harness, and have a dedicated AI security team, a separate console for that team can be justified. That describes a small number of AI-heavy companies, and they know who they are.

Why “Just Ship It to SIEM” Fails

Saying “AI is just another log source” in 2026 is as naive as saying “Sysmon into SIEM is as good as EDR” was in 2014. (I am a constructive cynic, not a full-on SIEM museum curator.)

I see four reasons, but, come on, this is kinda obvious:

  • Data becomes control flow. Application logs assume deterministic code paths. When an agent reads an untrusted email or a poisoned wiki page, the content can redirect what the agent does next. AgentDojo built a benchmark of 97 tasks and 629 security test cases around exactly this. A log line written after the tool call cannot make the allow-or-block decision. It has to be made at the harness, before the call runs. A key argument for “?DR” is a need for control on the spot.
  • Timing. A SIEM rule that runs every few minutes will notice that an agent read an untrusted document and then called an export API. By then the export has happened. Detection after the fact is still worth having, but it does not help much for rapid sequence of automated actions.
  • Response granularity. If the only lever your SOC has is revoking the shared service-account token, containment means an outage for every legitimate user of that application. You need to be able to end one agent session or block one tool call.
  • Sensitivity, then volume. An illustrative example with round numbers (yours will differ): 500 agents running 200 tasks a day is 100,000 runs. If each run has 10 steps carrying about 50 KB of prompt history, retrieved documents and tool output, that is 500 KB per run, or about 50 GB a day of unstructured text. This is fine, for now. Still, having the harness evaluate locally and emit only structured and useful logs, analyzed on the spot is better AND cheaper.
Potentially Useful Actions Based on This

This was fun — we concluded the world does need AIDR, but it may not be what people call that name.

To reduce confusion, do these:

  1. Open the trench coat on every “AIDR” pitch. Ask which raccoon the vendor builds. Score the gate against the seven rows above. Judge workforce AI control as a policy tool against the DLP and CASB you already own (this isn’t AIDR). Evaluate cross-domain correlation against your SIEM collect and detect capabilities.
  2. Inventory the agents whose harness you do not own. For each SaaS agent, find out which audit logs and kill switches the vendor exposes, and get those logs into SIEM. Here you do need SIEM, not AIDR.
  3. Add an AI-telemetry question to your next MDR or SIEM review. Ask whether their detection content uses gen_ai tool-call telemetry and correlates it with identity and data-access logs. No tool removes the learning cost of knowing which data an agent is allowed to touch.
  4. Keep raw prompts out of SIEM by default. Follow an Output-Driven SIEM approach: have gateways and harnesses emit structured OpenTelemetry spans with a conversation ID, tool names and guardrail verdicts, and keep redacted payloads in local trace storage for on-demand retrieval.

As much harder extra credit:

  1. Test your “R” at the session level. Run an API or Die audit on your agent orchestrators and codify Context as Code for agent identities. If your SOC or MDR cannot end a single agent session, remove a single tool permission, or quarantine a poisoned document without revoking the application’s master key, you have no usable response.
So, Is AIDR the Next EDR?

One raccoon of three is, and what it gives you is “the next EDR”, perhaps. That is also the math behind “two-thirds wrong.” Some of the AIDR fans are wrong about two raccoons of three.

Every new computing substrate replays the same sequence. First we pretend the old log pipelines are enough. Then somebody sells a new console for the new domain. Then operations forces a settlement: sensors and inline controls live in the new runtime, and cross-domain detection and investigation stay in SIEM. AI is running that sequence faster than cloud did.

Just do not give the trench coat its own island in your SOC.

Agree? Disagree?

[A.C. — note to self: this is v7.5 Gemini skill using 4 Argon, take 2]

  • WhatDR or What Detection Domain Needs Its Own Tools?
  • The Model Has Preferences, but the Harness Got Controls (Part 1)
  • How to Solve the Mystery of AI Defense in Depth

items.title: Black October Made Attack Path Management a “Now” Problem
items.summary: On the November 10, 2026, Patch Tuesday, Microsoft released fixes for 1,093 vulnerabilities, its second Patch Tuesday in a row with a four-digit count. Sixty-three are rated critical. Attackers are already exploiting one of them. Dustin Childs of the Zero Day Initiative flagged 30 as potentially wormable. The same day, Gartner published a special report [login required] arguing that “Black October” is the new normal. According to Gartner, any one of October’s major incidents would likely have been the worst of a typical year. PHP2Shell memory leaks forced U.S. and EU government websites offline. Attackers breached commercial refrigeration portals in Europe, causing fires and facility shutdowns. Attackers moved about $6.3 billion out of Binance hot wallets across ten blockchains, most of it in roughly 20 minutes. Binance’s early investigation suggests the attack may have started with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Using the agentic AI framework ARTEX and stolen ConnectWise application credentials, Storm-0940 attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, reaching privileged access in some in under three hours. Vulnerability deep dive: Signed, Sealed, and Relayed, NTLM-style: Bypassing LDAP Signing Through Reauthentication According to Gartner, disclosed vulnerabilities reached nearly 49,000 in 2025, and the firm expects more than 70,000 this year. The industry’s average time to remediate sits at 43 days. At that pace, this week’s fixes would close out around December 23, more than two weeks after December’s Patch Tuesday. AI is surfacing vulnerabilities faster than anyone can patch them, and it’s putting working exploits in the hands of attackers at every skill level. Gartner’s conclusion is that fixing CVEs one at a time is already impractical and that security programs have to become preemptive. STAY TUNED: We’ll share dates for a webinar series exploring how AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation are changing cybersecurity, and how defenders can adapt. Attack path management belongs in “Now” Attack paths are chains of identities, privileges, and misconfigurations that let an attacker move from an initial foothold to critical assets. Attack path management (APM) is the practice of finding those chains and breaking them, starting with the choke points where one fix closes the most paths. It complements vulnerability management by showing which weaknesses lead to something that matters. Gartner advises security and IT leaders to make the move from reactive to preemptive in phases. The first phase, “Now,” focuses on optimizing existing controls and strengthening cyber hygiene: securing the identity fabric, eliminating standing privilege, and reducing technical debt. The second, “Next,” shifts from CVE prioritization to attack path management. Attack path analysis helps teams prioritize the “Now” work: which standing privileges, trust relationships, and legacy exposures put critical assets most at risk? Every organization I talk to has more identity hygiene debt than it can pay down in a year. Zero standing privilege is the right goal, but a tiny fraction of organizations have achieved it. The practical question is what privileges, on which identities, to fix first. Without a graph of an attacker’s paths, teams answer it with gut feel or tribal knowledge. With the graph, defenders can see that removing one group membership or one misconfigured delegation collapses thousands of paths at once. We call those choke points, and they’re where hygiene work pays off fastest. BloodHound Enterprise’s job is to eliminate paths to critical identities and resources, regardless of how the attacker got in. Gartner also recommends measuring security performance by attack paths eliminated instead of vulnerability counts. That has been the core idea behind the BloodHound Enterprise release in 2021. As Microsoft’s John Lambert wrote in 2015, defenders think in lists while attackers think in graphs. BloodHound Enterprise handed defenders back control by tailoring the attack graph to focus on those choke points that remove millions of paths at once. We need to be measuring the reduced exposure of critical assets, not just the count of findings closed. Why attack path management can’t wait ARTEX illustrates why the connections between exposures matter. In the ARTEX campaign, Storm-0940, a China-aligned actor, took over the cloud identities of ConnectWise’s Cloud Backup applications. Customers had already granted those applications privileged access to their Microsoft 365 tenants, so the attacker could sign in as a trusted app without a user sign-in. Using the agentic AI framework ARTEX, it attempted that access against more than 2,250 tenants and, in some, reached privileged access in under three hours. A backup application with broad tenant permissions is a familiar finding. Once its credentials were stolen, it became a path into every tenant that trusted it. November’s Patch Tuesday vulnerabilities illustrate the same need to consider downstream access. Microsoft rates the actively exploited Outlook zero-day, CVE-2026-124194, Moderate, with a CVSS score of 6.5. It can expose NTLM authentication material, creating opportunities for credential abuse beyond Outlook. The critical Exchange Server RCE, CVE-2026-118207, requires a low-privilege login. A compromised Exchange server can expose more than mailboxes when it holds broad rights in Active Directory. The Windows LDAP RCE, CVE-2026-119958, requires no authentication, and Childs warned it could be especially destructive on domain controllers. These vulnerabilities offer different routes into or through an environment. Their consequences depend on both the exploit and what the compromised identity or system can reach. The same Exchange exploit can be a contained incident in one environment and a path to control plane compromise in another, depending on the rights that server holds. Gartner lists this as the second of six structural realities from Black October: exposure outweighs isolated CVE severity. Where to begin? Internet exposure and active exploitation remain essential prioritization signals. Attack path analysis adds another: what the attacker can reach post-compromise. Combine those signals to identify vulnerable systems that can reach critical assets and the changes that most reduce that exposure. Start mapping attack paths now and use the map to prioritize hygiene work. AI agents belong on the same map Gartner’s identity data points in the same direction. In the surveys cited by Gartner, only 21% of organizations had created an AI agent governance framework, and 50% lacked defined operational boundaries for agents or relied on predefined human access. AI agents operate through identities and credentials, sometimes shared with people or other workloads. Those access relationships can become part of an attack path. With OpenGraph, teams can extend BloodHound Enterprise beyond Active Directory and Entra ID to model relationships across platforms such as Okta, GitHub, and Jamf. Attack paths cross product boundaries. The identities used by service accounts and AI agents belong on the same map as your control plane admins. If one of them can reach your most critical assets, find that path before an attacker does. What preemptive means in practice For an attack path management program, preemptive means putting five practices into operation: Identify your critical assets. Continuously track which identities can reach your most critical assets. Prioritize the fixes that most reduce exposure to critical assets with the least operational disruption. Report progress in a metric a board understands: how far exposure to critical assets went down. Run that cycle at the pace of environment change, but at least daily. Gartner calls the attacker-defender capability gap permanent. The attacker is going to retain the upper hand if we don’t change our programs, not just to keep pace, but to fundamentally disrupt this advantage. Attackers only win when they understand the relationships in an environment better than defenders. However, the defender can proactively map and remove attack paths before the breach takes place. Black October won’t be the last month like it. Teams that already understand their attack paths can act on the exposures that matter most before the next incident begins.

items.title: Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 CTF: New challenges, new leaderboards
items.summary: Key takeaways Put your digital forensics skills to the test: Compete in a three-hour Magnet Virtual Summit Capture the Flag featuring new forensic datasets, realistic investigative scenarios, and challenges for all experience levels. Choose how you compete: Join the Unassisted or AI-Assisted Leaderboard for a chance to win prizes, with additional cipher challenges offering an early opportunity to earn points. Get ready for the challenge: Join a virtual preparation workshop on February 8, download the forensic images in advance, and compete live on February 11. By Jessica Hyde, Founder & Owner of Hexordia I am thrilled to announce the launch of the Magnet Virtual Summit Capture the Flag (CTF), proudly sponsored by Hexordia ! This competition is a fun, interactive way to put your digital forensics skills to the test. Participants will work with forensic images from multiple simulated pieces of evidence and answer a variety of challenge questions based on the data. You are welcome to use any tools you prefer to solve the questions, which are assigned point values reflecting their complexity. The challenges are thoughtfully designed to accommodate all levels of expertise, from beginners to seasoned practitioners. We are incredibly enthusiastic about the entirely new data sets and questions we are preparing, and we eagerly await your participation! It has been an absolute pleasure collaborating with our exceptional group of interns, Matteen Mahfooz and Alex Vejandla from George Mason University, and our Hexordia team member, Adam Hachem. Furthermore, we are delighted that multi-CTF champion Kevin Pagano has also returned to join the team to construct this year’s competition. New leaderboard structure & prizes With this year’s CTF, we are introducing a brand-new leaderboard structure. The Magnet Virtual Summit CTF aims to replicate real-life scenarios in digital forensics and the use of artificial intelligence will be permitted, as it’s becoming an increasingly prevalent tool in investigations. Before starting the competition, please choose whether you will be competing on the Unassisted Leaderboard or the AI-Assisted Leaderboard. The AI-Assisted Leaderboard is available for participants using AI tools during the three-hour competition window only. Unassisted Leaderboard: First place, second place, and third place prizes AI-Assisted Leaderboard: First place prize Returning for the 2027 challenge: Cipher questions Back by popular demand for the 2027 challenge, keep a close watch on our social media channels in the weeks leading up to the main event! We will once again be releasing a series of intriguing cipher questions on the Unassisted Leaderboard. Successfully solving these preliminary puzzles may provide valuable insights or clues that could assist you during the main event. The points awarded for the flags will also count towards your total. This is an excellent way to start flexing your investigative muscles early! Don’t worry, if you miss a week’s cipher, as it will stay open through the live event to solve. They’ll be posted on both boards during the main event. Challenge preparation workshop Monday, February 8 at 12:00PM ET Want to sharpen your skills before the competition? Join Kevin Pagano and me for a virtual workshop featuring tips, strategies, and practical advice to help you succeed in the CTF. You can register as part of your Magnet Virtual Summit session selection . Capture the Flag details The challenge itself will be held online on Thursday, February 11, from 11:00 AM – 2:00 PM ET and is open to all registered attendees of Magnet Virtual Summit. To ensure all participants have adequate time for initial preparation, the forensic images will be distributed to all registrants by February 9. This allows for downloading, initial processing, and evidence review prior to the start of the competition. This event is open to participants worldwide. Ready to compete? Register for the Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 CTF here . We strongly encourage you to register without delay, as the evidence images will be distributed in advance to facilitate preparation. Additionally, make sure to follow our updates on LinkedIn , where we will share posts that may contain helpful hints or important references. Please make sure to register with Magnet Forensics by February 8, at 4:00 PM ET as well as the CTF board itself with the same email address. We are truly looking forward to your participation in the Magnet Virtual Summit CTF. Best of luck to all competitors!

Key takeaways
  • Put your digital forensics skills to the test:
    Compete in a three-hour Magnet Virtual Summit Capture the Flag featuring new forensic datasets, realistic investigative scenarios, and challenges for all experience levels.
  • Choose how you compete:
    Join the Unassisted or AI-Assisted Leaderboard for a chance to win prizes, with additional cipher challenges offering an early opportunity to earn points.
  • Get ready for the challenge:
    Join a virtual preparation workshop on February 8, download the forensic images in advance, and compete live on February 11.

By Jessica Hyde, Founder & Owner of Hexordia

I am thrilled to announce the launch of the Magnet Virtual Summit Capture the Flag (CTF), proudly sponsored by Hexordia!

This competition is a fun, interactive way to put your digital forensics skills to the test. Participants will work with forensic images from multiple simulated pieces of evidence and answer a variety of challenge questions based on the data.

You are welcome to use any tools you prefer to solve the questions, which are assigned point values reflecting their complexity. The challenges are thoughtfully designed to accommodate all levels of expertise, from beginners to seasoned practitioners. We are incredibly enthusiastic about the entirely new data sets and questions we are preparing, and we eagerly await your participation!

It has been an absolute pleasure collaborating with our exceptional group of interns, Matteen Mahfooz and Alex Vejandla from George Mason University, and our Hexordia team member, Adam Hachem. Furthermore, we are delighted that multi-CTF champion Kevin Pagano has also returned to join the team to construct this year’s competition.

New leaderboard structure & prizes

With this year’s CTF, we are introducing a brand-new leaderboard structure. The Magnet Virtual Summit CTF aims to replicate real-life scenarios in digital forensics and the use of artificial intelligence will be permitted, as it’s becoming an increasingly prevalent tool in investigations.

Before starting the competition, please choose whether you will be competing on the Unassisted Leaderboard or the AI-Assisted Leaderboard. The AI-Assisted Leaderboard is available for participants using AI tools during the three-hour competition window only.

  • Unassisted Leaderboard: First place, second place, and third place prizes
  • AI-Assisted Leaderboard: First place prize
Returning for the 2027 challenge: Cipher questions

Back by popular demand for the 2027 challenge, keep a close watch on our social media channels in the weeks leading up to the main event! We will once again be releasing a series of intriguing cipher questions on the Unassisted Leaderboard. Successfully solving these preliminary puzzles may provide valuable insights or clues that could assist you during the main event. The points awarded for the flags will also count towards your total. This is an excellent way to start flexing your investigative muscles early! Don’t worry, if you miss a week’s cipher, as it will stay open through the live event to solve. They’ll be posted on both boards during the main event.

Challenge preparation workshop

Monday, February 8 at 12:00PM ET

Want to sharpen your skills before the competition? Join Kevin Pagano and me for a virtual workshop featuring tips, strategies, and practical advice to help you succeed in the CTF. You can register as part of your Magnet Virtual Summit session selection.

Capture the Flag details

The challenge itself will be held online on Thursday, February 11, from 11:00 AM – 2:00 PM ET and is open to all registered attendees of Magnet Virtual Summit.

To ensure all participants have adequate time for initial preparation, the forensic images will be distributed to all registrants by February 9. This allows for downloading, initial processing, and evidence review prior to the start of the competition. This event is open to participants worldwide.

Ready to compete?

Register for the Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 CTF here. We strongly encourage you to register without delay, as the evidence images will be distributed in advance to facilitate preparation.

Additionally, make sure to follow our updates on LinkedIn, where we will share posts that may contain helpful hints or important references. Please make sure to register with Magnet Forensics by February 8, at 4:00 PM ET as well as the CTF board itself with the same email address.

We are truly looking forward to your participation in the Magnet Virtual Summit CTF. Best of luck to all competitors!
