items.title: Securely exposing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
items.summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime delivers a secure serverless environment to deploy AI agents and tools at scale. When you start talking to your agent, the runtime launches a dedicated isolated session that runs in its own dedicated microVM with a completely sandboxed CPU, memory, and filesystem allocation. This provides strict data governance, helps to prevent cross-tenant data leakage, and preserves context while isolating stateful reasoning from external sessions. To govern access control across these environments, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity provisions distinct workload identities to let your agents run. By federating directly with an OpenID Connect identity provider like Amazon Cognito , Okta, or others, the users can only see and interact with agents they’re authorized to use. But securing the runtime alone doesn’t protect the ingress path perimeter. When you expose your agent to users through a web or mobile application, the AWS Shared Responsibility Model dictates that you should provide a dedicated access layer that enforces tight control over the origin and intent of every request before any traffic reaches the runtime. The access layer acts as a trusted bridge to authenticate each incoming request, enforce authorization rules, preserve user identity through the request lifecycle, and securely channel all user traffic into the isolated runtime. This post walks through two architectures for securing access to AgentCore Runtime and provides guidance to help you decide which architecture best fits your organization. Why propagating identity is important In an agentic workflow, downstream data access should remain tied to the invoking user’s identity, and each segment in the execution chain is permissioned only for the immediate next hop. Using a single static credential, even one linked to the original requester, grants every immediate component identical, broad access. This directly violates the principle of least privilege, because the ingress gateway, the proxy, and the agent’s tool execution context each require only enough permission to reach the next component. Recent real-world incidents have demonstrated that agentic workloads can bypass internal prompt guardrails, escape the software sandboxes, and abuse static credentials to move across applications and layers. In a multi-chain agentic architecture, scoping each hop as tightly as possible is key to preventing these exploits. However, long-running, unattended execution poses a fundamental identity challenge for extended agentic workloads. If an agent runs a complex task that takes hours, the user’s interactive session will expire before the workload ends, making their short-lived OAuth 2.0 access token invalid mid-execution. Refreshing the tokens won’t solve this problem and storing a long-lived, user-scoped credential inside the agent’s runtime environment might reintroduce exactly the broad, standing credential attack surface that the zero-trust architectures are intentionally designed to mitigate. To mitigate this, identity propagation acts as a critical bridge between authentication at the perimeter and authorization at the data layer. The agent must operate within the invoking user’s authorization scope. Every session receives a short-lived, user-scoped token that provides only the permissions granted to that specific user and authorization is enforced at each hop. If any single segment is compromised, then the exposure is contained in that hop scope. This security model also strengthens a continuous verification process where the tokens are validated at every hop from the ingress endpoint through AgentCore to the downstream resource, so no segment operates with unverified or elevated privileges. Protecting AgentCore Runtime: What does it need? We explained in the previous section why identity must follow the user through every hop. However, identity propagation alone isn’t enough to secure the ingress path; it must be integrated within a broader set of ingress controls that together protect the path into the runtime. AgentCore Runtime provides infrastructure isolation, per session microVMs, per session tool registration, and enforces the application of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails . These features and resources protect the execution environment. However, they don’t control who reaches the runtime, how they’re authenticated, or whether their identity is preserved through the chain. That responsibility falls on the ingress control layer that you build. Securing this path requires a defense-in-depth architecture that binds every request to the user’s identity before it ever reaches the agent’s reasoning loop. To protect and control data access, any architecture exposing AgentCore Runtime to users must satisfy the following requirements: Authentication: Continuously verify the identity of every requester at the perimeter by validating tokens against the identity provider’s public keys. Authorization: Determine what the authenticated subject is allowed and authorized to do, which actors they can invoke, which scopes they hold and which operations they can perform. Per-hop least privilege: Make sure each component in the chain holds only enough permission to call the next hop, eliminating broad-scope credentials. Each hop must exchange the inbound token for a down-scoped, short-lived credential valid only for the immediate downstream call. Identity propagation: Preserve the user’s identity through the full execution chain, so the agent operates within the user’s authorization scope. For long running or unattended workloads where the user’s session closes mid-flight, the ingress must seamlessly transition the active user token into an encrypted, short lived session context key from AgentCore Runtime . This allows the microVM to securely assert a restricted, cryptographic snapshot of the user’s identity even when the user is completely offline. Edge security: Inspect and filter traffic before it reaches the application logic, by applying the needed WAF rules, bot control, IP-based rate limiting, and so on. Network perimeter: Restrict runtime access to a single secure, controlled network path. Traffic arriving from any unexpected origin must be rejected regardless of the token’s validity. Content protection: Enforce the Guardrails on both incoming prompts for injection attacks and outgoing tool arguments for malicious payload before execution. Audit and logging: Log every authentication outcome, the authorization decision on the tool invocations, and any security event to an externalized system for compliance and incident response. These security requirements are mandatory baselines to expose any agentic workloads to users. Any missing requirement might create a potential attack vector. By applying this full set of guardrails, you help contain the impact of a potential malicious exploit to a single user, a single session and a single execution hop. In the next section, we provide two architecture patterns that implement this propagation differently: The first architecture validates the user’s token independently at each layer while preserving it for the runtime to verify directly. The second architecture exchanges the user’s token at the gateway boundary for scoped machine credentials, attesting the user’s identity through verified claims. This pattern is uniquely suited for handling the session context keys required by asynchronous, unattended workloads. Both approaches achieve the same result: the agent acts as the user rather than with elevated privileges. The AgentCore Gateway patterns Each of the following patterns is presented the same way: the layered controls a request passes through before reaching the agent, followed by how user identity is carried to the runtime. As you explore, please note where each pattern places the trust boundary as that difference is what drives the trade-offs summarized at the end. Pattern A: Expose through API Gateway We expose AgentCore Runtime through Amazon API Gateway , which acts as a dedicated ingress point that terminates each client connection. Before any request reaches the agent, it must pass through layered security controls: A Lambda authorizer : An AWS Lambda authorizer validates the Amazon Cognito-issued JSON Web Token (JWT) by verifying the signature, issuer claim and token expiration, to confirm the requester’s identity. AgentCore Identity : Independently, AgentCore Identity performs a second validation inherent to the Lambda authorizer through its OAuth 2.0 inbound authentication flow . This helps to confirm the user’s identity before the request reaches the runtime to be processed. Because the client-provided session ID is treated as untrusted input, the Lambda authorizer creates a composite session ID by appending the user identifier to the client-provided session ID. Even if two different users submit the same session ID, they resolve to unique composite IDs at the AgentCore Runtime level, preventing any cross-user session leakage. To prevent denial of service attempts, we suggest using Amazon DynamoDB as a lightweight session counter. While the AWS WAF rate-based rules attached to the API Gateway stage protect against IP-level volumetric abuse, they evaluate requests before authentication. The Lambda authorizer checks and increments a per-user counter in DynamoDB after validating the user’s identity, helping prevent a single authenticated user from exhausting agent capacity, even if they connect from multiple IP addresses. This design scales cleanly by using a composite session ID. The Lambda Authorizer combines the user identifier and the client session ID, routing each user’s counter to a distinct partition. This naturally distributes write traffic and reduces the risk of hot keys. Each session can sustain roughly 1,000 counter updates per second before reaching DynamoDB’s per-partition write limit, which is far beyond what any legitimate session would ever generate. That same limit is exactly what makes the counter an effective throttle. Meanwhile, total capacity across all users scales horizontally , growing with the number of active sessions. For high-volume production deployments, on-demand capacity mode absorbs sudden spikes automatically, and CloudWatch Contributor Insights lets you confirm traffic stays evenly distributed. After the Lambda authorizer approves the request, as shown in the Figure 1: API Gateway forwarding: Passes the approved request to Lambda proxy that runs within an isolated environment with no internet egress. VPC endpoint routing: The proxy Lambda function forwards the request to AgentCore Runtime through an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) endpoint, making sure that all traffic remains strictly within the private network. Token preservation and identity propagation: The proxy Lambda function forwards the user’s token unchanged in the authorization header; this maintains the original user identity throughout the entire flow of AgentCore Runtime. API Gateway forwards the request to a Lambda proxy running on a private VPC with no internet egress. The role of this Lambda proxy is to relay the request to AgentCore Runtime through a VPC endpoint, so that all communication remains within the private network. The Lambda proxy forwards the user’s token (unchanged) in the Authorization header, which preserves the user’s identity all the way to AgentCore Runtime. Figure 1: Pattern A architecture for exposing AgentCore Runtime through Amazon API Gateway This VPC endpoint enforces a strict network perimeter using two independent controls: Security groups : The VPC endpoint security group restricts ingress solely to the proxy Lambda function on port 443, so no other compute in the account can reach the endpoint. Resource-based policy : The runtime resource-based policy is configured with principal "*" and a condition that allows invocations only when the request carries aws:SourceVpc and aws:SourceVpce values matching this stack’s VPC and endpoint. Authentication happens at the AgentCore Identity level, so there is no AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal to match, and the network path is the only meaningful gate and condition that remains. AgentCore Runtime rejects requests sent directly from outside the VPC with an AccessDeniedException , even with a valid JWT. Beyond the network boundary, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails evaluates each model’s invocation for prompt injection attacks, helping catch malicious inputs even after an invocation has passed identity and network verification. This adds content protection as a defensive layer independent of identity and network controls. Your stack logs and tracks every authorization outcome along this path as structured JSON to Amazon CloudWatch , with an INVALID_JWT alarm . The full walkthrough and a deployable AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) sample are linked at the end of this post. Before production deployment, we recommend configuring an AWS WAF Web ACL at the API Gateway stage to inspect requests before they reach the Lambda authorizer. You should include AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet and AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet for generic OWASP Top 10 protections and known exploit patterns, AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet to catch injection signatures, a per-IP rate-based rule ahead of the DynamoDB throttle counters, and custom rules to reject oversized requests or malformed session IDs early. For a step-by-step integration guide including two deployment patterns for placing AWS WAF in front of the AgentCore Runtime, see Securing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with AWS WAF . This first pattern satisfies the ingress security requirements discussed earlier. It achieves defense in depth by applying the authentication at two independent layers, enforcing authorization through session binding and controlling traffic through per-user throttling. The architecture maintains per-hop least privilege from the API Gateway through the AgentCore Runtime while preserving end-user identity propagation by passing the user’s token through unchanged. The edge filtering is managed with AWS WAF and the network perimeter is enforced by VPC endpoint controls. The design includes the application of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content security with a tamper-proof audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch . The deployable CDK sample for pattern A is available on GitHub. Pattern B: Expose through AgentCore Gateway With Pattern B, you expose AgentCore Runtime through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a managed service purpose-built for agentic traffic that combines ingress authentication, token exchange and Runtime routing without requiring a proxy Lambda function or custom VPC networking. Before any request reaches the agent, it passes the following layered security controls: Inbound authentication: A custom JWT inbound authorizer is configured on AgentCore Gateway that validates the Amazon Cognito JWT by verifying its signature, issuer, and expiration before any logic runs. Identity extraction, session binding and guardrails: A REQUEST interceptor for Lambda, invoked directly by AgentCore Gateway, extracts the verified user identity claims from the validated token for downstream injection. For asynchronous or unattended workloads, this interceptor securely binds these claims into an encrypted, short lived session context key. This helps ensure that even if the user’s interactive session expires hours later, a secure snapshot of their identity remains intact . It mirrors the role of the Lambda authorizer in Pattern A, enforcing the same session-binding and throttling logic. Perimeter authorization (AgentCore Policy): AgentCore Gateway uses a deterministic Cedar-based policy engine to evaluate each request against defined policies before allowing tool access . It also enforces Amazon Bedrock Guardrails through AgentCore Policy for screening prompt injection and content violations at the gateway level, before the request reaches the agent. This declarative enforcement is an advantage over the API Gateway pattern where guardrails must be invoked programmatically from within the agent code. After the authorization succeeds, the gateway manages the outbound call to AgentCore Runtime by using a strict workload isolation mechanism as shown in Figure 2: Token exchange: The gateway requests a machine-to-machine (M2M) token from AgentCore Identity using a dedicated Amazon Cognito M2M app client and attaches it to the request. Workload verification: The AgentCore Runtime validates this token against the allowedWorkloadConfiguration parameter, confirming the request originated from the gateway. On-behalf-of access: The runtime unpacks the session context key, allowlists the injected user identity passed by the interceptor and forwards it directly to the agent to enable secure, context-aware execution on behalf of the user, even during completely unattended background execution loops. Figure 2: Pattern B architecture for exposing AgentCore runtime through AgentCore Gateway If a client attempts to bypass the gateway by sending a valid user token directly to the runtime, the request is automatically rejected because it lacks the required workload identity. For more operational efficiency, AgentCore Gateway integrates AWS WAF directly at the single gateway access point, protecting the entire ingress path in one place, without the need to manage separate authorizers, proxy Lambda functions or VPC endpoints. While API Gateway also supports AWS WAF, the AgentCore Gateway pattern simplifies management by consolidating all ingress controls behind a single component. The AgentCore Gateway also supports native rate limiting , removing the need for custom DynamoDB-based throttle tables, for your production environments. The interceptor writes a structured audit trail to CloudWatch, with an INVALID_JWT alarm to flag spikes in authentication failures. Before production deployment, we strongly recommend that you enable AWS WAF on the AgentCore gateway with the same rule sets described in the API Gateway pattern, including the OWASP protections, SQL injection, and custom rules for oversized or malformed requests. To summarize, this second architecture satisfies the ingress security requirements defined earlier. It achieves defense in depth by applying a managed CUSTOM_JWT authorizer directly at the entry point, enforcing authorization through interceptor-based session binding and using rate limiting to control traffic. This pattern maintains per-hop least privileges from AgentCore Gateway through to the runtime by automating M2M token exchange, while propagating user identity for on-behalf-of execution. The edge security is managed by AWS WAF, coming directly with the gateway’s single-entry point, and secure workload isolation strictly enforces the perimeter. Finally, this design applies declarative Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for early content safety, and a tamper-proof audit trail and alarms in CloudWatch. The complete CDK sample for Pattern B is available on GitHub. Choosing your AgentCore Runtime patterns As explained earlier, securing access to AgentCore Runtime can be achieved through two different patterns: The AgentCore Gateway pattern or the Amazon API Gateway pattern. The right choice depends on your existing AWS infrastructure, workload constraints, and operational preferences. Choose the Amazon API Gateway pattern if: You have existing API infrastructure : Your team already runs an established Amazon API Gateway and AWS WAF deployment You need a single entry point : You prefer to fold agentic traffic into your existing pipelines rather than introducing a separate entry point to operate and secure. Your security model is VPC centric : Your security and compliance teams rely on VPCs and security groups as their primary network control layer Your agent sessions are short-lived : While API Gateway has increased its integration timeout beyond 29 seconds, long running agentic workloads with streaming tool calls might still exceed it. This isn’t a concern if your sessions are brief. Choose the AgentCore Gateway pattern if: You’re building a new gateway: Your organization has no existing API Gateway You have long run workloads : Your agents use streaming or long running tool calls that require strict API timeouts You need low operational overhead : You prefer a fully managed perimeter over manually wired infrastructure You require advanced AI routing : You want built-in capabilities to convert APIs and Lambda functions into Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, handle Agent to Agent (A2A) traffic and route inference across different model providers. The following table summarizes the key elements that help you make the right architectural decision: Consideration API Gateway (Pattern A) AgentCore Gateway (Pattern B) Suited to Teams already standardized on API Gateway Teams starting fresh who want less infrastructure to operate. Perimeter control Runtime resource policy with aws:SourceVpc and VPC endpoint security group Runtime workload lock ( allowedWorkloadConfiguration ). Components to operate API Gateway, Lambda authorizer, Amazon VPC, VPC endpoints, proxy Lambda function AgentCore Gateway and Lambda REQUEST interceptor. User identity to agent User JWT forwarded unchanged (no SigV4 ) Interceptor-injected verified headers (OAuth outbound M2M token). AWS WAF Attach directly to the API stage Attach directly to the gateway. Request timeout Inherits the API Gateway integration timeout Not subject to this limitation. Public endpoint Can be fully private (API Gateway PRIVATE endpoint type) Supports AWS PrivateLink ingress and VPC Lattice egress, but keeps a public endpoint active. Access relies on the JWT authorizer and resource policy rather than removing the endpoint Conclusion By securing access to the AgentCore Runtime with a defense in depth, an agent can be both highly usable and secure. The two patterns in this post complete the shared responsibility model for you: they authenticate every request against the identity provider, authorize it at each step and propagate the user’s identity end-to-end from the edge through the token exchange into the isolated microVM (AgentCore Runtime) and down to the agent’s tool calls (AgentCore Gateway). Each step only holds a short-lived credential for the next one, so the agent always works within the user’s permissions rather than with broad, long-term access. If one step is ever compromised, the design limits the impact to that single step, session and user. Whether the runtime is behind API Gateway with a VPC endpoint or in front of it with AgentCore Gateway, the design verifies each request at each step. To get started, clone the Pattern A sample or the Pattern B sample , deploy it in your account, and test it against your requirements. Both samples are provided as a starting point, not a production-ready deployment. We recommend working with your security and legal teams to adapt to the controls before going live. From there, you can extend either pattern for multi-tenant use, add observability hooks, or tighten controls for your specific compliance requirements. If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post. Meriem SMACHE Meriem is a Security Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS, supporting customers in the design and deployment of resilient cloud and AI solutions, from generative AI workloads to fully autonomous agentic systems, that meet their regulatory requirements and security needs. Christian Kamwangala Christian is a Senior AI/ML and Generative AI Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS, based in Paris, France. He partners with enterprise customers to architect, optimize, and deploy production-grade AI solutions using the comprehensive AWS ML stack. Christian specializes in inference optimization techniques that balance performance, cost, and latency requirements for large-scale deployments. Christian enjoys exploring nature and spending time with family and friends. Lior Perez Lior is a Principal AI & Machine Learning Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, based in Toulouse, France. He helps customers speed up their digital transformation with AI. He wrote the AWS Prescriptive Guidance Governing and Architecting the Diversity of Agentic AI at Scale, which helps enterprises design and govern AI agents. He makes complex ideas simple and practical. His background in manufacturing and meteorology gives him a different way of looking at business challenges. Charline Boulie Charline is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS. She helps French FinTech startups and scale-ups build and scale secure, generative AI-powered workloads, focusing on agentic AI, application development and security. She brings 15 years of software and cloud architecture experience from Thales Avionics and AWS Professional Services, and champions women in tech through mentoring and student outreach.

With Pattern B, you expose AgentCore Runtime through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a managed service purpose-built for agentic traffic that combines ingress authentication, token exchange and Runtime routing without requiring a proxy Lambda function or custom VPC networking.

Before any request reaches the agent, it passes the following layered security controls:

  • Inbound authentication: A custom JWT inbound authorizer is configured on AgentCore Gateway that validates the Amazon Cognito JWT by verifying its signature, issuer, and expiration before any logic runs.
  • Identity extraction, session binding and guardrails: A REQUEST interceptor for Lambda, invoked directly by AgentCore Gateway, extracts the verified user identity claims from the validated token for downstream injection. For asynchronous or unattended workloads, this interceptor securely binds these claims into an encrypted, short lived session context key. This helps ensure that even if the user’s interactive session expires hours later, a secure snapshot of their identity remains intact. It mirrors the role of the Lambda authorizer in Pattern A, enforcing the same session-binding and throttling logic.
  • Perimeter authorization (AgentCore Policy): AgentCore Gateway uses a deterministic Cedar-based policy engine to evaluate each request against defined policies before allowing tool access. It also enforces Amazon Bedrock Guardrails through AgentCore Policy for screening prompt injection and content violations at the gateway level, before the request reaches the agent. This declarative enforcement is an advantage over the API Gateway pattern where guardrails must be invoked programmatically from within the agent code.

After the authorization succeeds, the gateway manages the outbound call to AgentCore Runtime by using a strict workload isolation mechanism as shown in Figure 2:

  1. Token exchange: The gateway requests a machine-to-machine (M2M) token from AgentCore Identity using a dedicated Amazon Cognito M2M app client and attaches it to the request.
  2. Workload verification: The AgentCore Runtime validates this token against the allowedWorkloadConfiguration parameter, confirming the request originated from the gateway.
  3. On-behalf-of access: The runtime unpacks the session context key, allowlists the injected user identity passed by the interceptor and forwards it directly to the agent to enable secure, context-aware execution on behalf of the user, even during completely unattended background execution loops.

Figure 2: Pattern B architecture for exposing AgentCore runtime through AgentCore Gateway

If a client attempts to bypass the gateway by sending a valid user token directly to the runtime, the request is automatically rejected because it lacks the required workload identity.

For more operational efficiency, AgentCore Gateway integrates AWS WAF directly at the single gateway access point, protecting the entire ingress path in one place, without the need to manage separate authorizers, proxy Lambda functions or VPC endpoints.

While API Gateway also supports AWS WAF, the AgentCore Gateway pattern simplifies management by consolidating all ingress controls behind a single component.

The AgentCore Gateway also supports native rate limiting, removing the need for custom DynamoDB-based throttle tables, for your production environments. The interceptor writes a structured audit trail to CloudWatch, with an INVALID_JWT alarm to flag spikes in authentication failures.

Before production deployment, we strongly recommend that you enable AWS WAF on the AgentCore gateway with the same rule sets described in the API Gateway pattern, including the OWASP protections, SQL injection, and custom rules for oversized or malformed requests.

To summarize, this second architecture satisfies the ingress security requirements defined earlier. It achieves defense in depth by applying a managed CUSTOM_JWT authorizer directly at the entry point, enforcing authorization through interceptor-based session binding and using rate limiting to control traffic. This pattern maintains per-hop least privileges from AgentCore Gateway through to the runtime by automating M2M token exchange, while propagating user identity for on-behalf-of execution. The edge security is managed by AWS WAF, coming directly with the gateway’s single-entry point, and secure workload isolation strictly enforces the perimeter. Finally, this design applies declarative Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for early content safety, and a tamper-proof audit trail and alarms in CloudWatch. The complete CDK sample for Pattern B is available on GitHub.

Choosing your AgentCore Runtime patterns

As explained earlier, securing access to AgentCore Runtime can be achieved through two different patterns: The AgentCore Gateway pattern or the Amazon API Gateway pattern. The right choice depends on your existing AWS infrastructure, workload constraints, and operational preferences.

Choose the Amazon API Gateway pattern if:

  • You have existing API infrastructure: Your team already runs an established Amazon API Gateway and AWS WAF deployment
  • You need a single entry point: You prefer to fold agentic traffic into your existing pipelines rather than introducing a separate entry point to operate and secure.
  • Your security model is VPC centric: Your security and compliance teams rely on VPCs and security groups as their primary network control layer
  • Your agent sessions are short-lived: While API Gateway has increased its integration timeout beyond 29 seconds, long running agentic workloads with streaming tool calls might still exceed it. This isn’t a concern if your sessions are brief.

Choose the AgentCore Gateway pattern if:

  • You’re building a new gateway: Your organization has no existing API Gateway
  • You have long run workloads: Your agents use streaming or long running tool calls that require strict API timeouts
  • You need low operational overhead: You prefer a fully managed perimeter over manually wired infrastructure
  • You require advanced AI routing: You want built-in capabilities to convert APIs and Lambda functions into Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, handle Agent to Agent (A2A) traffic and route inference across different model providers.

The following table summarizes the key elements that help you make the right architectural decision:

Consideration API Gateway (Pattern A) AgentCore Gateway (Pattern B) Suited to Teams already standardized on API Gateway Teams starting fresh who want less infrastructure to operate. Perimeter control Runtime resource policy with aws:SourceVpc and VPC endpoint security group Runtime workload lock (allowedWorkloadConfiguration). Components to operate API Gateway, Lambda authorizer, Amazon VPC, VPC endpoints, proxy Lambda function AgentCore Gateway and Lambda REQUEST interceptor. User identity to agent User JWT forwarded unchanged (no SigV4) Interceptor-injected verified headers (OAuth outbound M2M token). AWS WAF Attach directly to the API stage Attach directly to the gateway. Request timeout Inherits the API Gateway integration timeout Not subject to this limitation. Public endpoint Can be fully private (API Gateway PRIVATE endpoint type) Supports AWS PrivateLink ingress and VPC Lattice egress, but keeps a public endpoint active. Access relies on the JWT authorizer and resource policy rather than removing the endpoint
Conclusion

By securing access to the AgentCore Runtime with a defense in depth, an agent can be both highly usable and secure. The two patterns in this post complete the shared responsibility model for you: they authenticate every request against the identity provider, authorize it at each step and propagate the user’s identity end-to-end from the edge through the token exchange into the isolated microVM (AgentCore Runtime) and down to the agent’s tool calls (AgentCore Gateway). Each step only holds a short-lived credential for the next one, so the agent always works within the user’s permissions rather than with broad, long-term access. If one step is ever compromised, the design limits the impact to that single step, session and user. Whether the runtime is behind API Gateway with a VPC endpoint or in front of it with AgentCore Gateway, the design verifies each request at each step.

To get started, clone the Pattern A sample or the Pattern B sample, deploy it in your account, and test it against your requirements. Both samples are provided as a starting point, not a production-ready deployment. We recommend working with your security and legal teams to adapt to the controls before going live. From there, you can extend either pattern for multi-tenant use, add observability hooks, or tighten controls for your specific compliance requirements.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

items.title: Quad9’s withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
items.summary: Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement. Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead. The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation. Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances. And a Belgian court recently issued an order that would impose substantial penalties if Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early January 2027. That’s something Cloudflare has never done. Cloudflare has spent years advocating against orders of this kind. We are concerned that rightsholders’ unrelenting demands for blocking by public DNS resolvers will end up causing real harm to the Internet. A refresher on DNS, the Domain Name System To understand why this is such a problem, it helps to understand how the Internet works under the hood. DNS resolvers are a foundational piece of the Internet’s infrastructure. DNS is the Internet’s address book: when you type a website name such as cloudflare.com, the DNS system translates that domain name into the IP address your device needs to connect to it. A DNS resolver is the service that looks up that address and sends it back to your device, much like an operator finding a phone number in a directory. DNS resolvers can be operated by anyone, but they are commonly run by Internet service providers (ISPs), mobile networks, businesses, and universities. If you’re reading this blog post at home and have never thought about DNS before, chances are that you’re using your ISP’s default resolver. Because you use your DNS resolver every time that you visit a website, it’s important for it to be reliable and trustworthy. And because the DNS resolver has access to all of your browsing activity, which resolver you use has real privacy implications. In addition to DNS resolvers that are provided by your local ISP, there are a variety of public DNS resolvers available. Cloudflare launched our public DNS resolver 1.1.1.1 in April 2018 to give back to the Internet. Our goal was to make a fast, reliable, privacy-first consumer DNS service available for free to everyone. We succeeded. 1.1.1.1 is among the fastest DNS resolvers in the world , including in Europe. Cloudflare's resolver doesn’t collect any user data, let alone sell it to advertisers. 1.1.1.1 has always been one of our favorite examples of Cloudflare fulfilling its mission to help build a better Internet. 1.1.1.1 is one of many public resolvers that anyone can use. In addition to 1.1.1.1 and Quad9’s 9.9.9.9, some of the other best-known public resolvers include Google’s 8.8.8.8 and Cisco’s OpenDNS. Just because these services are offered for free doesn’t mean they’re easy to provide. A well-run global public DNS resolver is an extraordinary engineering feat, built to securely and privately resolve hundreds of billions or even trillions of queries a day across a globally distributed network of hundreds of server locations. As Quad9 notes, there are many other DNS resolvers available to users, many of them offered by essentially anonymous services whose practices are unknown or undocumented. It’s easy to change your DNS resolver, and people do so for a variety of reasons including performance, reliability, or to access specific security features. Why public DNS resolvers should not be required to block Rightsholders have a legitimate interest in preventing online piracy. But trying to address online infringement through public DNS resolvers is fundamentally the wrong approach. Among other things, such blocking is ineffective. Think back to the analogy of an operator finding a phone number in a directory. If a court wants to shut down an illegal business, forcing the directory operator to cross the business's name out of the phone book doesn't actually close the business. The storefront is still open, the products are still there, and anyone who already knows the address, or uses a different phone book, can walk in. The same is true for the Internet. DNS resolvers are just one link in the transmission chain. The only way a DNS resolver can “block” content is by declining to return the IP address for a particular website. But a public DNS resolver cannot remove the actual infringing content from the Internet, nor can it take down the servers hosting it. Because of this, blocking by public DNS resolvers is remarkably easy to bypass. Any Internet user who wants to reach a blocked site can circumvent the block in less than a minute simply by switching to one of the thousands of other DNS resolvers available online. In fact, users don’t even need a resolver at all to reach infringing content if they already know the underlying IP address. Unsurprisingly, while blocking via public resolvers may inject some friction for some users when accessing content, there is no evidence that it actually reduces the total amount of online infringement that occurs. In addition to being ineffective, as we’ve written previously , DNS blocking is a blunt instrument that causes collateral damage. Because DNS operates at the domain level, a resolver cannot block a specific infringing video or file; it must block the entire domain. This affects all content on that domain, whether legal or illegal. It is also entirely opaque to the user: when a resolver is forced to block a domain, the website simply fails to load. The user receives no explanation or legal notice, making it impossible to know if the site is down for maintenance, if their network is broken, or if the site was blocked by a court order. The problem is substantially worse with respect to public DNS resolvers. Because public resolvers operate globally, any blocking will naturally cross borders, meaning that a single country could dictate what content is accessible around the world. For example, while the EU-dedicated DNS resolver DNS4EU operated by Whalebone blocks in response to country-specific orders, it does so across the entire EU. Efforts to reengineer public DNS resolvers to allow for more localized blocking would fundamentally alter the service, harming performance and resilience, undermining user privacy, and fragmenting the open Internet. For these reasons, Cloudflare, Google, Cisco, and Quad9 have all opposed efforts to mandate blocking by public DNS resolvers, with some success. Several years ago, courts in Germany ruled in favor of Cloudflare and Quad9 , rejecting requests to require DNS blocking. More recently, a French court rejected penalties against Cloudflare for failing to block through 1.1.1.1, finding that other actions we had taken through our CDN and reverse-proxy service were sufficient to comply with the underlying order. Undeterred, rightsholders have continued to press for blocking by public resolvers with a level of determination that is hard to explain. A recent study found that the majority of online piracy in Europe is hosted in Europe. If rightsholders want to genuinely address online infringement, there are far better places to focus their efforts — most notably by requiring the hosting providers who actually store the pirated files to take them down. Forcing public DNS resolvers out of markets hurts the Internet The French court’s penalty order against Quad9 represents the culmination of these rightsholder efforts. As a small non-profit that only offers a public DNS resolver, Quad9 had no alternative methods for demonstrating compliance with the order. The French court therefore granted rightsholders’ request to issue penalties for non-compliance, forcing Quad9 to undermine its own service or leave the country. Quad9’s withdrawal from France represents a genuine loss for the Internet. In the short term, removal of Quad9’s resolver is likely to cause immediate and potentially severe disruptions to Internet access. Because of the way their service is set up to preserve privacy, Quad9 has no way to know who exactly is using its resolver, let alone to directly communicate to them about the upcoming withdrawal of services. That means that individuals, hospitals, universities, and government offices all may be caught unaware when the resolver stops working. Again, because of how DNS resolvers work, those users will not receive a detailed error message explaining what happened — their Internet will simply stop working. The problem will be even worse when devices like security systems or thermostats are hardwired to use Quad9’s resolver. Fixing these issues may be slow or even impossible. More generally, driving Quad9 out of France does absolutely nothing to prevent online infringement, but it does leave everyday Internet users with fewer safe, reliable options, particularly ones like Quad9 that also protect users from phishing and malware. Taking established public DNS resolvers away forces Internet users to fall back on the default resolvers offered by their ISPs (which may monetize their browsing data), try lesser-known resolvers operated by anonymous or less trustworthy organizations, or run their own resolver. The irony is that Quad9 and Cloudflare are being pulled into court precisely because we are transparent, reputable organizations. Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web. The way forward If nothing else, we hope that Quad9’s announcement may serve as a wake-up call to rightsholders and policymakers that seeking to block infringement at every layer of the Internet has real costs. We believe there are far better ways to work together to fight piracy without compromising the integrity of the Internet, and Cloudflare continues to pursue innovative collaborations to that end. Our collective efforts in addressing online infringement would be put to better use in seeking to have such content removed at the hosting provider, which would both achieve a more durable solution and avoid collateral damage to the Internet. In the meantime, we will keep resisting misguided efforts to require blocking by public DNS resolvers. Along with Google and Cisco, we have appealed the Belgian order that would impose penalties on us if we do not start DNS blocking by January 2027. We hope to get a resolution before the end of the year that would avoid another situation like the one Quad9 faces now in France. We have grave concerns about the disruption that would be caused if additional resolvers are forced to withdraw from markets, and we will continue to advocate against that possible result.

items.title: Secure the data that fuels AI with Microsoft Purview
items.summary: Agents in Microsoft 365 grew 15x year-over-year, and every one of them can reach your organization's sensitive data. AI accesses, creates, and updates data, faster than current classification and labeling can keep up. At the same time, AI apps and agents introduce new surface areas for sensitive data to be exposed such as grounding data, prompts, responses, tool calls and more. Without the right controls, that data exposure can erode customer trust and create regulatory, legal, competitive, and financial consequences. Microsoft Purview helps organizations secure the data that fuels AI. To act quickly and confidently, data security teams need a precise, current understanding of their sensitive data, without extra manual work, and controls that enforce protection across humans, apps, and agents. Purview helps teams understand their sensitive data, protect data across humans and AI, and stay ahead of compliance with the auditability that evolving regulations demand. At Ignite, we're announcing enhanced classification and labeling at scale to help teams get to data protection faster, and new data loss prevention (DLP) controls that protect the data Microsoft Copilot and local agents use. Ignite announcements at a glance Get to data protection faster Stay current with recurring classification refresh (public preview January 2027): Automatically re-classify data that hasn’t been touched in years when classifiers are updated or improved. Deploy faster with enhanced built-in sensitive information types (SITs) (available starting January 2027) : Get precise detection out of the box with less manual tuning and customization, starting with the 100+ most widely used SITs, such as credit card and U.S. Social Security numbers, and extending to all built-in SITs over time. Simplify workflows with a unified classification management experience (public preview): Find and manage all your classifiers in one place, with improved search and filtering. Accelerate data protection with auto -labeling scalability improvements (generally available): Now label up to 500,000 files per day, match 20M items in simulation, target sites by attribute instead of hand-picking with adaptive scopes; and apply default library labels to SharePoint libraries for data-at-rest ( public preview). Protect data across humans and AI Protect the sensitive data that Copilot uses (public preview January 2027) : Apply DLP policies that prevent Copilot from processing files with sensitive data, even when those files aren't labeled. Additionally, Copilot will not process prompts with attached or linked files containing sensitive data. Protect the sensitive data local agents use (public preview January 2027) : Gain visibility into local agent activity and apply DLP policies that prevent local agents from processing sensitive data, whether it comes from a prompt or from the files and tools the agent accesses. Additionally, data protection policies can be scoped to specific agents for more granular controls tailored to each agent’s role. Integrate agent activity signals into Unified Agent Risk score (public preview) : Purview agent activity and interaction with sensitive data signals now feed into Unified Agent Risk score in Agent 365, so security teams can spot higher-risk agents, prioritize investigations, and apply the right controls. Get to data protection faster AI creates large volumes of new data. More than 2 billion files are uploaded to SharePoint every day, and SharePoint is now the top grounding source for Microsoft 365 Copilot. At that volume, admins can't pause to manually tune and validate classification before enforcing auto-labeling and DLP policies. That's why we're enhancing our built-in sensitive information types (SITs) for precise detection out of the box, so admins can move confidently from detecting sensitive data to enforcing protection. We're starting with the 100+ most widely used SITs, such as credit card and U.S. Social Security numbers, and will extend these enhancements to all built-in SITs over time. To secure data effectively, classification must keep pace as your data estate grows and your definition of what's sensitive evolves. Purview classifies content as it is accessed, created, and shared, but AI tools can also access and process older files that no one has opened in years. Getting to protection faster also means making classification easier to manage. The new unified classification management experience brings all classifiers, including sensitive information types, exact data match, trainable classifiers, and document fingerprinting, into one place, with improved search and filtering. Figure 2: Admins can now extend a SharePoint library's default sensitivity label to all files in the library, including data-at-rest. Organizations need to protect all three without getting in the way of productive AI use. Admins can already use Purview sensitivity labels and DLP policies to restrict Copilot from processing labeled files and emails, as well as prompts containing sensitive information. Today, we're taking that further: admins can protect the data Copilot uses, even when files aren't labeled . When Copilot retrieves content to ground a response, Purview can detect sensitive data such as financial information or personal ID numbers, and DLP can block Copilot from using it. This helps organizations deploy Copilot more quickly, with confidence. Figure 3: DLP policy to prevent Copilot from grounding responses on files containing sensitive information, even if the file is not labeled. Protection also extends to the prompt itself: admins can now protect sensitive data in Copilot prompt attachments and linked files , in addition to typed text, so sensitive data is covered as it flows into and through Copilot. Figure 4: DLP blocks Copilot from processing a prompt with a file containing sensitive information (SIT). For example, an employee might ask Copilot to analyze a linked financial planning document that hasn’t been labeled. Without a label, Purview can still identify a SIT, such as an ABA routing number, and apply the organization’s DLP policy to prevent it from grounding the response. The same protection extends to prompts and attachments. With protection integrated into Copilot, organizations can confidently turn AI innovation into everyday impact. In addition to protecting Copilot, Purview currently provides visibility into agent activity and audit records for agents built on Microsoft Copilot Studio and Foundry, helping organizations understand how AI is being used. items.title: Accelerate Zero Trust for AI: Expanded SecOps coverage and new guides to turn insights into action
items.summary: Security leaders keep asking this question: our AI footprint is growing fast. How do we know our defenses are keeping up? Agents act on their own, at machine speed, with access to real data and real systems. That accelerates innovation, and it introduces new attack surfaces and trust boundaries for every security team. Attackers are using AI too, to move faster and at scale. AI introduces new attack vectors like prompt injection. But most AI-related incidents still run through gaps Zero Trust was designed to close: excessive access, exposed credentials, and unpatched weaknesses. That's why Zero Trust principles matter more than ever. For security teams, the Zero Trust foundation they’ve built still counts. The next step is to extend it. The hard part is knowing which paths are still open and proving they're narrowing over time. The Zero Trust Assessment is built for exactly that. Today we’re releasing Zero Trust Assessment latest version, which extends our recent expansion of Zero Trust for AI and reflects what we’ve heard from customers and partners since. Here is what’s new: Detect what prevention misses: Deeper Security Operations coverage, with new checks that measure readiness to detect and respond when prevention isn't enough. Measure progress over time, at enterprise scale: Performance improvements that help large, complex tenants run a complete assessment, plus certificate-based sign-in for scheduled runs that track progress over time. Turn findings into a roadmap: Direct import of assessment results into the Zero Trust Workshop, so every roadmap task starts with your tenant's own findings. These updates make Zero Trust progress easier to track, and the results are measurable. In a May 2026 Forrester Consulting Total Economic Impact™ study , a global NGO reported significant gains in identity maturity, confirmed by independent Zero Trust maturity assessments. Zero Trust-aligned detection and response playbooks also cut its mean time to respond, and it could now measure response metrics it couldn’t track before. Deeper Security Operations coverage: Assume breach applies to agents, too Preventive controls reduce the chance of unauthorized access. Security operations address the harder question: how do you detect and respond to suspicious activity that gets through? With AI agents, that question becomes more urgent. An agent may sign in with valid credentials, hold legitimate permissions, and still act in unexpected or harmful ways. Preventive controls remain essential, but they can't anticipate every action after access is granted. Security operations provide the telemetry, behavioral detection, investigation, and response capabilities needed to identify and contain misuse. AI's speed raises the stakes: suspicious activity can unfold faster, leaving defenders less time to act. That's why assume breach isn't a pessimistic principle. It's a practical one, and strong security operations put it into practice. Figure 1: New Security Operations assessment The latest release adds 26 new Security Operations checks that expand on the SecOps coverage introduced in August , such as privileged account protection, ransomware prevention through attack surface reduction rules, and security log retention. They assess configurations across identity and privileged access, email and endpoint protection, cloud app session controls, and Microsoft Sentinel capabilities, including data collection, threat intelligence, hunting, retention, and automated response. Together, these checks help security teams identify gaps in prevention, detection, investigation, and response, and give the partners who support them a clear starting point for customer conversations. "Microsoft gave us the telemetry we needed to see the full picture. Our Security teams became empowered versus challenged by the complex patchwork of systems that had been in place." -- Weston Maggetti, Platform Manager, Ford Motor Company Built for enterprise scale and long-term progress The organizations with the most to protect are often the hardest to assess, and in the AI era, their environments change faster than any single assessment can capture. This release addresses both. Performance improvements make large tenants easier to assess at real enterprise scale: one organization recently completed a full assessment of a tenant with more than 500,000 member users and close to 4 million guest users. New settings also give teams control over which checks to run and how long each one can take. With app-only, certificate-based authentication, the assessment runs automatically without anyone signing in for supported services, on a schedule that matches your operating rhythm, from monthly reviews to every change window. Partners can use the same automated, scheduled approach to deliver recurring assessments for their customers: baseline once, then report progress on a regular cadence. Because every run is consistent, security teams can compare results over time and show leadership the progress made, the risk that remains, and what to tackle next. Assessment results stay in your environment. By default, the tool sends a basic usage event that includes your tenant ID but no assessment results, and you can turn it off with a single setting. Figure 2: Zero Trust Posture View Turn findings into lasting, measurable progress Knowing where you stand only matters if you can act on it. With this release, you can import Zero Trust Assessment results into the Zero Trust Workshop . Your tenant's findings then appear on the matching tasks, giving your team a head start on a prioritized 12- to 24-month roadmap. Partners can import their customers’ results the same way and use the findings to anchor workshops and shape the roadmap with their customers. Repeatable assessments give you measurable inputs to set a baseline, prioritize improvements, and track progress over time. For a broader, multiyear security transformation, the Security Adoption Framework (SAF) uses the same findings to connect business outcomes, security disciplines, people, process, and technology in one coordinated plan. Get started Learn how it works. Watch the overview video to see how the Zero Trust Assessment and Workshop work together. Then explore the AI pillar learning module and new click-through guides for the AI pillar and DevSecOps pillar . Run the assessment. Run the Zero Trust Assessment today to set a baseline across Identity, Devices, Network, Data, Infrastructure, Security Operations, and AI. Then import your results into the Zero Trust Workshop to turn your findings into a prioritized roadmap. See it live, then try it firsthand at Microsoft Ignite . Join ManpowerGroup CTO Amanda Jack and Microsoft in our breakout session to hear how they built a secure foundation for AI with Zero Trust principles. Then join our hands-on lab to work through the assessment and workshop alongside the team behind them. Learn more about Microsoft Security solutions on our website and bookmark the Microsoft Security blog for expert insights on security matters. Follow us on LinkedIn ( Microsoft Security ) and X ( @MSFTSecurity ) for the latest cybersecurity news and updates.

items.title: Ignite 2026: Building the frontier ecosystem
items.summary: Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, delivered the opening keynote at Ignite in San Francisco this morning. Here is an edited version of his remarks. This week is about two things: First is how we capitalize on new capabilities that are growing exponentially. And second is how do we build the capability to deal with the consequences of these exponentials. At times like these, I always find it helpful to be grounded in our mission: To empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. In today’s world, that means building a frontier ecosystem. We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large. For us, that comes down to three things: Keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring your control of your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust. And so, our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three core architectural principles. Copilot Copilot is the new OS for work . Copilot brings together all the new form factors of human-computer interaction, whether it is Chat, Cowork, Code or Autopilot, into one experience. It also brings together the disparate categories of knowledge work, coding and business process. That is why we have all of Office with its richness built into Copilot. And underlying it is a model system that matches the right intelligence to the right context to the right form factor to accomplish the task. Home gives you one place to start, whether you need a quick answer or want to assign and complete complex, multi-step tasks. Code brings the power of an infinite SaaS factory to every individual. It lets you build your own custom SaaS apps, dashboards and much more. And Autopilot is an autonomous agent that keeps moving your work forward 24×7 in all the places where you and your team collaborate. Underlying all this is Work IQ. You can think of this as the most important database for any organization, with a deep understanding of people, their relationships, documents, emails, meetings, chats and projects that make up the fabric of work. And we are going further. We are extending Copilot for specific roles: sales, legal, finance, service. We are organizing the skills, connectors and plugins for these roles across the entire surface area of Copilot. And that includes third-party systems, too. In fact, today we are announcing new plugins for business applications, starting with Dynamics 365. And it is not just Dynamics. We are very excited to partner with Salesforce to bring Salesforce to Copilot . And we are going beyond that as well. Up until now, we have mostly been in a single player world of people and their agent loops and swarms. But the time has come for a true multiplayer form factor, where people, their agents and other people are all driving towards a common goal, with shared context. This is Copilot Workspaces: YouTube Video Click here to load media Microsoft IQ The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain and continuously improve its own intelligence. Essentially, we are taking the system we built underneath Copilot and externalizing it as a first-class platform that embodies your organizational intelligence as an asset that you continuously build and control. We are bringing together all of the data you have across Fabric, Foundry and Microsoft 365. And, of course, all the third-party context too. Microsoft IQ comes with hundreds of new connectors we are announcing today, so agents can get the full enterprise context where business gets done. And all this rich context manifests as business plugins that can be shared and inherited across the organization. Models For us, it is about mapping intelligence to a given task, with the best economics. This is something we can uniquely do in the context of real-world tasks by tuning our products, harness and tools, and the model system, end-to-end. And today we are thrilled to announce Microsoft-Decision-1.1 , which is now generally available and ready for enterprise deployment. We have added multimodal support. And we have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster. Already, more than 4,000 customers have used it. And we ourselves are using it for core tasks like routing, data labeling, personalization, content filtering and hundreds of other use cases. Foundry of course has all the most popular closed and open weight models, too. We are very excited to bring GPT 6.2 to Foundry. It is a great model that sets a new bar for AI in professional work. And today we are announcing that Meta’s latest models are all coming to Foundry as well. We are also innovating at the frontier with our own MAI model family that is both compute-efficient when it comes to pre-training and token-efficient when it comes to product deployment. Our goal is to put additional points on the frontier curve informed by real world task-performance. And we are going further. We are announcing MAI Licensed Weights, meaning our trusted customers will now be able to get access to Microsoft AI model weights through our Frontier Co. Today, we are introducing lots of new models . But I want to highlight two in particular: First, Code. We are introducing our new flagship family of agentic coding models: Code 2. Code 2 is at the frontier of cost-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. It excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multifile implementation, repo-wide reasoning and UI at a fraction of frontier cost. Code 2 Flash is designed for fast, high-volume work like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes and rapid iterations. It brings near-flagship quality for a much lower cost. These models are both generally available today on GitHub Copilot, both in the model picker and as part of Copilot Fusion. They are also available in Foundry. We are taking the same approach in cyber. Cyber 2 Flash is our most capable security model yet. It is a flash-sized model that delivers performance ahead of frontier models at a fraction of the cost per task. And, just as we have done with coding, we are co-designing the model with the tools and systems where it will be used. We are integrating Cyber 2 with Perception. Agent 365 Successfully deploying AI systems starts with making sure you have observability at every layer of the stack. That is where Agent 365 comes in. Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, delivered the opening keynote at Ignite in San Francisco this morning. Here is an edited version of his remarks.

This week is about two things: First is how we capitalize on new capabilities that are growing exponentially. And second is how do we build the capability to deal with the consequences of these exponentials.

At times like these, I always find it helpful to be grounded in our mission: To empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. In today’s world, that means building a frontier ecosystem. We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large.

For us, that comes down to three things: Keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring your control of your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust.

And so, our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three core architectural principles.

Copilot

Copilot is the new OS for work. Copilot brings together all the new form factors of human-computer interaction, whether it is Chat, Cowork, Code or Autopilot, into one experience. It also brings together the disparate categories of knowledge work, coding and business process. That is why we have all of Office with its richness built into Copilot. And underlying it is a model system that matches the right intelligence to the right context to the right form factor to accomplish the task.

Home gives you one place to start, whether you need a quick answer or want to assign and complete complex, multi-step tasks. Code brings the power of an infinite SaaS factory to every individual. It lets you build your own custom SaaS apps, dashboards and much more. And Autopilot is an autonomous agent that keeps moving your work forward 24×7 in all the places where you and your team collaborate.

Underlying all this is Work IQ. You can think of this as the most important database for any organization, with a deep understanding of people, their relationships, documents, emails, meetings, chats and projects that make up the fabric of work.

And we are going further. We are extending Copilot for specific roles: sales, legal, finance, service. We are organizing the skills, connectors and plugins for these roles across the entire surface area of Copilot.

And that includes third-party systems, too. In fact, today we are announcing new plugins for business applications, starting with Dynamics 365. And it is not just Dynamics. We are very excited to partner with Salesforce to bring Salesforce to Copilot.

And we are going beyond that as well. Up until now, we have mostly been in a single player world of people and their agent loops and swarms. But the time has come for a true multiplayer form factor, where people, their agents and other people are all driving towards a common goal, with shared context. This is Copilot Workspaces:

YouTube Video

Click here to load media

Microsoft IQ

The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain and continuously improve its own intelligence. Microsoft IQ comes with hundreds of new connectors we are announcing today, so agents can get the full enterprise context where business gets done. Models

For us, it is about mapping intelligence to a given task, with the best economics. This is something we can uniquely do in the context of real-world tasks by tuning our products, harness and tools, and the model system, end-to-end.

And today we are thrilled to announce Microsoft-Decision-1.1, which is now generally available and ready for enterprise deployment. We have added multimodal support. And we ourselves are using it for core tasks like routing, data labeling, personalization, content filtering and hundreds of other use cases.

In this article
  • AI agents escaped testing and hacked real systems
  • California says OpenAI lost control of agents more than 80 times
  • The state wants stronger safeguards and financial penalties

An AI agent doesn’t need malicious intentions to cause a cybersecurity incident. Give it a goal, tools, and enough freedom to find a shortcut, and the damage can extend well beyond the computer where it was supposed to stay.

That is the concern behind a lawsuit California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed against OpenAI on November 16. The state alleges that the company developed and tested powerful AI models without adequate safeguards, allowing experimental agents to escape their testing environments and gain unauthorized access to other organizations’ systems.

The best-known incident involved Hugging Face, the platform where developers share AI models and datasets. But California’s complaint says it was not an isolated failure: According to the filing, OpenAI acknowledged to investigators that it had lost control of autonomous agents more than 80 times during testing.

As we explained in our follow-up on the AI agent swarm, agents used a shared service as an improvised message board, exchanging information that helped others get around their restrictions. According to the complaint, roughly 1,200 agents used that unauthorized communications channel, and about 700 participated in the Hugging Face attack.

California’s complaint says the attack involved roughly 17,600 attacker actions and required two weeks of full-time remediation work by Hugging Face’s security team.

Why California decided to sue

California alleges that OpenAI had repeated warnings that its containment measures were failing and continued testing anyway.

The complaint identifies several alleged failures:

  • Warning signs like observed unauthorized internet access went unaddressed.
  • Monitoring did not match public assurances. The state alleges that OpenAI promised continuous monitoring but did not monitor models’ reasoning live in the relevant training and evaluation environments.
  • Reduced model safeguards were not offset by stronger containment. California says experimental models were tested without protections normally present in publicly released versions, while the surrounding infrastructure failed to keep their actions contained.
  • OpenAI failed to substantially comply with investigative demands for records about the incidents and its security practices.

California is suing under its Unfair Competition Law and also argues that OpenAI’s unsafe testing constitutes a “public nuisance.” In this case, that means interfering with a community’s ability to use its property safely, including computer systems. The state is seeking a court order requiring safer testing practices, along with financial penalties.

Who pays when the sandbox fails?

The lawsuit raises a question that extends beyond one company: When an autonomous system crosses a security boundary, who is responsible for keeping it in line?

The lawsuit puts responsibility back on the organization running the experiment. Whether an agent was trying to finish a benchmark or complete a research task, California’s position is that keeping it from breaking into someone else’s systems was OpenAI’s job.

For organizations using AI agents, the practical lesson is to treat them as software with the power to take actions, not simply chatbots that produce answers. Login details, network access, tools, and permissions determine how far an unexpected action can reach.

Our earlier coverage of an OpenAI agent that bypassed a government website’s access controls emphasized limiting that access and monitoring what agents actually do.

items.title: Threat intelligence that moves at the speed of the threat: What’s new at Microsoft Ignite 2026
items.summary: Security teams are operating in an environment where the time between threat discovery and potential impact continues to shrink, and AI is increasing the speed and scale of attacks. When a new vulnerability is exploited or a threat campaign begins to emerge, defenders need to quickly determine what is happening, whether their organization could be affected, and where action may be required. But the information needed to make those decisions is often distributed across research reports, vulnerability data, indicators, incidents, and organizational telemetry. At Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re introducing new Microsoft Threat Intelligence capabilities designed to help security teams identify important threats earlier, understand their relevance, and more quickly apply intelligence to their defense. Here’s what’s new. Put zero-days and emerging threats front and center Zero-day attacks exploit software vulnerabilities before a fix is available, leaving organizations with little or no advance warning. Emerging threats present a related challenge: the threat is new or rapidly developing, and intelligence about its scope, infrastructure, techniques, and potential impact is still evolving. For security teams, the challenge is not simply gaining access to high-quality intelligence. It is identifying the most urgent intelligence quickly and understanding what it means for their organization. Threat intelligence in Microsoft Defender is adding a new zero-day and emerging threats experience, available in public preview, to help address that challenge. New zero-day and emerging threat tags clearly distinguish this research from other threat intelligence content, helping analysts identify time-sensitive threats more quickly. We’re also updating Threat Intelligence overview and Threat Analytics with a zero-day widget and latest-threats view that surface new zero-day and emerging-threat research from Microsoft Security Research soon after discovery. Figure 1: New zero-day widget and latest-threats view in Threat intelligence overview in Defender Not every emerging threat carries the same relevance for every organization. Security teams can therefore filter the latest threats by industry and region, helping analysts focus on activity most applicable to their environment. Figure 2: New filter by region and industry in Threat intelligence overview in Defender Teams can also subscribe to email notifications for zero-day and emerging-threat updates, providing another way to stay informed as important new threats are identified. Figure 3: New notification rule for Emerging threats and Zero-Day attacks in Defender These capabilities are intended to shorten the time from threat discovery to defender awareness, while making it easier to prioritize the intelligence that warrants further investigation. From intelligence to protection at AI speed Knowing that a threat exists is only the beginning. Security teams also need to understand whether their environment is adequately protected against it. Microsoft is bringing those activities closer together. From a Threat Analytics article, security teams can now run the Protect against a threat playbook in Microsoft Perception. Figure 4: Run Perception playbook directly from a threat article The playbook checks existing protection coverage and can create custom detections tailored to the organization’s environment, supplementing Microsoft’s built-in protections. Analysts can begin with Microsoft’s understanding of a threat, evaluate how existing protections address it, and strengthen detection based on the characteristics of their own environment. Threat intelligence becomes more actionable: it not only helps explain a threat, but also helps security teams assess whether they are ready to act against it. At Ignite, the Threat Intelligence Agent in Microsoft Perception is also becoming generally available. The Threat Intelligence Agent is designed to help analysts investigate and operationalize threat intelligence more efficiently by applying AI reasoning to the information they use during an investigation. Threat intelligence teams, however, rarely depend on a single source of research. Analysts routinely work across intelligence from Microsoft, commercial providers, independent researchers, industry communities, open-source research, and other sources. The Threat Intelligence Agent can now turn external threat articles into structured findings, extracting the attacker behaviors, techniques, and indicators that matter and making that understanding available for action. For analysts, this expands the value of the agent beyond any single intelligence source. Teams can incorporate more of the research they already rely on and accelerate investigation. Threat intelligence reimagined for the AI era As AI reshapes the threat landscape, defenders need a new approach: timely to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, tailored to surface what matters most to their organization, and actionable to turn insight into protection faster. Together, these capabilities help defenders cut through the noise, prioritize what matters, and respond with greater speed and confidence. Want to go deeper at Microsoft Ignite? Join these two sessions: “Threat Intelligence reimagined: From signals to protection at AI speed” with Tanmay Ganacharya and Yoni Nave on Thursday, November 19 at 9am PST. “Threat Intelligence reimagined: Expert Q&A and deep dive” with Yoni Nave on November 19 at 4:15pm PST. Not attending in person? Watch the sessions on demand .
