items.title: Preparing for a Post-Quantum Future with TLS in Windows
items.summary: The post-qu a ntum cryptography (PQC) transition has already begun . A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could eventually compromise the public-key cryptography widely used to secure data and communications today . But organizations do not need to wait for that future to arrive before the risk becomes relevant. Encrypted traffic can be collected now and potentially decrypted later, while replacing cryptography across applications, infrastructure, and identity will take years. Windows is helping organizations take a practical first step. Earlier this year, we introduced post-quantum hybrid key exchange in the Windows Transport Layer Security (TLS) stack. With the October 2026 security update, Windows expands that foundation with pure post-quantum key exchange and authentication . Support in Windows 11 24H2 and later, as well as Windows Server 2025 helps organizations begin addressing risks to long-lived data while preparing certificate infrastructure and applications for a broader post-quantum transition. The two parts of the TLS transition TLS is foundational to secure communications across websites, applications, and services. Its public-key cryptography serves two critical functions: key exchange, which helps protect the confidentiality of a connection, and authentication, which helps establish trust in the peer you're communicating with. Both need to evolve for a post-quantum future, but the transition is different for each. Start by protecting t oday's d ata from f uture d ecryption Key exchange is where the risk is more immediate. A threat actor doesn't need a quantum computer today to create a future problem. The collection of encrypted traffic today for potential decryption in the future is known as a harvest-now, decrypt-later (HNDL) attack. items.summary_html:
The post-quantum cryptography (PQC) transition has already begun. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could eventually compromise the public-key cryptography widely used to secure data and communications today. But organizations do not need to wait for that future to arrive before the risk becomes relevant. Encrypted traffic can be collected now and potentially decrypted later, while replacing cryptography across applications, infrastructure, and identity will take years.  

Windows is helping organizations take a practical first step. Earlier this year, we introduced post-quantum hybrid key exchange in the Windows Transport Layer Security (TLS) stack. With the October 2026 security update, Windows expands that foundation with pure post-quantum key exchange and authentication. Support in Windows 11 24H2 and later, as well as Windows Server 2025 helps organizations begin addressing risks to long-lived data while preparing certificate infrastructure and applications for a broader post-quantum transition.  

The two parts of the TLS transition  

TLS is foundational to secure communications across websites, applications, and services. Its public-key cryptography serves two critical functions: key exchange, which helps protect the confidentiality of a connection, and authentication, which helps establish trust in the peer you're communicating with. Both need to evolve for a post-quantum future, but the transition is different for each. 

Start by protecting today's data from future decryption 

Key exchange is where the risk is more immediate. A threat actor doesn't need a quantum computer today to create a future problem. The collection of encrypted traffic today for potential decryption in the future is known as a harvest-now, decrypt-later (HNDL) attack. That makes post-quantum key exchange an important place to start for sensitive data that needs to remain confidential well into the future. 

Prepare the certificate ecosystem for post-quantum authentication 

Authentication requires a broader ecosystem transition. Certificates and digital signatures help establish that you're connecting to the peer you intended to reach. Today, that trust commonly depends on quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms that will also need to transition over time. 

For authentication, the challenge is preparing the certificate and Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) ecosystem before post-quantum authentication is needed at scale. Organizations need to map certificate dependencies, modernize PKI and certificate lifecycle processes, and determine where post-quantum authentication fits in their environments. 

Different authentication scenarios may ultimately require different approaches. X.509 certificates using ML-DSA provide a path for organizations to begin evaluating post-quantum authentication in enterprise PKI and service-to-service environments. For the Web PKI, larger post-quantum signatures can create performance challenges at scale. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is developing Merkle Tree Certificates (MTC) as a new certificate construction intended to reduce this overhead while preserving security properties comparable to today's X.509 and Certificate Transparency model. Microsoft is exploring MTC support in Windows alongside X.509-based PQC capabilities as we prepare Windows for the evolving post-quantum authentication ecosystem. 

Together, post-quantum key exchange using ML-KEM and authentication using ML-DSA certificates allow organizations to begin the transition of both key exchange and authentication in Windows. 

Start your post-quantum TLS transition  Begin with hybrid post-quantum key exchange 

We recommend starting with hybrid post-quantum key exchange, which combines classical and post-quantum cryptography. Where specific requirements call for pure PQC, organizations can also use pure ML-KEM key exchange. 

Assess your authentication readiness 

In parallel, assess readiness for post-quantum TLS authentication across the certificate ecosystem. Applications, PKI infrastructure, and systems that issue, validate, or depend on certificates may also need to adapt. 

To get started, see these Microsoft Learn resources

  • TLS supported groups and post-quantum key exchange in Windows 
  • Post-Quantum Cryptography in Active Directory Certificate Services 
  • Post-quantum authentication: Why organizations should start testing certificate ecosystems now 
TLS is one step in a broader Windows transition 

Post-quantum TLS is an important milestone, and it’s where most organizations will start.  But TLS is one piece of a larger transition. The same cryptography protects data, identities, and device trust across Windows, and we're working on all of it together. 

That work starts with a crypto-agile foundation. We're adding additional post-quantum algorithms to Cryptography Next Generation (CNG) as global standards evolve and pairing them with hybrid and composite approaches designed to make it easier to adapt as algorithms evolve. And because not every application relies on TLS, Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) extends that protection to applications beyond it. 

On top of that foundation, we're working with standards bodies, silicon providers, and partners to bring Wi-Fi, and IPsec to post-quantum, with Wi-Fi already underway. We're also evolving identity and PKI end to end, across Active Directory Certificate Services (ADCS), Windows Hello, Kerberos, and smart cards. ADCS already supports ML-DSA and will add composite PQ certificates, so classical and post-quantum trust can run side by side during the transition. 

The same shift reaches the chain of trust beneath Windows. Signing for software, Windows Update, and servicing is moving toward post-quantum signatures, with firmware and Secure Boot advancing alongside UEFI, silicon, and OEM partners. Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) already supports TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange on supported configurations, and work continues across data protection, TPM, Pluton, measurement, and attestation.

Looking ahead 

The post-quantum transition will take time. The important step is to begin. Start by identifying data that must remain confidential over the long term, deploy hybrid post-quantum TLS key exchange, and map the applications and certificate infrastructure that will need to evolve. 

TLS is an important step, but it’s only the beginning. Windows is building a crypto-agile foundation across the platform and working with the industry to help organizations adopt post-quantum protection as standards and ecosystems mature. 

Learn More 

To learn more about Post-quantum readiness and Windows security at Ignite, check out these resources: 

  • Read about other Windows security announcements at Ignite 2026 at the Windows Experience blog 
  • Check out the new Windows Security Guide to better understand how we are thinking about security across the platform 

For more on post-quantum cryptography, visit our other resources:  

  • Post-quantum authentication: Why organizations should start testing certificate ecosystems now  
  • Preparing the Windows ecosystem for next-generation code signing  
  • Windows, TLS 1.3 and Post Quantum Crypto FAQ

items.title: Artifact Signing with Signing Transparency: Private Preview
items.summary: In October, we shared how AMD and Microsoft are exploring independently verifiable hardware provenance through Artifact Signing with Signing Transparency. Now, we’re taking the next step with a controlled private preview, inviting a select group of customers to evaluate Signing Transparency in Artifact Signing against their own supported workflows. The preview brings Microsoft's Signing Transparency (MST) into the Artifact Signing experience in Azure portal, with availability in limited regions. It gives selected customers an opportunity to evaluate supported signing and verification workflows with our team and help shape the experience. The opportunity extends beyond semiconductor provenance to software, firmware, and other supply chain evidence. Have a signing or verification challenge to explore? Express interest in the private preview . Why signing transparency matters Digital signatures are foundational to software and supply chain security. They help establish who signed an artifact and whether the signed content has changed. Artifact Signing makes this practical at scale by simplifying how signatures are produced with validated identities for signing artifacts. But increasingly, enterprises also need durable evidence about the decisions, processes, and assurances associated with that artifact, evidence that can be independently verified across organizational and trust boundaries. Microsoft's Signing Transparency extends signing with a standards-based transparency layer for that evidence. It creates tamper-evident, cryptographically verifiable records of signed statements, allowing customers, partners, and auditors to independently verify that evidence was registered and has not been altered. This provides a stronger foundation for security, compliance, release, and supply chain decisions without requiring every relying party to depend solely on assertions from the organization that produced the evidence. Importantly, Signing Transparency is an implementation of the I ETF Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust (SCITT) architecture. SCITT defines a standards-based approach for registering and verifying signed statements about supply chain artifacts and processes. By implementing this architecture, Signing Transparency provides a foundation for interoperable evidence that can be independently verified across enterprise and ecosystem boundaries. For enterprises, this can strengthen governance and provide more verifiable inputs into trust decisions. For software publishers, hardware manufacturers, security providers, and other ecosystem participants, it creates a common standards-based model for producing and consuming evidence that can travel with an artifact across its lifecycle. Signing Transparency in action: strengthening semiconductor supply chain trust AMD, an early design partner, helped us explore semiconductor provenance as a demanding test case: are manufacturing records authentic, and do they belong to the processor being evaluated? The proof of concept brought together AMD Device Provenance , Artifact Signing, and Signing Transparency to explore how manufacturer-issued evidence could be signed, recorded, and independently validated. That work illustrates the value of connecting evidence creation with independent verification across organizational boundaries. The same need is relevant to software publishers, firmware suppliers, and teams assessing third-party artifacts. The AMD demonstration remains a proof of concept, not a product commitment or a statement of private preview scope. “AMD Device Provenance is standards-aligned and designed to help customers independently verify the provenance of AMD hardware. Our collaboration with Microsoft shows how manufacturing evidence can connect with signing and transparency services to strengthen trust across the semiconductor supply chain.” – Ravi Kuppuswamy, SVP, Compute & Enterprise AI, AMD.

How the private preview works 

 

Figure 1. Enabling Signing Transparency in the Azure portal. Manage Signing Transparency for individual Private Trust certificate profiles and access the associated ledger from your Artifact Signing account.

Have a signing or verification challenge you would like to explore? Tell us about your scenario through the private preview interest form: Express interest in the Artifact Signing with Signing Transparency private preview. items.title: Microsoft Purview: Data Loss Prevention (DLP) vs. Insider Risk Management (IRM)
items.summary: Navigating the Microsoft Purview compliance suite often leads to a common question: what sets Data Loss Prevention (DLP) apart from Insider Risk Management (IRM)? Although these two solutions frequently overlap in organizational security strategies, they address entirely different challenges. In this article, we will explore the core distinctions between them, highlighting how DLP safeguards your sensitive data, while IRM detects and manages risky user behavior before it leads to an incident. The fundamental difference is that DLP focuses on protecting sensitive data, while Insider Risk Management focuses on identifying and managing risky user behavior. Both are Microsoft Purview security and compliance capabilities, but they address different dimensions of data security. Data Loss Prevention (DLP): Determines whether sensitive information is being shared, transferred, or used in ways that violate organizational policies and can automatically prevent those actions. Insider Risk Management (IRM): Analyzes patterns of user activity and contextual signals to identify potential insider threats, including accidental data exposure, intellectual property theft, and other security violations. Side-by-side comparison Capability Purview DLP Purview Insider Risk Management Primary objective Prevent unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data Detect, investigate, and mitigate insider risks Primary focus Data and how it is handled User activities, behavioral patterns, and risk context Key question Is sensitive information leaving the organization or being shared inappropriately? Is a user exhibiting potentially risky behavior? Detection approach Content inspection, sensitivity labels, sensitive information types, and policy conditions Correlation of user activities, risk indicators, and contextual signals Typical triggers Sensitive data emailed externally, copied to USB, uploaded to unauthorized destinations Unusual downloads, repeated data exfiltration activities, or risky actions associated with departing employees Prevention capabilities Directly blocks, restricts, audits, or warns about policy violations Primarily detects and investigates; can initiate mitigation and integrate with DLP for preventive controls Risk analysis Evaluates data and activities against configured policies Correlates activities and indicators to identify potential insider risk Investigation DLP alerts, activity details, and incident reports Risk alerts, user activity timelines, investigation cases, and escalation workflows User awareness Policy tips, warnings, and notifications Primarily analyst-facing; privacy-preserving investigation workflows Privacy controls Role-based access and compliance controls Pseudonymization by default, role-based access, and auditing Typical stakeholders Security, compliance, and data protection teams Insider risk, security investigations, compliance, and authorized HR/legal stakeholders Practical example: An employee downloading confidential customer information Consider a financial services organization where an employee downloads confidential customer records and attempts to transfer them to a personal cloud storage account. Scenario A: Using Purview DLP The organization has configured DLP policies to protect customer information. What happens? An employee accesses an Excel file containing customer financial information. The employee attempts to upload the file to an unauthorized cloud storage service. DLP evaluates the content and activity against the configured policies. If the file contains protected information and the policy conditions match, DLP can block the upload. A policy notification or alert may be generated. Outcome: Sensitive customer information is prevented from leaving through the restricted channel. Important: DLP does not need to determine whether the employee has malicious intentions. It enforces the configured data protection policy. Scenario B: Using Purview Insider Risk Management Now consider the same employee, but with additional activities: Downloads unusually large amounts of confidential information. Copies files from multiple sensitive SharePoint locations. Attempts to transfer information to personal storage. Repeatedly performs activities associated with potential data exfiltration. What happens? IRM collects relevant activity signals from supported sources. It correlates those signals using configured insider risk policies. It identifies potentially risky patterns across activities. It generates risk alerts when the configured detection criteria are met. Authorized investigators can review the activity context, investigate, and determine appropriate next steps. Outcome: The organization can investigate whether the employee's behavior represents a potential insider threat. Important: IRM identifies potential risk, not proven malicious intent. An alert is not evidence that an employee has committed wrongdoing. IRM supports risk investigation and escalation workflows, including integration with Microsoft Purview eDiscovery. The biggest architectural difference: Data-centric vs. user-centric security This is probably the most important distinction when explaining these capabilities to enterprise customers. Purview DLP: Data-centric protection DLP essentially evaluates: Data sensitivity + Activity + Destination + Policy = Enforcement decision For example: Is the document classified as confidential? Does it contain credit card numbers? Is it being shared externally? Is the destination permitted? Should the activity be allowed, audited, or blocked? DLP focuses on whether a particular action involving data violates a protection policy. Purview IRM: User-centric risk detection IRM evaluates: User activities + Risk indicators + Context + Correlation = Potential insider risk For example: Is the user performing multiple potentially risky activities? Are there unusual patterns of sensitive data access or transfer? Are activities associated with a configured risk scenario? Does the combination of signals warrant investigation? IRM provides broader context around potential insider risk rather than evaluating only an individual data-sharing transaction. Can DLP and Insider Risk Management work together? Absolutely. In fact, Microsoft provides an integration called Adaptive Protection that combines their strengths. Adaptive Protection uses Insider Risk Management signals to dynamically adjust DLP enforcement based on the risk level associated with a user. This is particularly valuable because traditional DLP policies can apply consistent restrictions, while Adaptive Protection enables more context-aware enforcement. Example: Adaptive Protection Imagine an organization with three insider risk levels. User risk level IRM assessment Example DLP enforcement Minor Limited indicators of potential risk Monitor activity and generate alerts Moderate More significant indicators of potential risk Increase monitoring and notify users Elevated Significant indicators warranting stronger controls Block specified external sharing activities These are illustrative policy choices, not mandatory Microsoft defaults. How it works: IRM evaluates relevant user activity and assigns a risk level. Adaptive Protection makes that risk level available to supported enforcement policies. DLP evaluates the risk level alongside its other policy conditions. DLP applies the configured controls. As the risk level changes, applicable enforcement can change dynamically. For example, an employee at an elevated insider risk level could be prevented from sharing certain content externally, while users at lower risk levels continue working with fewer restrictions. This is where the two solutions become particularly powerful together. Does Insider Risk Management replace DLP? No. They are complementary, not competing solutions. Consider these customer requirements: Customer requirement Recommended capability Prevent employees from emailing credit card numbers externally DLP Block confidential files from being copied to USB drives DLP Prevent sensitive information from being uploaded to unauthorized cloud applications DLP Identify potential intellectual property theft IRM Investigate suspicious patterns of employee data access and transfer IRM Identify potential data exfiltration associated with departing employees IRM Apply stricter DLP restrictions to users exhibiting elevated insider risk IRM + DLP with Adaptive Protection Protect sensitive data while investigating suspicious user activity DLP + IRM One important nuance: DLP can detect and report risky activities, and IRM can contribute to mitigation. The distinction is their primary purpose and operating model , not an absolute separation between detection and prevention. Which capability should customers implement first? For customers beginning their Microsoft Purview data security journey, I would generally recommend the following sequence. Phase 1: Establish data protection with DLP Start by identifying sensitive information and understanding where it resides. Define sensitive information types and classification requirements. Implement sensitivity labels where appropriate. Configure DLP policies for Microsoft 365 workloads. Extend protection to endpoints and other supported locations. Initially use audit or simulation capabilities to assess impact before enabling blocking. Business outcome: Reduce accidental and unauthorized sensitive data exposure. Phase 2: Introduce Insider Risk Management Once the organization has foundational visibility and protection, introduce insider risk detection. Identify relevant insider risk scenarios. Establish investigation ownership and privacy safeguards. Configure appropriate risk indicators and policies. Develop alert triage and investigation workflows. Integrate with existing security and compliance processes. Business outcome: Improve the ability to detect and investigate potentially harmful insider activities. Phase 3: Enable Adaptive Protection Connect the two capabilities to establish risk-based enforcement. Configure insider risk levels. Map risk levels to DLP policy conditions. Apply proportionate restrictions based on risk. Continuously tune detection and enforcement. Business outcome: Stronger security controls where risk is elevated, with less disruption for lower-risk users. The actual deployment order should depend on the customer's highest-priority risks, licensing, regulatory obligations, and organizational readiness. How I would position this to a customer For your CAIP and Security cross-solution conversations, I would use this positioning: Microsoft Purview DLP protects sensitive information from inappropriate sharing or movement, while Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management identifies potentially risky user activities that could lead to data loss, intellectual property theft, or security incidents. Together, through Adaptive Protection, they enable organizations to move from static data protection policies toward dynamic, risk-aware security controls. Executive-level analogy Think of these solutions as two different security mechanisms: DLP is the security checkpoint: It examines what information is moving and determines whether that movement should be permitted. IRM is the security intelligence function: It analyzes patterns of activity to identify potential insider threats that warrant investigation. Adaptive Protection connects them: It enables the checkpoint to adjust restrictions based on the risk intelligence available. My recommendation When discussing Microsoft Purview with enterprise customers, I would avoid positioning DLP and IRM as alternative products. Instead, position them as three layers of a comprehensive data security strategy : Understand the data: Discover, classify, and label sensitive information. Protect the data: Use DLP to prevent unauthorized exposure. Understand and respond to insider risk: Use IRM and Adaptive Protection to identify potential threats and dynamically strengthen enforcement. Bottom line: DLP answers, "How do we prevent sensitive data from leaking?" IRM answers, "How do we identify potentially risky insider activity?" Adaptive Protection answers, "How do we automatically adjust protection based on that risk?" References: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/dlp-learn-about-dlp https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/insider-risk-management https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/insider-risk-management-adaptive-protection https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/insider-risk-management-adaptive-protection-guide

Absolutely. In fact, Microsoft provides an integration called Adaptive Protection that combines their strengths.

Adaptive Protection uses Insider Risk Management signals to dynamically adjust DLP enforcement based on the risk level associated with a user.

This is particularly valuable because traditional DLP policies can apply consistent restrictions, while Adaptive Protection enables more context-aware enforcement.

Example: Adaptive Protection

Imagine an organization with three insider risk levels.

User risk level

IRM assessment

Example DLP enforcement

Minor

Limited indicators of potential risk

Monitor activity and generate alerts

Moderate

More significant indicators of potential risk

Increase monitoring and notify users

Elevated

Significant indicators warranting stronger controls

Block specified external sharing activities

These are illustrative policy choices, not mandatory Microsoft defaults.

How it works:

  1. IRM evaluates relevant user activity and assigns a risk level.
  2. Adaptive Protection makes that risk level available to supported enforcement policies.
  3. DLP evaluates the risk level alongside its other policy conditions.
  4. DLP applies the configured controls.
  5. As the risk level changes, applicable enforcement can change dynamically.

For example, an employee at an elevated insider risk level could be prevented from sharing certain content externally, while users at lower risk levels continue working with fewer restrictions.

This is where the two solutions become particularly powerful together.

Does Insider Risk Management replace DLP?

No. They are complementary, not competing solutions.

Consider these customer requirements:

Customer requirement

Recommended capability

Prevent employees from emailing credit card numbers externally

DLP

Block confidential files from being copied to USB drives

DLP

Prevent sensitive information from being uploaded to unauthorized cloud applications

DLP

Identify potential intellectual property theft

IRM

Investigate suspicious patterns of employee data access and transfer

IRM

Identify potential data exfiltration associated with departing employees

IRM

Apply stricter DLP restrictions to users exhibiting elevated insider risk

IRM + DLP with Adaptive Protection

Protect sensitive data while investigating suspicious user activity

DLP + IRM

One important nuance: DLP can detect and report risky activities, and IRM can contribute to mitigation. The distinction is their primary purpose and operating model, not an absolute separation between detection and prevention.

Which capability should customers implement first?

For customers beginning their Microsoft Purview data security journey, I would generally recommend the following sequence.

Phase 1: Establish data protection with DLP

Start by identifying sensitive information and understanding where it resides.

  • Define sensitive information types and classification requirements.
  • Implement sensitivity labels where appropriate.
  • Configure DLP policies for Microsoft 365 workloads.
  • Extend protection to endpoints and other supported locations.
  • Initially use audit or simulation capabilities to assess impact before enabling blocking.

Business outcome: Reduce accidental and unauthorized sensitive data exposure.

Phase 2: Introduce Insider Risk Management

Once the organization has foundational visibility and protection, introduce insider risk detection.

  • Identify relevant insider risk scenarios.
  • Establish investigation ownership and privacy safeguards.
  • Configure appropriate risk indicators and policies.
  • Develop alert triage and investigation workflows.
  • Integrate with existing security and compliance processes.

Business outcome: Improve the ability to detect and investigate potentially harmful insider activities.

Phase 3: Enable Adaptive Protection

Connect the two capabilities to establish risk-based enforcement.

  • Configure insider risk levels.
  • Map risk levels to DLP policy conditions.
  • Apply proportionate restrictions based on risk.
  • Continuously tune detection and enforcement.

Business outcome: Stronger security controls where risk is elevated, with less disruption for lower-risk users.

The actual deployment order should depend on the customer's highest-priority risks, licensing, regulatory obligations, and organizational readiness.

How I would position this to a customer

For your CAIP and Security cross-solution conversations, I would use this positioning:

Microsoft Purview DLP protects sensitive information from inappropriate sharing or movement, while Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management identifies potentially risky user activities that could lead to data loss, intellectual property theft, or security incidents.

Together, through Adaptive Protection, they enable organizations to move from static data protection policies toward dynamic, risk-aware security controls.

Executive-level analogy

Think of these solutions as two different security mechanisms:

  • DLP is the security checkpoint: It examines what information is moving and determines whether that movement should be permitted.
  • IRM is the security intelligence function: It analyzes patterns of activity to identify potential insider threats that warrant investigation.
  • Adaptive Protection connects them: It enables the checkpoint to adjust restrictions based on the risk intelligence available.
My recommendation

When discussing Microsoft Purview with enterprise customers, I would avoid positioning DLP and IRM as alternative products.

Instead, position them as three layers of a comprehensive data security strategy:

  1. Understand the data: Discover, classify, and label sensitive information.
  2. Protect the data: Use DLP to prevent unauthorized exposure.
  3. Understand and respond to insider risk: Use IRM and Adaptive Protection to identify potential threats and dynamically strengthen enforcement.

Bottom line: DLP answers, "How do we prevent sensitive data from leaking?" IRM answers, "How do we identify potentially risky insider activity?" Adaptive Protection answers, "How do we automatically adjust protection based on that risk?"

Nearly two weeks later, about 29 million services remained vulnerable. Behind those servers are banks, healthcare providers, energy companies, and much of the infrastructure the internet runs on. And that same day brought five other major disclosures across the industry. Explore coordinated agents and shared intelligence with Microsoft Perception Turning a flaw like the PHP one into a working attack once took a specialist team months. Within roughly a day of PHP2Shell’s disclosure, security researchers had developed a working, weaponized exploit. By the following week, that research had expanded to cover additional PHP versions and configurations. The time from discovery to exploit is shrinking from months to minutes. The physics of cybersecurity are changing, and fast. AI is amplifying risk. Attackers can now find and exploit gaps faster than defenders can close them. Attacks are becoming fully automated. AI has moved from assisting attackers, to executing their tasks, to planning and running entire campaigns on its own. Agents are the new insiders. While not inherently malicious, they perform tasks and business workflows at machine speed, around the clock, and have broad access to data, apps, tools, and other agents. Frontier Transformation starts with business outcomes and a simple idea: technology was invented to serve humanity, not the other way around. To help organizations bring their ideas to life and innovate safely in the agentic era, we need a new cyber stack, built for agentic security. A new cyber stack, built to fight AI with AI The Microsoft cyber stack has three layers: Signals, sensors, and actuators . This foundational layer is powered by sensors and actuators in Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Sentinel, the network, the operating system, the browser, and our hyperscale cloud. Sensors tell you something is wrong. Actuators let you do something about it: contain a device on the network, revoke an identity’s access, or block an agent at the authorization layer. And because we know we’re not the only security solution provider in your environment, we connect to the wider ecosystem through more than 500 connectors. Together, Microsoft and partner sources produce more than 165 trillion signals a day, 2 which, enriched by Microsoft and customer threat intelligence, fuel the context layer. Context . This layer organizes those signals, together with each customer’s own environment, into agent-ready, real-time understanding of the digital estate that is optimized for precision, recall, and token efficiency. Agents, harness, and models . On top are specialized security agents that work together as teams through playbooks, directed by a harness, and a multi-model approach that uses the right model for each task, designed to ensure effective and efficient security outcomes, at scale. Delivering agentic security at Microsoft Ignite At Microsoft Ignite 2026 , we’re delivering innovation across every layer of the stack. It starts with Microsoft Perception , now generally available . Perception brings the top of the stack together. It orchestrates red, blue, and green team agents through playbooks, working together in a closed loop to deliver security outcomes. Red team agents simulate attacks from an attacker’s perspective before a breach occurs. Blue team agents detect, triage alerts, and investigate attacks, freeing analysts to focus on the critical decisions that matter most. Green team agents fix and remediate. Perception is built to help security teams move at machine speed, drive outcomes rather than tasks, and automate while staying in control. Your team sets the guardrails and signs off on high-impact actions, and automated triggers launch playbooks when an incident meets the criteria you set. New cost management dashboards and a cost estimator help you track AI usage, forecast spending, and connect costs to measurable security outcomes. Agents are only as good as what they can see and what they can do. That’s why we are investing as much in the foundation as in the layers above it. Read the Microsoft Perception Tech Community blog Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender , generally available for core capabilities , is part of that foundation. ISOC brings security information and event management (SIEM) capabilities, user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA), threat intelligence, and threat protection and disruption together so you can start your journey to the agentic security operations center (SOC). Eligible Defender Suite, Microsoft 365 E5, and Microsoft 365 E7 customers receive all Microsoft Sentinel SIEM features, 90-day default data retention for Defender data, more than 500 connectors, reduced ingestion rates, and a built-in data lake. The complete breadth of SIEM capabilities is now in preview. Learn more about the latest updates in Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel Read on to learn how Microsoft Perception, ISOC in Defender, and new capabilities across the stack work together to help customers secure their foundations, secure agentic insiders, and defend with agents. Secure your foundations Defending against AI-speed attacks starts with closing the doors attackers walk through first, and the scale of that work is increasing. In 2026, more than 96,000 vulnerabilities 3 have been published to the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) Program, more than double 2024’s roughly 40,000 and more than 20 times the level of 2010, 4 driven in part by AI-assisted vulnerability discovery tools. Yet only 26% of vulnerabilities in the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog were remediated in 2025, as remediation typically extends into weeks and months. AI finds those gaps faster than teams can close them. Today we’re announcing new capabilities to help. Strengthen your security foundation with Perception . In preview in January 2027 , new AI Readiness Initiatives in Perception turn Secure Now guidance into actionable plans with shared progress tracking, helping organizations close critical security gaps, and prepare for AI adoption. Initiatives focus on scenarios that help reduce AI-amplified risk such as modernizing authentication and deploying monthly updates. Prioritize and reduce exposure with Perception agents and playbooks . Focus on the risks that matter most and coordinate remediation using threat intelligence and business context. Two new playbooks bring together green team agents, including the Posture Prioritization Agent, now generally available, and the Risk Reduction Agent, now in public preview. Coverage spans Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud. Vulnerability shielding , available in preview , helps protect vulnerable assets from exploitation by applying targeted, temporary protection to buy defenders time before they can apply a permanent patch. During routine operations the Risk Reduction Agent proactively suggests shielding when patches aren’t immediately available. During an active attack, vulnerability shielding helps reduce exposure to certain vulnerabilities by applying targeted, temporary protections while organizations prepare immediate remediation. In supported scenarios, these protections can include adjustments to network accessibility and permissions to help limit exposure. Secure data across humans and agents with Microsoft Purview . Enhanced data classification drives precise protection with less manual effort, generally available in January 2027. Also entering preview in January: grounding protection for Copilot based on sensitive information types, which lets customers adopt Copilot without labeling every file first, and expanded data loss prevention (DLP) controls for prompts to Copilot and local agents running on Windows, which help protect sensitive data from leaking while customers use AI. Learn how Microsoft Purview accelerates data protection for the AI era. Defend with agents A SOC where people work through a queue of alerts by hand can’t keep up with increasingly autonomous attacks. Perception brings specialized red, blue, and green agents, and playbooks that automate common SecOps workflows, so defenders can get ahead. Stop threats at machine speed with new Perception playbooks and agents . Accelerate threat detection, investigation, and response with new playbooks and four blue team agents, now generally available: Alert Triage Agent, Attack Investigation Agent, Detection Authoring Agent, and Threat Intelligence Agent. Helping teams move from detection to response faster, with less manual effort. See it in action: Watch agents triage an incoming alert, investigate the attack end to end, and then improve detection rules that help identify similar threats in the future . Stay ahead of attackers with new Perception playbooks and agents . Proactively find and validate weaknesses with playbooks that coordinate red team agents, including the Recon Agent, now generally available, and the Web App Pen Test Agent, now in preview, helping security teams identify and address vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. See it in action: think like an attacker with the Protect web app playbook, which runs a pen test against your app, surfaces the weaknesses that matter, and drives the fix through to your code in GitHub. Use Perception in your flow of work . Teams can now invoke Perception playbooks in Defender, connect through Model Context Protocol (MCP) and APIs to SIEM, security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR), and IT service management tools, and bring in signals from AWS, Okta, and Salesforce. These integrations are in preview. We are also expanding the preview of Codename MDASH , our agentic code scanner, which helps customers find and fix vulnerabilities. MDASH can now analyze repositories up to 5 GB, run in regulated clouds, and MDASH code scans can be used by the Web App Pen Test Agent to prioritize and fix vulnerabilities. MDASH adds more of the MAI Cyber family, including MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash and MAI-Cyber-2 in preview, 5 improving efficiency while maintaining the quality of security findings. Learn more about MAI-Cyber-2 . Sign up to explore Codename MDASH with optional MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash access Secure agentic insiders Agents are the new insiders. They operate continuously, collaborate with other agents, change shape, and pursue goals in ways that can surprise the people who deployed them. To mitigate this risk we must discover agents, onboard them to management, secure and contain them, and do it continuously—even as their behavior and context change. Building on our October 2026 announcement, at Ignite we are introducing new capabilities to help customers secure agentic insiders, around the clock. Continuously contain agentic insiders with new Perception playbooks and agents . Investigate and remediate AI posture risks and anomalous agent behavior with new playbooks and green team agents. Microsoft Entra ID Governance dynamic permissions grant task-scoped, time-bound access, while Conditional Access dynamic controls adjust protections as risk changes. These capabilities remain in limited preview . Discover, govern, and secure agents with Microsoft Agent 365 and Microsoft Entra Suite capabilities for agentic insiders . Discovery expands by 35 local agent types, to 60 in total, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot, plus third-party cloud agents on AWS and Google Cloud. Discovered agents receive a Microsoft Entra Agent ID and can be governed with Conditional Access. Intune policies contain supported local agents on the device. Additionally, Microsoft Autopilot agents get their own Agent user account and ID, so admins can enable Conditional Access, ID Protection, and access governance to the work an Autopilot does under its own identity. Defender and Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention protect runtime and sensitive data access, and Dynamic Agent Risk assesses each agent’s exposure, blast radius, and runtime behavior. Available in preview. While these capabilities can enable customers to secure and contain agents, they will not give them insight into how the model behind an agent behaves. Without that visibility it is hard for customers to answer three basic questions about consequential AI activity: What was the AI asked and authorized to do? What happened between the request and the outcome? Can we independently verify it? That’s why Microsoft is announcing the next phase of our commitment to responsible AI: the AI Transparency Initiative . We believe every organization should be able to see what its AI accesses and does, independently verify those actions, and control what it is permitted to do, whatever model or provider it runs on. To that end, we are expanding our participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) SI Agent Standards Initiative, 6 plus drawing on our own research to develop open, industry-wide standards for AI transparency, security, and governance. We’re shaping this approach with more than 40 organizations including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard, and Volvo Cars. And we will implement this work across Microsoft AI models and products, including Microsoft Foundry and Copilot. The more agency we give AI, the more transparency we should expect in return. Sign up to help shape the AI Transparency Initiative Changing how security work gets done AI is changing how attacks happen, and how security work gets done. Developers, IT, and security teams now share responsibility for building, managing, and securing AI, so Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft Agent 365, and Perception share the same signals and context. Inside the SOC, analysts need agents to defend at machine speed, which is why we’re building agentic security into the tools they already use. Technology alone won’t get us there. Securing our own environment through the Secure Future Initiative has taught us a great deal, and our Frontier Security Engineers, services teams, and partners are working side by side with customers to put those lessons to work. Join us at Microsoft Ignite , online or in person, to learn how Microsoft Perception, ISOC in Defender and new capabilities across the stack can help secure your organization at machine speed. We’d love to see you there. Explore what’s new Secure Now . Microsoft Perception . ISOC in Microsoft Defender . Codename MDASH Partnership . Introducing MAI-Cyber-2 . Secure Agentic Insiders . Learn how Microsoft Purview accelerates data protection for the AI era . AI is changing access. See how Microsoft Entra helps you stay ahead . See how Intune extends endpoint management, supports AI governance on devices, and helps administrators respond to exposure findings . To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website . Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn ( Microsoft Security ) and X ( @MSFTSecurity ) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity. 1 PHP: News Archive – 2026 . 2 2026 Microsoft Digital Defense Report—Decoding emergence . 3 https://cvetodo.com/2026-cves . 4 CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures . 5 Signing up does not guarantee access. Submissions are reviewed, and customers are onboarded based on need and prioritization. Customers should work with their account team to be formally nominated for the preview. 6 SI Agent Standards Initiative | NIST .

items.title: Frida 17.27.0 Released
items.summary: Attaching to apps that are already running now works on non-rooted Android, Gadget carries its version so tools can tell which one they have, and idund comes to macOS, where it can make a short-lived client some fifteen times faster to reach an iOS device. iOS 27.2 users also get a fix for tunnels being torn down. And as promised last time, the XNU agent now runs live on CI. Jailed Android On a device without root, we get into a debuggable app by injecting Gadget over JDWP. That used to require spawning the app. attach() now works for an app that is already running: we break on Binder.execTransact() , trigger it with a dumpsys meminfo call into the app, load Gadget on that binder thread, then clean up and detach from JDWP. Each process gets its own Gadget files and socket, so another process of the same package can’t have its mapped Gadget overwritten, and a later attach() reuses a Gadget that is already loaded. Picking a Gadget when attaching Backends that attach by injecting Gadget, on jailed iOS and non-rooted Android, let you pick a custom one. Until now that was only possible through spawn() . There is now a gadget_path session option: import frida device = frida . get_usb_device () session = device . attach ( pid , gadget_path = " /path/to/frida-gadget.so " ) Which Gadget is this? Gadget now embeds its name, version and architectures, in the same JSON payload our Barebone agents carry: a .package section on PE, a __TEXT,__package section on Mach-O, and a package note on ELF. PE also gets a VERSIONINFO resource, and Mach-O a current_version , so the version shows up in the platform’s own tools. The new BinaryMetadata.from_file() reads it back, from PE, Mach-O, including universal ones, and ELF, without loading the binary: import frida metadata = frida . BinaryMetadata . from_file ( " frida-gadget.dylib " ) print ( metadata . name , metadata . version , metadata . architectures ) Idun idund , the per-user daemon that shares the tunnel to an iOS device between processes, now also runs on macOS. Without it, each process holds its own assertion with the system’s pairing daemon, and interrupts the system’s own connection to the device’s service discovery with its handshake. It also pays for tunnel setup, unless another app on the system is already using the device. With idund holding the tunnel, a short-lived client that would have paid for it goes from about 0.5 s down to 30 ms, and the system is interrupted once per tunnel rather than once per process. Two fixes came out of this, both about the device keeping one discovery connection per source address. On iOS 27.2, the device remembers the UUID of its last discovery peer, and when a different one handshakes, it re-attaches and closes every service listener it advertised. We used a random UUID per handshake, so each new discovery connection tore down the services of the previous one, resetting connections inside the tunnel and refusing new tunnels until the device was replugged. We now present a stable UUID, the one that also backs the pairing identity, and on macOS the system’s own. And clients of idund no longer open a discovery connection of their own, which evicted the daemon’s; it hands them the service directory from its handshake, and refreshes it on their behalf. Barebone The XNU agent’s tests now run on CI, booting the iOS 26.1 restore ramdisk under Inferno , fresh for each test. Two hooking tests are skipped there for now, as they pass on a fast host but lose a wake under the timing of the slow CI runner. Bindings python: Named constructors such as from_file() are now always static factories, matching frida-node, and are reachable from the public types rather than only through _frida . This fixes ControlService() raising NotImplementedError , and turns XnuKernelcache and Gio.InetAddress construction into from_blob() and new_any() . python: Wrapping a returned handle no longer runs the type’s __init__() , which crashed for types only constructible through factories, and leaked a second object for others. node: Only new maps to the JavaScript constructor. Named constructors are static factories, like BinaryMetadata.fromFile() , and so are the kernel image types’ fromBlob() and Gio.InetAddress.newAny() . net: The native library’s exports are now generated from frida-core’s public header. The hand-maintained list had drifted, and on macOS and Linux the library exported only what frida-core happened to reference, leaving out the Compiler among others. swift: Regenerated for the new APIs. Enjoy! Changelog droidy: Support attaching to running apps. droidy: Wait for Gadget to start listening, as connecting right after injecting could fail with “closed” when configured to resume on load. droidy: Give JDWP enum properties valid defaults, fixing a crash when creating a breakpoint event. api: Add SessionOptions.gadget_path , honored by the jailed iOS and non-rooted Android backends. api: Add BinaryMetadata.from_file() . gadget: Embed version metadata. idun: Support macOS in the daemon. idun: Present a stable host UUID to the device’s service discovery, and the system’s own on macOS, fixing tunnels being torn down on iOS 27.2. idun: Share the service directory with daemon clients. pe-module: Let get_data_at_rva() report the size, and use it to bound the mapper’s copies. macho-module: Validate load commands and slices, check command sizes and strings, bound the __LINKEDIT tables, export trie, and rebase and bind repeats, skip out-of-range section and linkedit data, reject segments whose VM range wraps, and bound the header-only loader. Thanks for reporting, @smoke-wolf ! elf-module: Skip sections with out-of-range data. leb: Don’t read past the end when skipping. barebone: Run the XNU live tests on CI. python: Map only new to __init__() , expose factory constructors in the public types, and skip __init__() when wrapping a handle. node: Keep named constructors out of new . net: Generate the native exports from frida-core’s public header, and wrap static factories and string array properties. swift: Regenerate bindings for the latest FridaCore.
items.summary_html:
Attaching to apps that are already running now works on non-rooted Android, Gadget carries its version so tools can tell which one they have, and idund comes to macOS, where it can make a short-lived client some fifteen times faster to reach an iOS device. iOS 27.2 users also get a fix for tunnels being torn down. And as promised last time, the XNU agent now runs live on CI.

Jailed Android

On a device without root, we get into a debuggable app by injecting Gadget over JDWP. That used to require spawning the app. attach() now works for an app that is already running: we break on Binder.execTransact(), trigger it with a dumpsys meminfo call into the app, load Gadget on that binder thread, then clean up and detach from JDWP.

Each process gets its own Gadget files and socket, so another process of the same package can’t have its mapped Gadget overwritten, and a later attach() reuses a Gadget that is already loaded.

Picking a Gadget when attaching

Backends that attach by injecting Gadget, on jailed iOS and non-rooted Android, let you pick a custom one. Until now that was only possible through spawn(). There is now a gadget_path session option:

import frida

device = frida.get_usb_device()
session = device.attach(pid, gadget_path="/path/to/frida-gadget.so")
Which Gadget is this?

Gadget now embeds its name, version and architectures, in the same JSON payload our Barebone agents carry: a .package section on PE, a __TEXT,__package section on Mach-O, and a package note on ELF. PE also gets a VERSIONINFO resource, and Mach-O a current_version, so the version shows up in the platform’s own tools.

The new BinaryMetadata.from_file() reads it back, from PE, Mach-O, including universal ones, and ELF, without loading the binary:

import frida

metadata = frida.BinaryMetadata.from_file("frida-gadget.dylib")
print(metadata.name, metadata.version, metadata.architectures)
Idun

idund, the per-user daemon that shares the tunnel to an iOS device between processes, now also runs on macOS. Without it, each process holds its own assertion with the system’s pairing daemon, and interrupts the system’s own connection to the device’s service discovery with its handshake. It also pays for tunnel setup, unless another app on the system is already using the device. With idund holding the tunnel, a short-lived client that would have paid for it goes from about 0.5 s down to 30 ms, and the system is interrupted once per tunnel rather than once per process.

Two fixes came out of this, both about the device keeping one discovery connection per source address. On iOS 27.2, the device remembers the UUID of its last discovery peer, and when a different one handshakes, it re-attaches and closes every service listener it advertised. We used a random UUID per handshake, so each new discovery connection tore down the services of the previous one, resetting connections inside the tunnel and refusing new tunnels until the device was replugged. We now present a stable UUID, the one that also backs the pairing identity, and on macOS the system’s own. And clients of idund no longer open a discovery connection of their own, which evicted the daemon’s; it hands them the service directory from its handshake, and refreshes it on their behalf.

Barebone

The XNU agent’s tests now run on CI, booting the iOS 26.1 restore ramdisk under Inferno, fresh for each test. Two hooking tests are skipped there for now, as they pass on a fast host but lose a wake under the timing of the slow CI runner.

Bindings
  • python: Named constructors such as from_file() are now always static factories, matching frida-node, and are reachable from the public types rather than only through _frida. This fixes ControlService() raising NotImplementedError, and turns XnuKernelcache and Gio.InetAddress construction into from_blob() and new_any().
  • python: Wrapping a returned handle no longer runs the type’s __init__(), which crashed for types only constructible through factories, and leaked a second object for others.
  • node: Only new maps to the JavaScript constructor. Named constructors are static factories, like BinaryMetadata.fromFile(), and so are the kernel image types’ fromBlob() and Gio.InetAddress.newAny().
  • net: The native library’s exports are now generated from frida-core’s public header. The hand-maintained list had drifted, and on macOS and Linux the library exported only what frida-core happened to reference, leaving out the Compiler among others.
  • swift: Regenerated for the new APIs.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • droidy: Support attaching to running apps.
  • droidy: Wait for Gadget to start listening, as connecting right after injecting could fail with “closed” when configured to resume on load.
  • droidy: Give JDWP enum properties valid defaults, fixing a crash when creating a breakpoint event.
  • api: Add SessionOptions.gadget_path, honored by the jailed iOS and non-rooted Android backends.
  • api: Add BinaryMetadata.from_file().
  • gadget: Embed version metadata.
  • idun: Support macOS in the daemon.
  • idun: Present a stable host UUID to the device’s service discovery, and the system’s own on macOS, fixing tunnels being torn down on iOS 27.2.
  • idun: Share the service directory with daemon clients.
  • pe-module: Let get_data_at_rva() report the size, and use it to bound the mapper’s copies.
  • macho-module: Validate load commands and slices, check command sizes and strings, bound the __LINKEDIT tables, export trie, and rebase and bind repeats, skip out-of-range section and linkedit data, reject segments whose VM range wraps, and bound the header-only loader. Thanks for reporting, @smoke-wolf!
  • elf-module: Skip sections with out-of-range data.
  • leb: Don’t read past the end when skipping.
  • barebone: Run the XNU live tests on CI.
  • python: Map only new to __init__(), expose factory constructors in the public types, and skip __init__() when wrapping a handle.
  • node: Keep named constructors out of new.
  • net: Generate the native exports from frida-core’s public header, and wrap static factories and string array properties.
  • swift: Regenerate bindings for the latest FridaCore.

items.title: Malicious iOS Scripts Now Behind 1 in 5 Advertiser Suspensions as Coruna Exploit Kit Hides Inside Ad Landing Pages
items.summary: Malicious iOS scripts accounted for roughly 20% of advertiser account suspensions in 2026 across advertising platforms protected by ADEX, according to the company’s newly released State of Ad Fraud 2026: ADEX Trust & Safety Report . It is the first year the anti-fraud platform has tracked device-targeted attacks as a standalone category, and the figure places iPhone-specific exploitation alongside cloaking as one of the leading reasons advertisers are removed from ad networks. The finding reflects a shift in how malware reaches mobile users. Rather than relying on malicious apps, operators are buying legitimate ad inventory and pointing it at landing pages that quietly fingerprint each visitor’s device before deciding what to serve. One URL, two very different pages At the center of the report is an investigation into approximately 50 advertiser accounts that ran campaigns with sharply different creatives and landing-page designs but near-identical delivery mechanics underneath. ADEX found hidden iframes checking visitors’ iOS versions and filtering scripts designed to screen out bots, crawlers, and manual reviewers. A platform moderator loading the page would see an ordinary offer; a user on a vulnerable iPhone would receive an exploit chain. That chain was assembled by the Coruna exploit kit, which selected payloads matched to the device’s iOS version and chipset. The kit has been documented in previous campaigns leveraging 23 exploits to compromise thousands of iPhones , and Apple has already shipped emergency updates for older devices specifically to blunt Coruna attacks . The documented chains in ADEX’s investigation covered iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1, meaning fully patched devices were not affected but any phone running outdated firmware remained exposed. The payload was delivered under a filename ending in .min.js, blending into the minified JavaScript libraries found on virtually every commercial website. The final implant targeted digital wallets and financial applications and scanned the device for cryptocurrency recovery seed phrases, a technique consistent with DarkSword and Coruna operations previously observed stealing wallet recovery phrases . Why the accounts were only visible together ADEX noted that reviewing each landing page in isolation would likely have missed the operation entirely. The connection between the 50 accounts emerged only from shared infrastructure: the same device-check logic, the same script patterns, and the same redirect behavior repeated behind constantly rotating designs and offers. The company passed its findings to affected clients for review and enforcement, and said the investigation has since allowed its moderation systems to recognize the same attack pattern even when it appears behind a brand-new landing page. The approach mirrors a broader trend in which attackers abuse legitimate ad platforms as a distribution layer, as seen when malicious Instagram ads were used to infect iPhones with spyware without any user interaction . In both cases, the ad network’s trust and reach become the delivery mechanism. Cloaking declines as a share, new categories emerge The report also shows the enforcement mix changing. Cloaking accounted for about 45% of advertiser suspensions in Q3 2026, down from roughly 75% across 2025. Messenger-based phishing, observed on services including WhatsApp and Telegram through third-party abuse, was broken out as its own category during the year. ADEX cautioned that platforms log a single primary reason for each suspension even when several techniques appear together. An iOS-targeted campaign typically also uses cloaking to hide its payload from reviewers, so the 20% figure for malicious iOS scripts likely understates how often device-targeting appears in practice. For traffic-quality teams, the report’s practical takeaway is to follow the delivery infrastructure rather than the creative. Shared scripts, servers, device checks, and redirect chains are harder to rotate than page designs, and they expose coordinated operations that individual account reviews cannot. The full State of Ad Fraud 2026: ADEX Trust & Safety Report is available from ADEX , a global anti-fraud and traffic-quality platform within AdTech Holding that analyzes billions of impressions, clicks, and conversions to protect AdTech products and partners from malware-driven and invalid traffic.

items.title: Using the AWS RMiT workbook and ISO Compliance Guides to support your BNM submissions
items.summary: Your next Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) notification submission needs auditable evidence of how Amazon Web Services (AWS) controls align with Risk Management in Technology (RMiT) requirements. Two resources now exist to support that work: the AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT and the compliance guides published by AWS Security Assurance Services (AWS SAS) . The AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT, available through AWS Artifact , maps each RMiT provision to AWS Control Objectives (AWS responsibilities under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model ) and AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices (your responsibilities). It tells you, for every RMiT requirement, what AWS is responsible for and what you implement. The compliance guides published by AWS SAS over the past year provide implementation guidance for International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards that complements the workbook. These guides show how to implement controls that meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks using AWS services, giving your technical and compliance teams a clear path from regulatory expectation to deployed architecture. Malaysian financial institutions can now trace from BNM regulatory requirement, through AWS control implementation, to the evidence that demonstrates it: AWS third-party attestations for AWS-side controls, and your own workload evidence for customer-side controls. BNM expects this specificity in notification documentation. AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT The workbook is a structured Excel document available through AWS Artifact . For each of the 394 RMiT provisions, it identifies: Whether the requirement is an AWS responsibility or a customer responsibility under the Shared Responsibility Model The specific AWS Control Objective that addresses the requirement (where AWS is responsible) The relevant AWS Well-Architected Framework best practice for customer implementation (where the customer is responsible) Supporting information and references for each mapping The following is a sample entry from the workbook: RMiT Requirement Responsibility Source AWS supporting information 10.49: A financial institution should ensure network resilience… AWS AWS Control Objectives AWS Control Section: Network Security. AWS maintains redundant network connectivity with multiple tier-1 transit providers across each Availability Zone. 10.49: (Customer responsibility) Customer Well-Architected REL 2: How do you plan your network topology? Implement multi-AZ deployments. Configure VPC flow logs and use AWS Network Firewall. The workbook currently includes 394 rows across all RMiT appendix requirements, with 208 mapped to AWS responsibilities and 186 to customer responsibilities. Why this matters now BNM revised RMiT guidelines effective 28 November 2025, and updated them on 25 September 2026 to add requirements for National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII) entities. Financial institutions operating under both BNM Outsourcing and BNM RMiT must demonstrate that their cloud service providers maintain controls aligned with regulatory expectations. Institutions preparing notification submissions for material cloud workloads need auditable evidence of this alignment. The revised guidelines set higher expectations for evidence quality. Institutions submitting notifications without clear, structured control mapping evidence might face extended review cycles and requests for additional information from BNM. Workloads that could be deployed in weeks remain in governance queues for months when supporting documentation lacks the specificity regulators expect. Compliance guides from AWS Security Assurance Services Start with the RMiT workbook to identify which provisions AWS addresses and which you implement. Then use the following compliance guides to design and implement your customer-side controls. The guides are implementation guidance for your teams. Audit evidence comes from two places. For AWS-side controls, use AWS third-party attestations, such as ISO certificates and System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports, available in AWS Artifact. For your workload, use evidence from your own environment, including configurations, logs, and AWS Config conformance pack results. Auditors can also use the guides as a reference for how a control is typically implemented on AWS. AWS SAS has published five compliance guides over the past year. Each guide provides control-level implementation guidance on the customer side of the Shared Responsibility Model, showing how AWS services can be configured to meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks. These guides were written by AWS SAS practicing security assessors and auditors holding Payment Card Industry Qualified Security Assessor (PCI QSA), Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), Certified Information Security Manager (CISM), ISO 27001 Lead Auditor, and Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP) certifications, drawing on experience from hundreds of cloud security assessments across financial services globally. The following is the list of guides AWS SAS practicing auditors have published, which include control mapping information relevant to BNM RMiT: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 on AWS (Information Security Management) – Maps Annex A controls to AWS services ISO 31000:2018 on AWS (Risk Management) – Integrates AWS services into risk identification, assessment, treatment, and monitoring ISO/IEC 42001:2023 on AWS (Artificial Intelligence Management Systems) – Supports institutions building responsible artificial intelligence (AI) on AWS Cloud Security Alliance Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) v4.1 on AWS (Cloud Security Controls) – Maps 207 control objectives to AWS American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) SOC 2 on AWS – Navigates SOC 2 compliance using AWS services How these resources work together A Malaysian financial institution preparing a BNM notification can use these resources together: The RMiT workbook identifies which RMiT provisions are AWS responsibilities and which are customer responsibilities. For AWS responsibilities, the workbook references the specific AWS Control Objective. AWS third-party reports in AWS Artifact, such as the AWS ISO/IEC 27001 certificate and SOC reports, attest to those AWS Control Objectives. For customer responsibilities, the ISO compliance guides show how to implement the corresponding controls using AWS services. The ISO 31000 guide can inform the risk management methodology you apply to your cloud workloads. AWS Config Conformance Packs for BNM RMiT provide automated, continuous monitoring of deployed controls. Resources also supporting this approach: The AWS User Guide for Financial Institutions in Malaysia examines the BNM Outsourcing and RMiT policy documents and sets out the steps to launch regulated workloads on AWS AWS Config Conformance Packs for BNM RMiT provide automated compliance monitoring through managed AWS Config rules mapped to specific RMiT controls Compliance teams across Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) financial services have already begun referencing the AWS Guide to BNM RMiT and associated resources in their cloud risk assessment processes and BNM notification documentation. Looking ahead: AI governance For institutions deploying generative AI and machine learning, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (Artificial Intelligence Management Systems) is relevant to BNM technology governance expectations. In November 2024, AWS became the first major cloud provider to announce ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI services. AWS passed its first surveillance audit in November 2025 with zero findings. The ISO 42001 compliance guide published in May 2026 supports institutions building their own responsible AI systems on their side of the AWS Shared Responsibility Model. How to get started Access the RMiT workbook through AWS Artifact and review with your compliance lead to identify which provisions apply to your material cloud workloads. Download the relevant ISO compliance guides to plan how you implement your customer-side controls. Download AWS ISO certificates and SOC reports from AWS Artifact for AWS-side evidence. Map your workload-specific controls using the workbook as the RMiT baseline and the ISO guides as implementation guidance. Implement automated compliance monitoring using the BNM RMiT conformance pack for AWS Config to maintain continuous visibility over your control posture. Engage your AWS account team or AWS SAS for additional guidance on implementing customer-side controls referenced in the workbook. As BNM updates its regulatory expectations, AWS will update these resources to reflect revised requirements. Subscribe to the AWS Security Blog for update notifications. Additional resources AWS Financial Services Compliance Center for Malaysia AWS Artifact (access the RMiT Workbook and ISO certifications) ISO/IEC 27001:2022 on AWS Compliance Guide ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management on AWS Compliance Guide ISO/IEC 42001:2023 on AWS Compliance Guide (AI Management Systems) Cloud Security Alliance CCM v4.1 on AWS Compliance Guide AICPA SOC 2 Compliance Guide on AWS AWS Guide to BNM RMiT AWS User Guide for Financial Institutions in Malaysia AWS Shared Responsibility Model AWS Well-Architected Framework Operational Best Practices for BNM RMiT (AWS Config) If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . Jonathan Jenkyn Jonathan (JJ) is a Senior Security and Compliance Solutions Architect with AWS Security Assurance Services and a published cybersecurity author. He has over 30 years of experience across penetration testing, incident response, cyber resilience, and security governance. He helps customers build practical security programs. He champions disability inclusion and neurodiversity at Amazon. Outside work, he runs, cycles, swims, and enjoys family time. Matthew Nixon Matt is a Principal in the AWS Asia Financial Services Security and Compliance team. He has 20 years of experience in technology risk, audit, and information security, including leading a cloud risk team in financial services. Matt co-founded an award-winning AI/ML startup, authored books on IT and cloud risk, and won the Singapore ISACA 2024 IT Risk Leader Award.
