Hackers Exploit Unpatched Microsoft Exchange Servers to Deploy Custom RATs Across Southeast Asia
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting unpatched Microsoft Exchange servers and vulnerable web servers to break into government networks across Southeast Asia, deploying custom remote access trojans built for quiet, long-term spying. The campaign combines server exploitation, targeted phishing, credential theft, and mailbox access to pursue sensitive government information. The activity has targeted government entities since at least July 2025. Investigators observed attackers deploying PerfectPioneer RAT before introducing its modular successor, KUKURAT, in March 2026. The operation focused on maintaining access and collecting intelligence, with targeted filenames suggesting an interest in international relations and internal political affairs. Researchers from Unit 42 identified both previously undocumented malware families and tracked the campaign as TGR-STA-0049, also known as REF7707, Earth Alux, and Ink Dragon. The investigation shows how the attackers steadily updated their tools while combining familiar intrusion methods with newer ways to hide network traffic and endpoint activity. Hackers Exploit Unpatched Microsoft Exchange Servers Server exploitation was the primary entry method. Attackers compromised vulnerable Exchange and web servers, planted web shells, and used that access to run reconnaissance commands and deploy malware. The report does not identify the specific Exchange vulnerabilities exploited, so the intrusions should not be attributed to a particular CVE or exploit chain. The approach echoes earlier Exchange server backdoor attacks involving other threat groups, although those incidents do not establish a connection to this campaign. Execution of the PerfectPioneer RAT from a web shell, as shown in Cortex XDR (Source – Unit42) Here, researchers observed a mixture of custom and publicly available web shells, including ASPXSpy, Godzilla, and Suo5 variants. Phishing provided a second route into targeted systems. Attackers used lookalike government domains and executable files disguised with PDF icons. Opening these files launched malware alongside a decoy document. One lure impersonated an official Myanmar election notice, while another delivery method ran a genuine GlobalProtect installer as malware executed in the background. PerfectPioneer is written in Go, and researchers recovered six variants. The most complete version supports file transfers, shell commands, process management, screenshots, keylogging, code injection, and SOCKS5 proxying. Some variants also contain an operator safety mechanism that blocks destructive or conspicuous commands, reducing the chance that an attacker’s mistake exposes the intrusion. Both malware families support HTTP/3 communications over QUIC, which uses UDP rather than TCP. This matters because some network defenses inspect TCP traffic more closely than UDP traffic. PerfectPioneer’s analyzed communication framework can fall back to HTTP/2, while KUKURAT has separate HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 variants. Blocking QUIC alone therefore does not remove the threat. KUKURAT Hides Activity While Attackers Steal Credentials and Email KUKURAT shifts most capabilities into separate DLL modules retrieved from the command server when needed. Written in C++, its code supports at least 12 named modules covering functions such as screenshots, keylogging, file management, scanning, remote execution, and lateral movement. This separates the small core agent from much of its operational functionality. Unlike the distinct TinyRCT government espionage campaign , this operation also features a coordinated camouflage engine. KUKURAT can generate harmless-looking web requests, imitate browser-related registry activity, and rapidly create and delete temporary files. Code snippet from the PerfectPioneer RAT’s isDangerousCommand code (Source – Unit42) These actions aim to bury meaningful signals among artificial noise rather than simply conceal a single malicious file. Attackers also deployed a watchdog component that could restart KUKURAT after it stopped responding. After compromising domain controllers, they modified domain log-on scripts so legitimate user authentication triggered malware downloads and execution on additional endpoints. Researchers also observed the use of established remote administration methods for movement inside compromised networks. Credential theft included LSASS memory dumping, DCSync, Mimikatz, ProcDump, and SharpDPAPI. The attackers then examined Exchange impersonation rights and, in observed cases, granted a compromised account broad mailbox access. Their document collection targeted office files, PDFs, and images, linking endpoint compromise directly to the campaign’s intelligence-gathering objective. The pattern reinforces lessons from other Exchange server exploitation campaigns without implying shared attribution. Defenders should patch exposed servers, investigate existing compromises, audit domain log-on scripts, and review Exchange permissions. Unit 42 additionally recommends inspecting or restricting QUIC traffic and monitoring suspicious credential-dumping behavior. Removing malware without addressing stolen credentials, mailbox permissions, and domain persistence may leave attackers with routes back into the environment. items.summary_html:
Hackers are exploiting unpatched Microsoft Exchange servers and vulnerable web servers to break into government networks across Southeast Asia, deploying custom remote access trojans built for quiet, long-term spying.

The campaign combines server exploitation, targeted phishing, credential theft, and mailbox access to pursue sensitive government information.

The activity has targeted government entities since at least July 2025. Investigators observed attackers deploying PerfectPioneer RAT before introducing its modular successor, KUKURAT, in March 2026.

The operation focused on maintaining access and collecting intelligence, with targeted filenames suggesting an interest in international relations and internal political affairs.

Researchers from Unit 42 identified both previously undocumented malware families and tracked the campaign as TGR-STA-0049, also known as REF7707, Earth Alux, and Ink Dragon.

The investigation shows how the attackers steadily updated their tools while combining familiar intrusion methods with newer ways to hide network traffic and endpoint activity.

Hackers Exploit Unpatched Microsoft Exchange Servers

Server exploitation was the primary entry method. Attackers compromised vulnerable Exchange and web servers, planted web shells, and used that access to run reconnaissance commands and deploy malware.

The report does not identify the specific Exchange vulnerabilities exploited, so the intrusions should not be attributed to a particular CVE or exploit chain.

The approach echoes earlier Exchange server backdoor attacks involving other threat groups, although those incidents do not establish a connection to this campaign.

Execution of the PerfectPioneer RAT from a web shell, as shown in Cortex XDR (Source – Unit42)

Here, researchers observed a mixture of custom and publicly available web shells, including ASPXSpy, Godzilla, and Suo5 variants. Phishing provided a second route into targeted systems.

Attackers used lookalike government domains and executable files disguised with PDF icons. Opening these files launched malware alongside a decoy document.

One lure impersonated an official Myanmar election notice, while another delivery method ran a genuine GlobalProtect installer as malware executed in the background.

PerfectPioneer is written in Go, and researchers recovered six variants. The most complete version supports file transfers, shell commands, process management, screenshots, keylogging, code injection, and SOCKS5 proxying.

Some variants also contain an operator safety mechanism that blocks destructive or conspicuous commands, reducing the chance that an attacker’s mistake exposes the intrusion.

Both malware families support HTTP/3 communications over QUIC, which uses UDP rather than TCP. This matters because some network defenses inspect TCP traffic more closely than UDP traffic.

PerfectPioneer’s analyzed communication framework can fall back to HTTP/2, while KUKURAT has separate HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 variants. Blocking QUIC alone therefore does not remove the threat.

KUKURAT Hides Activity While Attackers Steal Credentials and Email

KUKURAT shifts most capabilities into separate DLL modules retrieved from the command server when needed. Written in C++, its code supports at least 12 named modules covering functions such as screenshots, keylogging, file management, scanning, remote execution, and lateral movement. This separates the small core agent from much of its operational functionality.

Unlike the distinct TinyRCT government espionage campaign, this operation also features a coordinated camouflage engine. KUKURAT can generate harmless-looking web requests, imitate browser-related registry activity, and rapidly create and delete temporary files.

Code snippet from the PerfectPioneer RAT’s isDangerousCommand code (Source – Unit42)

These actions aim to bury meaningful signals among artificial noise rather than simply conceal a single malicious file. Attackers also deployed a watchdog component that could restart KUKURAT after it stopped responding.

After compromising domain controllers, they modified domain log-on scripts so legitimate user authentication triggered malware downloads and execution on additional endpoints. Researchers also observed the use of established remote administration methods for movement inside compromised networks.

Credential theft included LSASS memory dumping, DCSync, Mimikatz, ProcDump, and SharpDPAPI. The attackers then examined Exchange impersonation rights and, in observed cases, granted a compromised account broad mailbox access.

Their document collection targeted office files, PDFs, and images, linking endpoint compromise directly to the campaign’s intelligence-gathering objective.

The pattern reinforces lessons from other Exchange server exploitation campaigns without implying shared attribution. Defenders should patch exposed servers, investigate existing compromises, audit domain log-on scripts, and review Exchange permissions.

Unit 42 additionally recommends inspecting or restricting QUIC traffic and monitoring suspicious credential-dumping behavior.

Removing malware without addressing stolen credentials, mailbox permissions, and domain persistence may leave attackers with routes back into the environment.

items.title: Autonomous Cyberattacks: New Trends and How to Prepare for It
items.summary: For years, “AI-powered attacks” meant better phishing emails. That era is over. In late 2025, Anthropic disclosed a state-sponsored espionage campaign in which an AI agent ran an estimated 80–90% of the tactical work against roughly 30 targets, with humans stepping in only at a handful of decision points. The attacker’s bottleneck is no longer headcount. It is tokens. For SOC analysts and detection engineers, this changes the math. Dwell time shrinks, attack volume scales with compute, and the TTPs we write rules for start to mutate on every run. Here is what autonomous attacks look like under the hood, and how to build a defense that moves at the same speed. Get Started For Free What are Autonomous AI Cyberattacks? An autonomous AI cyberattack is an intrusion where an AI agent plans, executes, and adapts the attack chain with minimal human direction. The operator sets an objective (“get domain admin at target X”) and the agent decides how to get there. The key difference from classic automation is reasoning. A script runs the same playbook every time. An agent reads tool output, notices a failed exploit, and tries another path. Think of it as moving from a loaded gun to a junior red teamer that never sleeps, works hundreds of targets in parallel, and costs a few dollars per hour of API time. How does Autonomous Attack work? Most autonomous attack frameworks run a simple loop: observe, plan, act, evaluate, repeat. An orchestrator model breaks the objective into small tasks and hands them to sub-agents wired to real tooling through frameworks like the Model Context Protocol (MCP): scanners, credential dumpers, browsers, shells. A typical run maps cleanly to MITRE ATT&CK: Reconnaissance (TA0043): the agent enumerates exposed services, scrapes employee data, and ranks targets by value. Initial Access (TA0001): it writes or adapts an exploit for a discovered weakness, tests it, and retries on failure. Credential Access and Lateral Movement (TA0006, TA0008): it harvests secrets, validates them, and pivots, logging every step for the operator. Collection and Exfiltration (TA0009, TA0010): it sorts stolen data by intelligence value before sending it out. The trick that makes this work is task decomposition. Each sub-task looks benign in isolation (“scan this host,” “test this login”), which is exactly how attackers have slipped past model safeguards. The defensive takeaway: the signal lives in the sequence and the tempo, not in any single event. How to defend against Autonomous AI Attacks? Agents are fast, but they are not subtle. They generate request rates no human operator could sustain, retry aggressively, and sometimes hallucinate credentials or findings. That noise is your advantage. Focus detection on: Behavior over indicators. IOCs from an agent-driven campaign may be unique per run. Write Sigma rules around behaviors such as rapid sequential discovery commands, burst authentication attempts across many accounts, or a new process spawning dozens of recon tools in seconds. Velocity and correlation. Chain low-severity events into high-confidence alerts. Ten benign actions within 60 seconds from one identity is a story worth telling. Identity and API telemetry. Agents live on tokens and service accounts. Monitor anomalous API usage, impossible-speed sessions, and unexpected calls to LLM endpoints from servers. Deception. Honeytokens and decoy credentials work beautifully against agents that greedily validate everything they find. How are LLMs used in Autonomous Attacks? LLMs play three roles in the modern attack stack: The brain. Commercial or open-weight models act as orchestrators, reasoning about what to do next and generating code on demand. The payload. Malware now queries models at runtime. CERT-UA’s LameHug, linked to APT28, used a hosted LLM to generate recon commands on the fly, and the PromptLock proof of concept showed ransomware writing its own Lua scripts via a locally run model. No static command strings means fewer signatures to match. The social engineer. Personalized phishing, voice cloning, and deepfake video now scale to thousands of targets at near-zero marginal cost. For detection engineers, this creates new telemetry worth hunting: outbound traffic to LLM APIs from non-user hosts, embedded API keys in binaries, local inference runtimes appearing on endpoints, and scripts that look freshly generated rather than copied from a known toolkit. items.summary_html:
For years, “AI-powered attacks” meant better phishing emails. That era is over. In late 2025, Anthropic disclosed a state-sponsored espionage campaign in which an AI agent ran an estimated 80–90% of the tactical work against roughly 30 targets, with humans stepping in only at a handful of decision points. The attacker’s bottleneck is no longer headcount. It is tokens.

For SOC analysts and detection engineers, this changes the math. Dwell time shrinks, attack volume scales with compute, and the TTPs we write rules for start to mutate on every run. Here is what autonomous attacks look like under the hood, and how to build a defense that moves at the same speed.

Get Started For Free

What are Autonomous AI Cyberattacks?

An autonomous AI cyberattack is an intrusion where an AI agent plans, executes, and adapts the attack chain with minimal human direction. The operator sets an objective (“get domain admin at target X”) and the agent decides how to get there.

The key difference from classic automation is reasoning. A script runs the same playbook every time. An agent reads tool output, notices a failed exploit, and tries another path. Think of it as moving from a loaded gun to a junior red teamer that never sleeps, works hundreds of targets in parallel, and costs a few dollars per hour of API time.

How does Autonomous Attack work?

Most autonomous attack frameworks run a simple loop: observe, plan, act, evaluate, repeat. An orchestrator model breaks the objective into small tasks and hands them to sub-agents wired to real tooling through frameworks like the Model Context Protocol (MCP): scanners, credential dumpers, browsers, shells.

A typical run maps cleanly to MITRE ATT&CK:

  1. Reconnaissance (TA0043): the agent enumerates exposed services, scrapes employee data, and ranks targets by value.
  2. Initial Access (TA0001): it writes or adapts an exploit for a discovered weakness, tests it, and retries on failure.
  3. Credential Access and Lateral Movement (TA0006, TA0008): it harvests secrets, validates them, and pivots, logging every step for the operator.
  4. Collection and Exfiltration (TA0009, TA0010): it sorts stolen data by intelligence value before sending it out.

The trick that makes this work is task decomposition. Each sub-task looks benign in isolation (“scan this host,” “test this login”), which is exactly how attackers have slipped past model safeguards. The defensive takeaway: the signal lives in the sequence and the tempo, not in any single event.

How to defend against Autonomous AI Attacks?

Agents are fast, but they are not subtle. They generate request rates no human operator could sustain, retry aggressively, and sometimes hallucinate credentials or findings. That noise is your advantage. Focus detection on:

  • Behavior over indicators. IOCs from an agent-driven campaign may be unique per run. Write Sigma rules around behaviors such as rapid sequential discovery commands, burst authentication attempts across many accounts, or a new process spawning dozens of recon tools in seconds.
  • Velocity and correlation. Chain low-severity events into high-confidence alerts. Ten benign actions within 60 seconds from one identity is a story worth telling.
  • Identity and API telemetry. Agents live on tokens and service accounts. Monitor anomalous API usage, impossible-speed sessions, and unexpected calls to LLM endpoints from servers.
  • Deception. Honeytokens and decoy credentials work beautifully against agents that greedily validate everything they find.
How are LLMs used in Autonomous Attacks?

LLMs play three roles in the modern attack stack:

  • The brain. Commercial or open-weight models act as orchestrators, reasoning about what to do next and generating code on demand.
  • The payload. Malware now queries models at runtime. CERT-UA’s LameHug, linked to APT28, used a hosted LLM to generate recon commands on the fly, and the PromptLock proof of concept showed ransomware writing its own Lua scripts via a locally run model. No static command strings means fewer signatures to match.
  • The social engineer. Personalized phishing, voice cloning, and deepfake video now scale to thousands of targets at near-zero marginal cost.

For detection engineers, this creates new telemetry worth hunting: outbound traffic to LLM APIs from non-user hosts, embedded API keys in binaries, local inference runtimes appearing on endpoints, and scripts that look freshly generated rather than copied from a known toolkit.

How to prepare your business for such attacks?

Preparation starts with an honest question: if an attacker could try every technique in your threat model tonight, in parallel, which ones would you catch?

  1. Map coverage to ATT&CK. Identify gaps against the techniques agents favor: discovery, credential access, and lateral movement. Prioritize by your real log sources, not a theoretical matrix.
  2. Shrink the exposed surface. Agents excel at finding forgotten assets. Continuous external attack surface management and fast patching of internet-facing systems remove their easiest wins.
  3. Harden identity. Enforce phishing-resistant MFA, rotate secrets, and kill standing privileges. Stolen credentials are fuel for every autonomous chain.
  4. Govern your own AI. Inventory internal agents, MCP servers, and LLM integrations. Every tool you give your own AI is a tool an attacker can hijack through prompt injection.
  5. Rehearse at machine speed. Run purple-team exercises with AI-assisted adversary emulation and measure time-to-detect in minutes, not days.
How to Transform Security to Autonomous Defense?

You cannot fight an agent with a ticket queue. Autonomous defense means letting machines handle the repetitive loop while analysts own judgment and strategy. In practice, that looks like:

  • Detection-as-code pipelines. Rules live in version control, are tested automatically, and deploy to every SIEM, EDR, and data lake in minutes. Sigma as a vendor-agnostic format makes this portable.
  • AI-assisted detection engineering. Use AI to translate threat reports into rules, convert queries across platforms, and tune noisy content. SOC Prime’s Uncoder AI does exactly this, turning CTI into ready-to-deploy detections and translating rules across dozens of SIEM, EDR, and data lake languages.
  • Continuous content refresh. New behaviors appear weekly. Threat Detection Marketplace on the SOC Prime Platform delivers curated, ATT&CK-mapped rules as emerging threats surface, so coverage evolves without waiting on a backlog.
  • Agentic triage with guardrails. Let AI agents enrich alerts, correlate context, and draft response actions, but keep humans approving anything destructive. Autonomy without oversight just gives the attacker a new target.

The goal is not to replace analysts. It is to compress the detect-to-respond cycle so your team works on the 5% of cases that actually need a human brain.

What are cybersecurity trends for Autonomous Attacks?
  • Exploit windows collapse. AI systems already find real vulnerabilities at scale, as DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge showed. Expect time from disclosure to weaponization to drop from weeks to hours.
  • Runtime-generated malware goes mainstream. LLM-querying payloads will push defenders further toward behavioral detection.
  • AI infrastructure becomes the target. Prompt injection, poisoned MCP servers, and hijacked agents will join the attack surface.
  • Defense goes agent-versus-agent. SOCs that pair human expertise with AI-driven detection engineering will keep pace. Those that don’t will be outrun.

items.title: COLD RELIC: A Case Study in Impersonation and Compromise
Agents didn’t break code review, they exposed it
items.summary: Every line of shipped code has an owner who is accountable for it, and that was true long before agents entered the picture. What agents have really changed is the volume of code. It now arrives faster than anyone can read it, and the traditional safeguard of a reviewer approving each diff was never as dependable as teams assumed. John Crickett, founder of Coding Challenges and a software veteran of several decades, explains on The Next Commit why delivery pressure is pushing developers to stop reading the code they ship, and why the reviewer approval they leaned on was never much of a safeguard. Teams can't outsource accountability to an AI tool. What they can do is ensure their verification practice keeps pace with the code, instead of quietly lapsing while everyone assumes it's still happening. Delivery pressure is quietly ending code review Most software developers who stop reviewing AI-generated code do so under the weight of delivery pressure, not by deliberate choice. Crickett sees developers splitting into three groups as agents take over more of the writing: One group has stopped reading the code and trusts the agent. A second group still reads everything because, as Crickett puts it, they "feel that they've got to own anything that goes to production." The third group is under pressure to ship, and Crickett says those developers either aren't reading the code "as fully as they'd like" or feel they're "losing the ability to." That third camp is the one worth worrying about, because those software developers ran out of time to review rather than deciding review doesn't matter. When review slips under that pressure, changes merge that nobody fully understands, and the next person to maintain the code inherits a system they cannot explain. Crickett is blunt about what that costs. "If you never look at the code or you don't have the ability to…You don't know whether it's good." Teams absolve themselves of accountability in the distance between the camp they want to be in and the camp delivery pressure forces them into. Neither a human reviewer nor another model can serve as the sole safeguard The review process that agents are supposedly breaking was already broken. Crickett walks through the honest math of code review: a reviewer easily scrutinizes five lines, finds 50 lines a bit harder, but a 500-line change “just gets a LGTM. Because most people cannot hold in their head five hundred lines of complex code change.” That approval is supposed to make the reviewer accountable for the change, and host Tom Howlett and Crickett both call that idea “a bit of a myth,” since nobody can answer for code they couldn’t follow. Crickett doesn’t fault the reviewer, because large pull requests are hard for anyone, and he calls it unrealistic “to expect that human code review works…We miss things and it doesn’t scale.” Agents turned the occasional 500-line change into a daily one. Pointing another model at the problem helps, and Crickett values LLM code review because it is cheap and repeatable. "If a human might only catch half the issues in a code review, an LLM might only catch say a third of the issues. The difference is the human will spend hours doing it and hates doing it. The LLM will spend minutes doing it and you can run it again. You can clear its context." Research on LLM judges shows where to draw the line. Ask one the same question twice and some of its verdicts change, and push back on it with another AI and more of them flip, because these models are trained to please. An LLM that catches a third of issues in minutes adds real value inside the loop, and the same LLM working as the only quality gate becomes a liability. Confidence needs both kinds of code verification Even as AI agents improve, the need for code verification is essential— an agent can write excellent code that still misses what the system needs. "It could write amazing code better than any human, for argument's sake, but still does the wrong thing," Crickett says. Suppose the agent ships flawless code that stores data insecurely, your site gets breached, and personal details leak. Nobody wrote bad code in that scenario, but someone left a gap between what they intended and what they specified, and the agent filled it without saying so. Those gaps open up easily in natural language, where, as Crickett points out, "you can change the whole meaning of a sentence by putting a comma in or not putting a comma in." A check that only asks "is this code well written" passes that change every time. Crickett's own answer is a "multi-point approach" that pairs LLM review with static analysis, compiler checks, tests, and exploratory testing, and a mix like that builds confidence when teams know what each check can prove. Deterministic analysis proves what rules can check: syntax and style, data and control flows, taint, architecture, and dependencies. It returns the same verdict every run and holds its answer when an agent argues back. This is what Sonar calls a zero-trust, multilayered code verification strategy: AI code review works alongside static analysis, compiler checks, tests, and exploratory testing. Agentic verification covers what rules can't, reasoning about intent and business logic, which is the check the breach scenario needed. Both kinds need to run independently of whatever generated the code, so every change meets the same bar whichever agent or model wrote it, and both need to leave evidence, a record of the intent, the standards, the checks, and the result that an auditor can read. In the CI verification loop, SonarQube sets the standard and Gitar enforces it at merge speed. Teams that want to stay in the camp that can still answer for what ships need verification built into every loop, from the guardrails that guide agents as they write to the checks that gate every pull request, because willpower and heroic review hours can't keep up with agents. Code is abundant. Confidence is scarce. Teams have to engineer it into every change. Listen to the full conversation with John Crickett on The Next Commit, and rethink how verification scales across your own development loops.

items.title: Why your software needs a CBOM
items.summary: Pick a service your team shipped this year. Which algorithm signs its tokens? What key size? Which line of code made that choice, and who wrote it? Most teams can't answer without a week of digging. For years that was fine. Cryptography worked, nobody touched it, and the libraries did the hard part. That is about to change. Quantum computers are expected to break RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, the public-key math behind TLS, code signing, single sign-on, and most of the internet. Governments have now set dates for moving off them. And every migration plan, in every guideline, starts with the same first step: find out what you have. That inventory has a name: a Cryptographic Bill of Materials, or CBOM. How does quantum computing threaten current encryption like RSA and TLS? In 2019, researchers estimated that breaking RSA-2048 would take a quantum computer with about 20 million physical qubits, running for about eight hours. In May 2025, Google's Craig Gidney cut that estimate to fewer than one million qubits , running for less than a week. In October 2026, Alice & Bob published an estimate of 22,593 physical qubits and about three days on its cat-qubit architecture, which assumes qubits that almost never suffer bit-flip errors. Those numbers fell mainly because of better algorithms and better error correction, and in Alice &Bob’s case a new type of qubit. These papers are estimates, not demonstrations. No quantum computer can do this today, and serious engineering problems remain. But the direction is hard to ignore. In the Global Risk Institute's Quantum Threat Timeline Report 2025, published in March 2026, 26 experts put the chance of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer within 10 years at 28% to 49%. You don't need to pick a date for "Q-Day" to see the problem. You only need to compare two timelines: how long until the threat is real, and how long your migration will take. What is a "harvest now, decrypt later" attack? The threat doesn't start when the first large quantum computer comes online. It started already. In a "harvest now, decrypt later" attack, an adversary records encrypted traffic today and stores it until it can be decrypted. NIST calls this one of the main reasons the transition is urgent. If your systems handle data that must stay confidential into the 2030s (health records, financial data, intellectual property, government information), then any of it sent today over quantum-vulnerable key exchange is already exposed. For that data, the deadline isn't 2030. It's the day it was sent. What are the NIST post-quantum cryptography deadlines and requirements? Governments started putting dates on post-quantum migration in 2022. Over the past two years, most major economies have set their own deadlines, and the US has pulled its most sensitive systems forward to 2030. NIST published its final transition report, IR 8547 , in October 2026. It deprecates quantum-vulnerable algorithms such as RSA and ECDSA after 2030, at every key size, and disallows them under NIST standards after 2035. The replacements are already standardized : ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). US federal agencies have had to submit a yearly inventory of the quantum-vulnerable cryptography in their most sensitive systems since May 2023, under OMB memo M-23-02. In June 2026, OMB memo M-26-15 went further: it asks agencies to keep a continuously updated inventory of all cryptographic assets that feeds a central cryptographic bill of materials. Executive Order 14412 now requires federal high-value assets and high-impact systems to use post-quantum key establishment by December 31, 2030 and post-quantum digital signatures by December 31, 2031. US national security systems follow the NSA's CNSA 2.0, which requires new acquisitions to be compliant from January 1, 2027, unless otherwise noted. The European Union's coordinated roadmap , published in June 2025, asks member states to complete first steps, including building cryptographic inventories, by the end of 2026, migrate high-risk use cases by the end of 2030, and migrate medium-risk use cases by the end of 2035, with low-risk systems moved as far as feasible. Similar timelines exist in the UK, Canada, Japan, and many other countries, and Australia's is earlier still: the end of 2030. The details differ. The first step doesn't. NIST's own announcement points beyond an organization's own systems to its "entire cryptographic supply chain." Regulators are also starting to name the CBOM itself. Executive Order 14412 directs CISA and NIST to publish minimum elements for a cryptographic bill of materials. OMB's M-26-15 asks agencies to feed their inventories into a central CBOM. The EU roadmap recommends a standard format such as CBOM, and Australia's signals directorate recommends CBOMs too. Why finding your cryptography is harder than it sounds If cryptography lived in one place, this would be easy. It doesn't. It's spread across thousands of files written over many years. It's in your own code, in the libraries you depend on, in configuration files, and in certificates loaded at runtime. The person who picked the cipher may have left years ago. And the code is changing faster than ever, now that AI coding agents write a growing share of it. Every new line can add a new place where cryptography is used. Searching the repository for "RSA" won't find all of it either. Look at this Java snippet: String transform = config.get("token.cipher"); // "RSA/ECB/PKCS1Padding" Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance(transform); cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, publicKey); The algorithm name never appears next to the call that uses it. It's also weak in a way that has nothing to do with quantum computers: RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding is a known risk today. A text search misses it. A developer survey misses it. A spreadsheet built last quarter is already out of date. This is why most teams can't answer the questions at the top of this post. It's not a skill problem. It's a visibility problem. What is a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM)? A Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) is a machine-readable inventory of the cryptography a piece of software uses, and where it uses it. The main open standard for CBOMs is CycloneDX, the open source bill of materials standard from OWASP that is also published as Ecma International standard ECMA-424 . CBOM support arrived in CycloneDX 1.6, and version 1.7 expanded it with a shared registry of algorithm families and elliptic curves, so different tools describe the same cryptography the same way. The OWASP Authoritative Guide to CBOM covers the full data model. A CycloneDX CBOM records four kinds of cryptographic assets: Algorithms , such as AES-256-GCM, RSA-2048, SHA-1, or ML-KEM-768, with properties like mode, key size, and security level. Protocols , such as TLS versions and the cipher suites they allow. Certificates , such as the X.509 certificates that prove identity and carry public keys. Related cryptographic material , such as keys, initialization vectors, nonces, and salts. A CBOM describes what kind of material is used, not the secret values. Each entry can also carry evidence: the file and line where the asset was found. Here is a simplified example for the snippet above: { "type": "cryptographic-asset", "name": "RSA-2048", "cryptoProperties": { "assetType": "algorithm", "algorithmProperties": { "algorithmFamily": "RSA-PKCS1", "primitive": "pke", "parameterSetIdentifier": "2048", "cryptoFunctions": ["encrypt"], "classicalSecurityLevel": 112, "nistQuantumSecurityLevel": 0 } }, "evidence": { "occurrences": [ { "location": "src/main/java/com/acme/payments/TokenEncryptor.java", "line": 42 } ] } } The last property tells the story. A NIST quantum security level of 0 means the algorithm meets none of NIST's post-quantum security categories: a large enough quantum computer could break it. And the evidence tells you exactly where to go to fix it. What is the difference between a CBOM and an SBOM? If you already produce a software bill of materials (SBOM), don’t assume it covers your cryptography. The two answer different questions. SBOM CBOM Answers What components does this software contain? What cryptography does this software use, and where? Lists Libraries, packages, versions, and licenses Algorithms, protocols, certificates, and key material Main use Vulnerability and license management Cryptographic risk and post-quantum migration Blind spot Shows that a crypto library is present, not how it is used Doesn't replace dependency and vulnerability tracking An SBOM might tell you that an application ships Bouncy Castle. Only a CBOM tells you that it uses RSA-2048 for encryption on line 42 of the payments service. Both use CycloneDX, so they fit side by side. What a CBOM lets you do An inventory isn't the goal. It's what makes every next step possible. Find what's at risk. Separate quantum-vulnerable algorithms like RSA and elliptic curves from those that are already safe, and from those that are broken today, like MD5 and SHA-1. Decide what to fix first. Rank work by how long the protected data must stay secret, how sensitive it is, and which regulations apply. Hand developers a real task. "Replace RSA somewhere in this service" is a project. "Change the call on line 42" is a ticket. Show progress with evidence. A standard file that updates as code changes is something auditors and regulators can read. A spreadsheet isn't. Build crypto-agility. Once you know where cryptography lives, swapping algorithms becomes a planned change instead of an emergency. One caution: a CBOM doesn't make you compliant on its own. It's evidence and a planning input. Compliance comes from the migration work it guides. What a good CBOM needs Not every inventory is equally useful. When you evaluate how to produce one, look for five things. Built from code, not surveys. The inventory should come from analyzing what the code actually does, including values that flow in from configuration. Consistent and repeatable. The same code should produce the same inventory every time, so changes in the CBOM reflect changes in the code. Explainable down to the line. Every entry should point to the file and line where it was found. If a developer can't find it, they can't fix it. Current with every change. Generate it in the pipeline, alongside the analysis that already runs on every branch, so it never goes stale between audits. In an open standard. Use CycloneDX so the CBOM works with your SBOM, your governance tools, and whatever comes next. Where Sonar stands Every line of code should be verified before it ships, whether a developer or an AI agent wrote it. Cryptography is part of that code. SonarQube already flags weak cryptography in code, including weak hashing, insecure cipher modes, and padding, short keys, and outdated TLS versions. With SonarQube Advanced Security , teams can also export an SBOM in CycloneDX or SPDX format to track the open source components they depend on. The next step is knowing exactly which cryptography that code uses, and where. That’s why we’re bringing CBOM generation to SonarQube, built from the same analysis that already runs on every branch. It will include cryptographic posture management: one view of the cryptography across all your projects, checked against a crypto baseline and post-quantum readiness policies, so you can see the gaps and track the migration. CBOM generation and cryptographic posture management are now in early access on SonarQube Cloud with a select group of customers. items.summary_html:
Pick a service your team shipped this year. Which algorithm signs its tokens? What key size? Which line of code made that choice, and who wrote it?

Most teams can't answer without a week of digging. For years that was fine. Cryptography worked, nobody touched it, and the libraries did the hard part.

That is about to change. Quantum computers are expected to break RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, the public-key math behind TLS, code signing, single sign-on, and most of the internet. Governments have now set dates for moving off them. And every migration plan, in every guideline, starts with the same first step: find out what you have.

That inventory has a name: a Cryptographic Bill of Materials, or CBOM.

How does quantum computing threaten current encryption like RSA and TLS?

In 2019, researchers estimated that breaking RSA-2048 would take a quantum computer with about 20 million physical qubits, running for about eight hours. In May 2025, Google's Craig Gidney cut that estimate to fewer than one million qubits, running for less than a week. In October 2026, Alice & Bob published an estimate of 22,593 physical qubits and about three days on its cat-qubit architecture, which assumes qubits that almost never suffer bit-flip errors.

Those numbers fell mainly because of better algorithms and better error correction, and in Alice &Bob’s case a new type of qubit. These papers are estimates, not demonstrations. No quantum computer can do this today, and serious engineering problems remain. But the direction is hard to ignore. In the Global Risk Institute's Quantum Threat Timeline Report 2025, published in March 2026, 26 experts put the chance of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer within 10 years at 28% to 49%.

You don't need to pick a date for "Q-Day" to see the problem. You only need to compare two timelines: how long until the threat is real, and how long your migration will take.

What is a "harvest now, decrypt later" attack?

The threat doesn't start when the first large quantum computer comes online. It started already.

In a "harvest now, decrypt later" attack, an adversary records encrypted traffic today and stores it until it can be decrypted. NIST calls this one of the main reasons the transition is urgent. If your systems handle data that must stay confidential into the 2030s (health records, financial data, intellectual property, government information), then any of it sent today over quantum-vulnerable key exchange is already exposed.

For that data, the deadline isn't 2030. It's the day it was sent.

What are the NIST post-quantum cryptography deadlines and requirements?

Governments started putting dates on post-quantum migration in 2022. Over the past two years, most major economies have set their own deadlines, and the US has pulled its most sensitive systems forward to 2030.

  • NIST published its final transition report, IR 8547, in October 2026. It deprecates quantum-vulnerable algorithms such as RSA and ECDSA after 2030, at every key size, and disallows them under NIST standards after 2035.
  • The replacements are already standardized: ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205).
  • US federal agencies have had to submit a yearly inventory of the quantum-vulnerable cryptography in their most sensitive systems since May 2023, under OMB memo M-23-02. In June 2026, OMB memo M-26-15 went further: it asks agencies to keep a continuously updated inventory of all cryptographic assets that feeds a central cryptographic bill of materials.  Executive Order 14412 now requires federal high-value assets and high-impact systems to use post-quantum key establishment by December 31, 2030 and post-quantum digital signatures by December 31, 2031.
  • US national security systems follow the NSA's CNSA 2.0, which requires new acquisitions to be compliant from January 1, 2027, unless otherwise noted.
  • The European Union's coordinated roadmap, published in June 2025, asks member states to complete first steps, including building cryptographic inventories, by the end of 2026, migrate high-risk use cases by the end of 2030, and migrate medium-risk use cases by the end of 2035, with low-risk systems moved as far as feasible.

Similar timelines exist in the UK, Canada, Japan, and many other countries, and Australia's is earlier still: the end of 2030. The details differ. The first step doesn't. NIST's own announcement points beyond an organization's own systems to its "entire cryptographic supply chain."

Regulators are also starting to name the CBOM itself. Executive Order 14412 directs CISA and NIST to publish minimum elements for a cryptographic bill of materials. OMB's M-26-15 asks agencies to feed their inventories into a central CBOM. The EU roadmap recommends a standard format such as CBOM, and Australia's signals directorate recommends CBOMs too.

Why finding your cryptography is harder than it sounds

If cryptography lived in one place, this would be easy. It doesn't.

It's spread across thousands of files written over many years. It's in your own code, in the libraries you depend on, in configuration files, and in certificates loaded at runtime. The person who picked the cipher may have left years ago. And the code is changing faster than ever, now that AI coding agents write a growing share of it. Every new line can add a new place where cryptography is used.

Searching the repository for "RSA" won't find all of it either. Look at this Java snippet:

String transform = config.get("token.cipher");  // "RSA/ECB/PKCS1Padding"
Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance(transform);
cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, publicKey);


The algorithm name never appears next to the call that uses it. It's also weak in a way that has nothing to do with quantum computers: RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding is a known risk today. A text search misses it. A developer survey misses it. A spreadsheet built last quarter is already out of date.

This is why most teams can't answer the questions at the top of this post. It's not a skill problem. It's a visibility problem.

What is a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM)?

A Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) is a machine-readable inventory of the cryptography a piece of software uses, and where it uses it.

The main open standard for CBOMs is CycloneDX, the open source bill of materials standard from OWASP that is also published as Ecma International standard ECMA-424. CBOM support arrived in CycloneDX 1.6, and version 1.7 expanded it with a shared registry of algorithm families and elliptic curves, so different tools describe the same cryptography the same way. The OWASP Authoritative Guide to CBOM covers the full data model.

A CycloneDX CBOM records four kinds of cryptographic assets:

  • Algorithms, such as AES-256-GCM, RSA-2048, SHA-1, or ML-KEM-768, with properties like mode, key size, and security level.
  • Protocols, such as TLS versions and the cipher suites they allow.
  • Certificates, such as the X.509 certificates that prove identity and carry public keys.
  • Related cryptographic material, such as keys, initialization vectors, nonces, and salts. A CBOM describes what kind of material is used, not the secret values.

Each entry can also carry evidence: the file and line where the asset was found. Here is a simplified example for the snippet above:

{
    "type": "cryptographic-asset",
    "name": "RSA-2048",
    "cryptoProperties": {
      "assetType": "algorithm",
      "algorithmProperties": {
        "algorithmFamily": "RSA-PKCS1",
        "primitive": "pke",
        "parameterSetIdentifier": "2048",
        "cryptoFunctions": ["encrypt"],
        "classicalSecurityLevel": 112,
        "nistQuantumSecurityLevel": 0
      }
    },
    "evidence": {
      "occurrences": [
        { "location": "src/main/java/com/acme/payments/TokenEncryptor.java", "line": 42 }
      ]
    }
  }


The last property tells the story. A NIST quantum security level of 0 means the algorithm meets none of NIST's post-quantum security categories: a large enough quantum computer could break it. And the evidence tells you exactly where to go to fix it.

What is the difference between a CBOM and an SBOM?

If you already produce a software bill of materials (SBOM), don’t assume it covers your cryptography. The two answer different questions.


SBOM

CBOM

Answers

What components does this software contain?

What cryptography does this software use, and where?

Lists

Libraries, packages, versions, and licenses

Algorithms, protocols, certificates, and key material

Main use

Vulnerability and license management

Cryptographic risk and post-quantum migration

Blind spot

Shows that a crypto library is present, not how it is used

Doesn't replace dependency and vulnerability tracking

An SBOM might tell you that an application ships Bouncy Castle. Only a CBOM tells you that it uses RSA-2048 for encryption on line 42 of the payments service. Both use CycloneDX, so they fit side by side.

What a CBOM lets you do

An inventory isn't the goal. It's what makes every next step possible.

  • Find what's at risk. Separate quantum-vulnerable algorithms like RSA and elliptic curves from those that are already safe, and from those that are broken today, like MD5 and SHA-1.
  • Decide what to fix first. Rank work by how long the protected data must stay secret, how sensitive it is, and which regulations apply.
  • Hand developers a real task. "Replace RSA somewhere in this service" is a project. "Change the call on line 42" is a ticket.
  • Show progress with evidence. A standard file that updates as code changes is something auditors and regulators can read. A spreadsheet isn't.
  • Build crypto-agility. Once you know where cryptography lives, swapping algorithms becomes a planned change instead of an emergency.

One caution: a CBOM doesn't make you compliant on its own. It's evidence and a planning input. Compliance comes from the migration work it guides.

What a good CBOM needs

Not every inventory is equally useful. When you evaluate how to produce one, look for five things.

  1. Built from code, not surveys. The inventory should come from analyzing what the code actually does, including values that flow in from configuration.
  2. Consistent and repeatable. The same code should produce the same inventory every time, so changes in the CBOM reflect changes in the code.
  3. Explainable down to the line. Every entry should point to the file and line where it was found. If a developer can't find it, they can't fix it.
  4. Current with every change. Generate it in the pipeline, alongside the analysis that already runs on every branch, so it never goes stale between audits.
  5. In an open standard. Use CycloneDX so the CBOM works with your SBOM, your governance tools, and whatever comes next.
Where Sonar stands

Every line of code should be verified before it ships, whether a developer or an AI agent wrote it. Cryptography is part of that code.

SonarQube already flags weak cryptography in code, including weak hashing, insecure cipher modes, and padding, short keys, and outdated TLS versions. With SonarQube Advanced Security, teams can also export an SBOM in CycloneDX or SPDX format to track the open source components they depend on.

The next step is knowing exactly which cryptography that code uses, and where. That’s why we’re bringing CBOM generation to SonarQube, built from the same analysis that already runs on every branch. It will include cryptographic posture management: one view of the cryptography across all your projects, checked against a crypto baseline and post-quantum readiness policies, so you can see the gaps and track the migration.

CBOM generation and cryptographic posture management are now in early access on SonarQube Cloud with a select group of customers. If you’d like to join, contact us for a demo and we’ll show you what it finds in your code.

The first federal deadlines are about four years away, and replacing cryptography across a large codebase takes years. Start the inventory now, while you still have time to plan the work instead of rushing it.

items.title: Hackers Use Fake Shipment ZIP Files and DLL Side-Loading to Deploy PureLogs and PureRAT Malware
items.summary: Hackers are using a shipment-themed ZIP archive to launch a Windows malware chain that combines a legitimate signed application, DLL side-loading, and hidden Python code. The attack disguises its components as shipping material, images, documents, and a browser updater before running a payload linked to PureLogs and PureRAT infrastructure. The case shows why a trusted digital signature does not make an entire software package safe. Here, the genuine application acts as the starting point, while a malicious library beside it drives execution. Similar business email malware campaigns have used delivery complaints and download lures to distribute these malware families, although the supplied findings do not establish a connection between those operations. Researchers from Unit 42, Shazan Khaja and Muhammet Algan, documented the activity in research dated November 16, 2026. They observed the infection chain on October 21 after a user downloaded the shipment-themed archive. Their findings trace execution from the extracted files to a decoded Windows payload communicating with infrastructure attributed to PureLogs and PureRAT campaigns. Hackers Use Fake Shipment ZIP Files and DLL Side-Loading Inside the archive, attackers placed a legitimate, validly signed, 32-bit Kingsoft PDF executable renamed to match the shipment lure. A malicious DLL sat alongside it. When the user launched the executable, Windows loaded that nearby library, handing control to attacker-supplied code without requiring changes to the signed program itself. The sequence unfolded within seconds. Windows Explorer wrote the DLL to disk at 03:02:53 UTC, consistent with archive extraction. The renamed application started at 03:03:06 and loaded the malicious library roughly one second later. Archive extraction for the next stage began at 03:03:09, showing how quickly execution followed the user’s action. This approach resembles other trusted application side-loading attacks in which genuine software loads a hostile neighboring library. However, the Kingsoft executable’s signature and hash are not evidence of infection on their own. Investigators need to examine its location, loaded libraries, and child processes rather than treating every copy as malicious. A downloaded ZIP archive disguised as a report uses DLL side-loading to decode and run a malicious Python script for #PureLogs / #PureRAT . Details at https://t.co/asDQbpBRpH pic.twitter.com/1pZw87RdpJ — Unit 42 (@Unit42_Intel) November 16, 2026 The DLL launched a command sequence that opened a decoy PDF while preparing the hidden payload. A signed WinRAR command-line program, disguised with an image extension, extracted a password-protected archive into the public user directory. The extracted package contained a Python runtime renamed to resemble Microsoft’s Edge updater. Several internal filenames used Korean-language phrases about chicken deliveries and refrigerator stock, unrelated to the shipment story. These strings help describe the package, but they do not establish the attackers’ identity or the victims’ location. The supplied research does not identify a threat actor or explain how the download link reached the user. Disguised Python Loader Decodes the Final Payload The renamed Python interpreter executed a one-line command that read another apparent PDF as raw bytes. Instead of displaying a document, it applied a repeating XOR key to recover Python code and passed that result to exec() . The document extension therefore concealed an encoded script rather than readable shipment information. The recovered script used randomized names and arithmetic expressions involving XOR, shifts, and addition to obscure its contents. It then decoded a large Base64 blob and applied another repeating XOR operation, producing a Windows Portable Executable file with an MZ header. These layers separated the visible lure from the final executable payload. Earlier reporting on Python DLL side-loading techniques provides context for this combination of trusted software and script execution. In this case, the decoded payload contacted the infrastructure listed below over TLSv1 on port 443. Unit 42’s findings associate that infrastructure with PureLogs and PureRAT campaigns, rather than independently proving that both families executed on the observed endpoint. For defenders, the strongest leads are behavioral: a signed application running from Downloads and loading a neighboring DLL, followed by command-shell activity, disguised archive extraction, and Python execution from a public directory. A Python command that decodes an apparent document and immediately executes its contents is another important investigation lead. items.title: ARTEX Detection: Hunting the AI Pentest Framework Turned Attack Platform
items.summary: Offensive AI is no longer a slide in a threat-landscape deck. It is sitting on attacker servers, wired to multiple LLM APIs, and probing production APIs at machine speed. ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework developed in China, is the clearest example so far: a red-team tool that threat actors have adopted to automate reconnaissance, vulnerability probing, and exploitation end to end. For SOC analysts and detection engineers, ARTEX detection is a new kind of problem. There is no single malware family to fingerprint. Instead, you face an LLM-driven operator that adapts payloads, rotates techniques, and generates traffic volumes no human pentester could. This article walks through the ARTEX analysis available so far, the behaviors worth alerting on, and how to detect ARTEX across web, endpoint, and Linux telemetry. Get Started For Free ARTEX Analysis ARTEX went public on GitHub as Autumn-27/ARTEX on July 26, 2026, under AGPL-3.0. It is written in Go, runs a Next.js console on PostgreSQL, and sits on top of ScopeSentry, the same author’s asset-discovery platform ( Censys ). The architecture explains the telemetry you will see. A Planner agent turns an operator goal, such as “gain admin panel access,” into attack intents. Worker agents claim those intents, run tools like nmap, and write results back into an asset graph and an exploration graph. The loop repeats until the goal is met, using Anthropic, OpenAI, or any OpenAI-compatible model endpoint. That loop is fast. Mandiant and GTIG recorded 27 events within 23 seconds, plus automated error correction used to land webshells, as covered in our report on how ARTEX leads a new wave of agentic offensive frameworks alongside PentAGI and CAIRN. The author disowned malicious use on October 8 and took the repository down, but forks and rebrands such as ScopeWeaver still circulate. As of early November, Censys counted 1,465 exposed ARTEX consoles, most on default port 8787. Reported Campaign What ARTEX affects Nov 9, 2026 Storm-3358 targets financial organizations SSRF and anonymous file uploads, then WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs plus cloud identity abuse Oct 27, 2026 Storm-0940 hits IT and software vendors Okta, Entra ID, and Cognito auth probing; account recovery abuse; IP and user-agent rotation Oct 21, 2026 ARTEX found on servers attacking Japanese companies API probing and WAF evasion in Japan and South Korea, driven by DeepSeek, Zhipu AI, and xAI models Oct 21, 2026 Storm-0940 ConnectWise supply-chain compromise (Microsoft) Sign-ins against 2,250+ tenants, peaking at 2,900 attempts per minute Oct 7, 2026 South Korean banks (CrowdStrike) A broker-facing loan service and an employee mobile system breached, data exfiltrated Detect ARTEX Detect ARTEX by behavior, not by name. Binaries get renamed and consoles get rebranded, but the explore-decide-execute loop leaves volumetric and sequential fingerprints across five log sources. Web server: 40x response spikes from a single IP, path traversal, file inclusion, and OS command injection patterns, and scripted files dropped into web directories. Wiz saw a fetch of /swagger/?format=openapi followed immediately by a random nonexistent URI, a clean mapping signature. Identity: failed-login bursts and access-denied spikes on Okta, Entra ID, and Cognito, password spraying, and abuse of account recovery workflows. Endpoint and Linux: web service accounts spawning shells, SSH known_hosts discovery, nmap, curl, or wget from unexpected parents, and netcat paired with RAT binaries. Cloud: an Azure write-then-delete of a throwaway blob, and AWS EC2 calls with –dry-run that test IAM permissions without changing state. Network: HTTP C2 to direct IPs on uncommon ports, and egress to LLM resellers or self-hosted proxies such as CLIProxyAPI and New API. ARTEX IOCs worth loading now include the ARTEX host 38.244.50[.]120 and LLM reseller xcai[.]pro (CrowdStrike), plus Storm-0940 infrastructure 144.172.64[.]60, .99, and .128 (Microsoft). Treat them as perishable: Censys watched 10 attacker open directories close and 15 new ones appear in two days. For ARTEX mitigation, rate-limit by account, session, and API key rather than IP alone, enforce API authorization server-side, and issue short-lived credentials. Decoys and tarpits work unusually well here, because an autonomous agent will happily burn its token budget on fake assets. Every Active Threats report linked above ships ready-to-deploy Sigma and AI rules plus simulation scripts, so you can validate coverage before ARTEX tests it for you. PHP2shell ARTEX PHP2Shell is the bug class an agentic framework loves most: pre-auth, widespread, and with public PoCs. CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are RCE chains in PHP core’s session.upload_progress, rated CVSS v4 9.2 and affecting PHP 5.4.0 through 8.5.11. PHP shipped fixes on October 21, 2026, a day early after the CVE IDs leaked ( Arctic Wolf ). The ARTEX PoC angle is concrete. An issue on an ARTEX fork proposed a php2shell-check skill that vendors three public verification scripts from the php2shell-poc research repo. Once a check like that exists as a skill, the Planner can queue it as just another intent against every PHP asset in the graph. The exposure is huge. Qualys counted 167 million PHP installations, 71% of them on end-of-life versions that will never get a vendor patch ( Qualys ). Amazon caught an exploitation attempt in its MadPot honeypots on October 17, four days before disclosure. To hunt PHP2Shell in ARTEX-style traffic, look for: Multipart POSTs carrying a PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field with attacker-chosen session IDs Follow-up file inclusion requests pointing at sess_ files in PHP session directories Inert PHP canaries and unique output markers, which scanners use to confirm evaluation PHP worker processes spawning shells, curl, or wget Patch first, upgrade end-of-life branches, and disable upload progress tracking where applications do not need it. FAQ What is ARTEX and how does it work? An open-source, LLM-driven pentest framework. Planner and Worker agents loop through recon, probing, and exploitation toward an operator-defined goal. When was ARTEX first discovered? It was released July 26, 2026. CrowdStrike first reported malicious use on October 7, 2026. What is the impact of ARTEX on systems? Data theft, RAT deployment, cloud identity takeover, and supply-chain compromise across finance, IT, and software vendors. Can ARTEX still affect me in 2026? Yes. Forks and rebrands remain active, and Censys still tracks 1,400+ exposed consoles. How can I protect myself from ARTEX? Patch fast (PHP2Shell first), rate-limit by identity, harden IdP flows, and deploy decoys. How can I detect ARTEX? Correlate volumetric web, identity, and cloud anomalies. Full details for ARTEX rules live in the SOC Prime reports linked above.

ARTEX went public on GitHub as Autumn-27/ARTEX on July 26, 2026, under AGPL-3.0. It is written in Go, runs a Next.js console on PostgreSQL, and sits on top of ScopeSentry, the same author’s asset-discovery platform (Censys).

The architecture explains the telemetry you will see. A Planner agent turns an operator goal, such as “gain admin panel access,” into attack intents. Worker agents claim those intents, run tools like nmap, and write results back into an asset graph and an exploration graph. The loop repeats until the goal is met, using Anthropic, OpenAI, or any OpenAI-compatible model endpoint.

That loop is fast. Mandiant and GTIG recorded 27 events within 23 seconds, plus automated error correction used to land webshells, as covered in our report on how ARTEX leads a new wave of agentic offensive frameworks alongside PentAGI and CAIRN.

The author disowned malicious use on October 8 and took the repository down, but forks and rebrands such as ScopeWeaver still circulate. As of early November, Censys counted 1,465 exposed ARTEX consoles, most on default port 8787.

ReportedCampaignWhat ARTEX affectsNov 9, 2026Storm-3358 targets financial organizationsSSRF and anonymous file uploads, then WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs plus cloud identity abuseOct 27, 2026Storm-0940 hits IT and software vendorsOkta, Entra ID, and Cognito auth probing; account recovery abuse; IP and user-agent rotationOct 21, 2026ARTEX found on servers attacking Japanese companiesAPI probing and WAF evasion in Japan and South Korea, driven by DeepSeek, Zhipu AI, and xAI modelsOct 21, 2026Storm-0940 ConnectWise supply-chain compromise (Microsoft)Sign-ins against 2,250+ tenants, peaking at 2,900 attempts per minuteOct 7, 2026South Korean banks (CrowdStrike)A broker-facing loan service and an employee mobile system breached, data exfiltrated Detect ARTEX

Detect ARTEX by behavior, not by name. Binaries get renamed and consoles get rebranded, but the explore-decide-execute loop leaves volumetric and sequential fingerprints across five log sources.

  • Web server: 40x response spikes from a single IP, path traversal, file inclusion, and OS command injection patterns, and scripted files dropped into web directories. Wiz saw a fetch of /swagger/?format=openapi followed immediately by a random nonexistent URI, a clean mapping signature.
  • Identity: failed-login bursts and access-denied spikes on Okta, Entra ID, and Cognito, password spraying, and abuse of account recovery workflows.
  • Endpoint and Linux: web service accounts spawning shells, SSH known_hosts discovery, nmap, curl, or wget from unexpected parents, and netcat paired with RAT binaries.
  • Cloud: an Azure write-then-delete of a throwaway blob, and AWS EC2 calls with –dry-run that test IAM permissions without changing state.
  • Network: HTTP C2 to direct IPs on uncommon ports, and egress to LLM resellers or self-hosted proxies such as CLIProxyAPI and New API.

ARTEX IOCs worth loading now include the ARTEX host 38.244.50[.]120 and LLM reseller xcai[.]pro (CrowdStrike), plus Storm-0940 infrastructure 144.172.64[.]60, .99, and .128 (Microsoft). Treat them as perishable: Censys watched 10 attacker open directories close and 15 new ones appear in two days.

For ARTEX mitigation, rate-limit by account, session, and API key rather than IP alone, enforce API authorization server-side, and issue short-lived credentials. Decoys and tarpits work unusually well here, because an autonomous agent will happily burn its token budget on fake assets. Every Active Threats report linked above ships ready-to-deploy Sigma and AI rules plus simulation scripts, so you can validate coverage before ARTEX tests it for you.

PHP2shell ARTEX

PHP2Shell is the bug class an agentic framework loves most: pre-auth, widespread, and with public PoCs. CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are RCE chains in PHP core’s session.upload_progress, rated CVSS v4 9.2 and affecting PHP 5.4.0 through 8.5.11. PHP shipped fixes on October 21, 2026, a day early after the CVE IDs leaked (Arctic Wolf).

The ARTEX PoC angle is concrete. An issue on an ARTEX fork proposed a php2shell-check skill that vendors three public verification scripts from the php2shell-poc research repo. Once a check like that exists as a skill, the Planner can queue it as just another intent against every PHP asset in the graph.

The exposure is huge. Qualys counted 167 million PHP installations, 71% of them on end-of-life versions that will never get a vendor patch (Qualys). Amazon caught an exploitation attempt in its MadPot honeypots on October 17, four days before disclosure.

To hunt PHP2Shell in ARTEX-style traffic, look for:

  • Multipart POSTs carrying a PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field with attacker-chosen session IDs
  • Follow-up file inclusion requests pointing at sess_ files in PHP session directories
  • Inert PHP canaries and unique output markers, which scanners use to confirm evaluation
  • PHP worker processes spawning shells, curl, or wget

Patch first, upgrade end-of-life branches, and disable upload progress tracking where applications do not need it.

FAQ

What is ARTEX and how does it work?

An open-source, LLM-driven pentest framework. Planner and Worker agents loop through recon, probing, and exploitation toward an operator-defined goal.

When was ARTEX first discovered?

It was released July 26, 2026. CrowdStrike first reported malicious use on October 7, 2026.

What is the impact of ARTEX on systems?

Data theft, RAT deployment, cloud identity takeover, and supply-chain compromise across finance, IT, and software vendors.

Can ARTEX still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Forks and rebrands remain active, and Censys still tracks 1,400+ exposed consoles.

How can I protect myself from ARTEX?

Patch fast (PHP2Shell first), rate-limit by identity, harden IdP flows, and deploy decoys.

How can I detect ARTEX?

Correlate volumetric web, identity, and cloud anomalies. Full details for ARTEX rules live in the SOC Prime reports linked above.

items.title: EU Accuses Temu of Failing to Stop Illegal Products, Citing Weak Security and Moderation Controls
items.summary: The European Commission has preliminarily found Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA), citing weak product checks, poor content moderation, and ineffective penalties against sellers. Announced on November 17, 2026, the findings question whether the marketplace takes effective steps to stop illegal products from reaching European buyers. The case concerns Article 35, which requires platforms to put concrete measures in place to reduce identified risks. These are preliminary findings, not a final ruling. Although the concerns involve platform security controls, the announcement does not describe a data breach, malware attack, or confirmed compromise of Temu’s systems. Investigators found that Temu requests product test reports for only a very small share of listings. Even when sellers must submit these reports, the company often does not check them. This leaves a gap between collecting safety documents and confirming that goods actually meet European Union safety requirements. Temu Breaching Digital Services Act Temu classifies toys, electronics, and cosmetics as high risk, but allegedly does not give them priority during physical inspections. The Commission also found that the company often failed to follow up on spot check results. Inspection levels did not increase as the number of product listings grew. The findings show why risk controls must grow alongside online services. Related Cybersecurity News coverage of EU platform oversight explains how DSA supervision extends to major digital services. For Temu, the immediate question is whether its checks can identify unsafe goods, rather than simply process an expanding volume of listings. According to the Commission, Temu’s moderation focuses mainly on listing information and compliance with its own terms, rather than product safety. Its system for comparing listings with previously flagged goods also gives insufficient attention to unsafe products. Separately, an approved corrective action plan requires Temu to examine moderation limits and possible seller manipulation. Human review presents another weakness. The number of moderators has not kept pace with listing growth, the Commission said. Taken together, these findings describe gaps across document checks, listing comparisons, physical inspections, and staff review. A listing that meets website rules does not necessarily prove the product itself is safe. The Commission also questioned penalties aimed at individual stores instead of the traders behind them. One trader can operate several stores, allowing sales to continue elsewhere after a closure. Investigators found that sellers could commit numerous serious violations, including failed product safety checks, before Temu suspended any of their stores. Temu can inspect the investigation file and respond in writing. The European Board for Digital Services will also be consulted. If confirmed, the findings could bring corrective orders and a fine reaching 6% of worldwide annual turnover. This differs from the DMA framework covered in Cybersecurity News’ Google enforcement report . The new case follows a €200 million fine in May 2026 over inadequate risk assessment. Approval of Temu’s October action plan addressed that earlier breach, not the latest findings. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .
