items.title: EU Sanctions 30 People and Two Entities Over Russian Disinformation and Cyberattacks
items.summary: On Monday, the Council of the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities for Russian information manipulation and malicious cyber activity. The influence side hits the Social Design Agency, the Moscow political-technology firm behind years of fake-news operations. The cyber side lists NoName057(16), the pro-Russian group that has spent four years knocking European websites offline with DDoS attacks. A sanctions listing won't take down a botnet, and nobody in Brussels expects it to. What it changes is the legal exposure for every European company that might pay, host, employ or do business with anyone on the list. It also puts a propaganda shop and a DDoS crew in the same announcement, which tells defenders how the EU now sees them - two arms of one hybrid campaign. What the Council announced The Council's announcement covers two separate legal regimes: Russia's destabilizing activities regime , created Oct. 8, 2024, adds the Social Design Agency, 24 of its staff and six pro-Kremlin commentators. It now lists 111 individuals and 21 entities. The EU's diplomatic service calls this the largest EU sanctions package targeting foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) to date. The EU's horizontal cyber sanctions regime , in force since 2019, adds NoName057(16). It now lists 27 individuals and 12 entities. The effects are the standard ones. Assets in the EU are frozen, EU citizens and companies may not make funds available to anyone listed, directly or indirectly, and listed individuals can't enter or transit the EU. The listings came on the same day as a separate package of 113 names aimed at Russia's war financing. Who's on the list The Social Design Agency runs the Doppelgänger campaign, which clones real news sites to spread fake stories. It has been under EU sanctions over the war in Ukraine since 2023. This listing moves it under the regime aimed at operations against the EU itself. The Council alleges that the agency's major operations need sign-off from Sergey Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff in Russia's presidential administration, and accuses it of cloning news sites, building Wikipedia-style platforms and staging physical provocations around the 2024 European Parliament elections. The 24 staff listed go well beyond management. Alongside Andrey Perla, named as the agency's "chief ideologue," the list includes caricaturists, monitors, a system administrator and the editor of "Pulse," an internal network of Telegram channels. Britain had already sanctioned 22 of them. The six commentators include RT correspondent Chay Bowes, accused of amplifying the Storm-1516 operation, and military blogger Yurii Podoliaka, who the EU says raised more than 1 billion rubles for Russian forces. NoName057(16) emerged in March 2022. The Council says it hit energy, finance, transport, and water sites with DDoS attacks, along with political parties and candidates during elections. Europol's Operation Eastwood took more than 100 of its servers offline in July 2025, and the group kept going. The target is the supply chain, not the operators The skeptical read is easy. A caricaturist in Moscow probably holds nothing in the EU worth freezing, and a DDoS crew that survived a 12-country police operation won't fold over an asset freeze. But influence and DDoS operations run on Western infrastructure. Domains, hosting, ad networks, payment rails, crypto exchanges and freelancers. Doppelgänger needed lookalike domains on Western registrars, which is why the U.S. Justice Department seized a batch of them in 2024. NoName057(16) paid its volunteers in cryptocurrency, Europol said. The "directly or indirectly" clause pushes the enforcement burden onto every EU company in those chains. The regime choice matters too. The destabilization regime gives Brussels extra tools for later, including bans on transactions involving physical infrastructure such as servers and network equipment. That is a lever aimed squarely at hosting providers. The pairing is the other signal. The Council's own descriptions put SDA provocations around elections next to NoName057(16) DDoS attacks on parties and candidates during elections. When a party's website goes down on election week, the outage is the smaller part of the attack. The headline it creates is the point. Who's affected Two groups of European organizations should read the list closely. The first is anyone who could end up providing money or services to a listed party, which includes banks, payment processors, crypto exchanges, hosting and cloud providers, domain registrars, ad networks, and PR or media firms that hire freelance writers and designers. Sanctions screening also has to cover entities owned or controlled by a listed person, even if they aren't named. The second is NoName057(16)'s target list, which includes government portals, energy, finance, transport and water operators, and political parties. For them, the sanctions change nothing operationally. The DDoS traffic will keep coming. Plan of action Refresh screening today. Pull the new names from the Official Journal acts (Council Implementing Regulations 2026/2558 and 2026/2550) into your sanctions screening, and rescreen vendors, freelancers and customers, not just payment counterparties. Hosting providers and registrars: tighten customer checks. Doppelgängers depend on lookalike domains and cheap hosting. Make sure abuse reports about cloned news sites reach someone who can act on them quickly. Watch for clones of your own brand. If you run a news outlet, a public body or a well-known consumer brand, monitor for lookalike domains and copied pages. Doppelgängers' method is to wear a trusted name. Plan for election-week DDoS. If you're a party, a public body or critical infrastructure, test DDoS protection on public sites before the next vote. NoName057(16) announces its targets on Telegram, so put its channels in your threat feeds. Prepare the message as well as the mitigation. A short holding statement that explains the outage and says whether any data was affected takes away most of the headline an attacker wanted. What we're watching NoName057(16) is changing tactics. U.S. prosecutors charged an alleged member in September, and researchers recently tied the group to a campaign that published personal details of senior European officials on the dark web, with crypto rewards offered for more. Doxxing aimed at officials and their families is a harder problem than a website outage. Spotting that exposure early matters. Cyble monitors dark web forums, leak sites, and Telegram channels for leaked credentials and personal data tied to your executives and staff, so your team can respond before the information is used against them. Request a demo to see how it works. The other question is whether Brussels uses the infrastructure-transaction bans the destabilization regime allows. If it does, hosting and network providers will feel these listings far more than the people named in them. Key takeaways On Nov. 16, 2026, the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities: the Social Design Agency with 24 staff and six commentators under its Russia destabilization regime, and NoName057(16) under its cyber regime. The operators will barely feel it. The burden falls on EU banks, hosting providers, registrars, ad networks, and crypto platforms, which may not deal with anyone listed, directly or indirectly. Listing a propaganda firm and a DDoS crew together reflects one playbook: election-period disruption built for headlines. Update screening lists now, monitor for clones of your brand, and plan DDoS defense and messaging before the next election. It also puts a propaganda shop and a DDoS crew in the same announcement, which tells defenders how the EU now sees them - two arms of one hybrid campaign.

The six commentators include RT correspondent Chay Bowes, accused of amplifying the Storm-1516 operation, and military blogger Yurii Podoliaka, who the EU says raised more than 1 billion rubles for Russian forces. 

NoName057(16) emerged in March 2022. The Council says it hit energy, finance, transport, and water sites with DDoS attacks, along with political parties and candidates during elections. Europol's Operation Eastwood took more than 100 of its servers offline in July 2025, and the group kept going.

The skeptical read is easy. A caricaturist in Moscow probably holds nothing in the EU worth freezing, and a DDoS crew that survived a 12-country police operation won't fold over an asset freeze. 

But influence and DDoS operations run on Western infrastructure. Domains, hosting, ad networks, payment rails, crypto exchanges and freelancers. Doppelgänger needed lookalike domains on Western registrars, which is why the U.S. Justice Department seized a batch of them in 2024.   1. Watch for clones of your own brand. If you run a news outlet, a public body or a well-known consumer brand, monitor for lookalike domains and copied pages. Doppelgängers' method is to wear a trusted name.

  • The operators will barely feel it. The burden falls on EU banks, hosting providers, registrars, ad networks, and crypto platforms, which may not deal with anyone listed, directly or indirectly.

items.title: Microsoft Windows 11 Secretly Tracks Which AI Coding Agents Developers Use Through Telemetry
items.summary: Windows 11 has a built-in component that notes which AI coding agents and developer tools you run. It sends that data to Microsoft if optional diagnostic data is on. Security researcher Xusheng Li, who works on Binary Ninja, shared the first finding on X on November 16, 2026. He then published a full technical write-up . Windows 11 AI Agent Tracking Li asked an AI helper to look through recent Windows files for undocumented features. It flagged a list of names inside MissionControlAggregator.dll, including codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, and cursor.exe. The same list held common tools like python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, and code.exe. Li opened the file in Binary Ninja and found that the names were used in simple comparisons. A feature flag called CLICodingAgentUsage guards the new checks. Binary Ninja Agent Strings (Image Source: Xusheng) The DLL does not scan your running programs. It listens to events Windows already creates, such as KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary. It also reads WSL launch events. A normal Windows copy of codex.exe can trigger a match, so the check is not limited to Linux tools. When a name matches, the component sets a bit in its saved state. Later, it sends a report called Segments.SubCohorts through Event Tracing for Windows . The report holds only yes-or-no flags, not runtime, focus time, or prompt text. Even so, a list of the AI tools a developer uses is private information. Li checked a Windows 11 ARM64 virtual machine on build 26200.9974. The feature was already on, and the DiagTrack telemetry service was running. DiagTrack started AggregatorHost.exe, which loaded the DLL. To test it, he copied cmd.exe and renamed it codex.exe. The name alone was enough to set the Codex bit. A report then showed CliAgentSubCohorts with a value of 4. A copy renamed gcc.exe set a separate developer-tool bit. Li did not stop at the local event, because local logs alone prove nothing. He found that a DiagTrack listener was subscribed to the report. The report also appeared in DiagTrack’s upload queue, marked as not required. That means Microsoft treats it as optional diagnostic data. On a clean US install of Windows 11 Home, optional data was on by default, and AllowTelemetry was set to 3. A baseline VM from the public ISO had the coding-agent feature off. So this is not proven to be active on every Windows PC. Windows Optional Diagnostic Settings (Image Source: Xusheng) Open Settings, then Privacy & security, then Diagnostics & feedback. Turn off Send optional diagnostic data. Microsoft’s own diagnostics and privacy guide says your device stays secure and works normally with only required data. It also says optional data can include device activity, which fits this case. Managed work PCs may hide this setting, so IT teams should check their own policies. AI coding tools already draw attention from bad actors. Cyber Security News recently reported that info-stealing malware now targets Claude, Cursor, and Codex data saved on developer machines. It also covered new threats against AI coding tools that steal credentials. A record of who uses which agent is not a secret key, but it shows where valuable code and tokens may sit. Microsoft has not yet explained why it collects this data. It may be for product planning, since Windows is adding more agent features. Until the company speaks, developers should check their diagnostic settings, read Li’s evidence, and decide what they are comfortable sharing. That means Microsoft treats it as optional diagnostic data. On a clean US install of Windows 11 Home, optional data was on by default, and AllowTelemetry was set to 3. A baseline VM from the public ISO had the coding-agent feature off. So this is not proven to be active on every Windows PC.

Windows Optional Diagnostic Settings (Image Source: Xusheng)

Open Settings, then Privacy & security, then Diagnostics & feedback. Turn off Send optional diagnostic data. Microsoft’s own diagnostics and privacy guide says your device stays secure and works normally with only required data.

It also says optional data can include device activity, which fits this case. Managed work PCs may hide this setting, so IT teams should check their own policies.

AI coding tools already draw attention from bad actors. Cyber Security News recently reported that info-stealing malware now targets Claude, Cursor, and Codex data saved on developer machines.

It also covered new threats against AI coding tools that steal credentials. A record of who uses which agent is not a secret key, but it shows where valuable code and tokens may sit.

Microsoft has not yet explained why it collects this data. It may be for product planning, since Windows is adding more agent features.

Until the company speaks, developers should check their diagnostic settings, read Li’s evidence, and decide what they are comfortable sharing.

items.title: CVE-2026-99288: NoisyTCP Linux Kernel Flaw Enables Remote Server Crashes
items.summary: A newly disclosed Linux kernel vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP , can enable an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash vulnerable Linux systems by sending specially crafted TCP traffic to an exposed listening service. The issue resides in the kernel TCP networking subsystem and can affect common server workloads such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH without requiring authentication or an unusual application configuration. The vulnerability remained in the Linux kernel for roughly 11 years after being introduced in October 2015. Red Hat rates the issue Important with a CVSS 3.1 score of 7.5 , noting that successful exploitation can cause an operating-system-level denial of service. Current public research does not demonstrate arbitrary code execution as a reliable attack outcome. The risk is particularly relevant to organizations operating internet-facing Linux infrastructure because exploitation occurs before authentication. If a vulnerable service running inside a container is targeted, the resulting kernel panic can affect the underlying host rather than only the individual container, potentially disrupting multiple workloads simultaneously. Organizations can strengthen their defenses against emerging vulnerability exploitation with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, helping security teams operationalize threat intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Detect CVE-2026-99288 by monitoring suspicious TCP behavior preceding kernel instability, unexpected host reboots, and Linux kernel panic events on externally reachable systems. Since NoisyTCP operates at the kernel networking layer, defenders should correlate host-level telemetry with network activity instead of relying exclusively on application logs. Contact Sales CVE-2026-99288 analysis CVE-2026-99288 affects the Linux kernel’s TCP established-socket lookup logic. TCP established ehash lookups operate without traditional locking, while the relevant socket caches use SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU, which allows memory to be reused before an RCU reader holding the previous address has completed its operation. After finding a matching tuple, functions such as __inet_lookup_established() and __inet6_lookup_established() obtain a reference and repeat the tuple validation. The vulnerable implementation does not verify whether the replacement object is already hashed. If memory is reused for another socket with the same tuple, a stale lookup can therefore acquire a reference to the new object before it is fully integrated into the expected socket state. One demonstrated attack path involves the reuse of a request socket through SYN cookies. While one receive context retains a stale reference to an existing request socket, another context can free that object and allocate a new SYN cookie request at the same slab address. Because the tuple remains the same, the stale lookup can acquire a reference to the replacement object and pass the tuple check. The newly created request socket, however, has not yet been hashed and has a NULL rsk_listener. When the Linux TCP receive path later attempts to use the listener, it dereferences the NULL pointer. This results in a kernel panic and causes the operating system to crash. Successful exploitation requires the stale lookup and socket reuse to occur concurrently in separate receive contexts. Researchers found that this can be achieved by exploiting differences in receive hashing between IPv4 fragments and ordinary TCP packets. Consequently, systems with two or more RX queues, or environments where Receive Packet Steering distributes traffic across multiple CPUs, can provide the concurrency necessary to trigger the race. The CVE-2026-99288 PoC demonstrates that exploitation time depends heavily on the target environment. Against Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running with default configurations on QEMU/KVM virtual machines, the researcher was able to reproduce the crash in approximately five seconds to two minutes. By comparison, triggering the issue on a quiet bare-metal Nginx server with eight RX queues took roughly 14 hours even with race timing tuned for the specific system. Virtualization can make the race more practical because vCPU preemption introduces additional scheduling variance. Nevertheless, the underlying weakness is not limited to virtual machines or a specific server application. Any directly reachable vulnerable Linux host exposing a TCP listener can potentially be targeted when the required concurrency conditions exist. The vulnerability originated in Linux kernel commit 079096f103fa, introduced on October 3, 2015 with Linux 4.4. The upstream correction, commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, was merged on November 3, 2026. The fix causes established socket lookups to reject unhashed objects, release the acquired reference, and restart the lookup instead of continuing with an unsafe reused socket. The Linux kernel CVE team lists 6.12.117, 6.18.63, and 7.3.4 among the stable kernel versions containing the correction. However, distribution vendors can backport patches independently, so administrators should rely on the advisory for their specific Linux distribution rather than assume that a version number alone determines exposure. For CVE-2026-99288 detection, security teams should correlate Linux kernel logs, system availability telemetry, and network activity. Potential indicators include kernel NULL pointer dereference events, kernel panics associated with tcp_v4_rcv, unexplained server reboots, and unusual bursts of TCP traffic immediately preceding system failure. Traditional CVE-2026-99288 IOCs such as malicious file hashes, payload URLs, or attacker-controlled domains are less relevant because exploitation can occur entirely through network traffic without dropping malware on the target. Defenders should therefore prioritize behavioral evidence, crash telemetry, TCP connection patterns, fragmentation activity, SYN traffic, and repeated host resets. As of November 17, 2026, there is no confirmed evidence that the vulnerability is being actively exploited in real-world attacks. Public research demonstrates remote denial of service, while Red Hat explicitly states that exploitation does not provide data modification or arbitrary code execution. Security teams seeking additional details for CVE-2026-99288 should consult the Linux kernel CVE announcement, vendor-specific advisories, and the original NoisyTCP disclosure because fixed package versions and backport availability can vary significantly across Linux distributions. CVE-2026-99288 Mitigation The most effective remediation is to install an updated kernel containing the upstream correction or the corresponding security backport supplied by the Linux distribution vendor. The Linux kernel CVE team recommends updating to the latest stable kernel rather than cherry-picking an individual change whenever possible. For CVE-2026-99288 mitigation, organizations should first inventory externally reachable Linux servers and identify systems exposing TCP services such as Nginx, Apache, SSH, proxies, gateways, and other network-facing workloads. Virtual machines with multiple RX queues, environments using RPS, and hosts supporting multiple critical containers should receive particularly high patching priority. Administrators should verify their running kernel rather than only checking whether the operating system’s package manager recently installed updates. A patched kernel package does not protect the system until the server has rebooted into that kernel. When immediate patching is not possible, Hyunwoo Kim and Red Hat document two temporary mitigations. One approach is to disable SYN cookies: sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0 This prevents the demonstrated path in which a request socket is reconstructed through a SYN cookie. However, disabling the feature reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, so administrators should carefully evaluate the operational and security trade-offs. The setting is maintained per network namespace and may therefore need to be applied individually to containers using separate namespaces. A second temporary measure is to reduce packet handling to a single RX queue and disable Receive Packet Steering and Receive Flow Steering. Since exploitation depends on separate RX contexts racing concurrently, serializing packet processing can prevent the demonstrated condition. This approach can affect network performance and should be evaluated before deployment in production environments. Organizations should additionally reduce unnecessary public exposure of administrative and infrastructure services, restrict TCP access to trusted networks where operationally possible, and ensure centralized collection of kernel logs and crash telemetry. These controls cannot substitute for patching but can help reduce attack surface and improve incident investigation. FAQ What is CVE-2026-99288 and how does it work? CVE-2026-99288, also known as NoisyTCP, is a Linux kernel TCP race condition affecting lockless established-socket lookups. Under specific timing conditions, recycled socket memory can be referenced before the replacement object has been fully initialized and hashed. A remote attacker can manipulate TCP traffic to trigger a NULL pointer dereference, resulting in a kernel panic and denial of service. When was CVE-2026-99288 first discovered? The precise date on which Hyunwoo Kim privately discovered the vulnerability has not been publicly disclosed. The correction entered the Linux networking development process in late October 2026 and was merged upstream on November 3. The Linux kernel CNA publicly announced the vulnerability on November 10, 2026, while Kim released the detailed NoisyTCP research after the coordinated disclosure embargo expired on November 15–16. What is the impact of CVE-2026-99288 on systems? Successful exploitation can remotely crash the Linux kernel and take the entire operating system offline without authentication. If the affected host runs containers or multiple services, a kernel panic can disrupt all workloads sharing that kernel. Current evidence demonstrates denial of service rather than reliable remote code execution. Can CVE-2026-99288 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Systems remain exposed when they run a vulnerable kernel that does not contain the upstream correction or a vendor backport. Because the underlying bug dates back to Linux 4.4 in 2015, many kernel branches and Linux distributions may be affected. Administrators should verify the latest security advisory for their distribution because patch availability continues to change as vendors release backports. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-99288? Apply a vendor-provided kernel update containing the NoisyTCP correction and reboot the system into the patched kernel. If immediate updating is impossible, evaluate temporary measures such as disabling SYN cookies or reducing packet processing to a single RX queue with RPS and RFS disabled. Organizations should also limit unnecessary TCP exposure and monitor Linux hosts for kernel panics, unexpected reboots, and suspicious network activity.

items.title: Uncovering GhostMap: The Rootkit Behind Shai-Hulud’s Rusty Cousin
items.summary: TL;DR: GhostMap is Aqua Nautilus’s research name for the Linux eBPF rootkit shared across examined IronWorm and Atomic Arch malware payloads. It blinds user-space applications by manipulating kernel data on the fly to hide malicious processes, files, and network sockets. In controlled experiments, Aqua Nautilus traced these evasion mechanics and proved their limits: while overwriting &mldr

items.title: “Amazon” job offer promises $5,000 a month, but it’s got all the signs of a scam
items.summary: Last month, Amazon announced plans to hire more than 300,000 people in the US for the holidays. That’s welcome news for job seekers, but scammers know that. We found several sites advertising a remote assistant job under Amazon-like names, with promises of up to $5,000 a month. None of the sites is run by Amazon. Amazon says all genuine job opportunities are posted on amazon.jobs ; hourly warehouse jobs are also listed at hiring.amazon.com . The offers we found are separate from Amazon’s holiday hiring push. The application doesn’t match the job description One careers page calls the role a “legitimate, fully remote position,” with “no commute, no office, no fixed desk.” Yet the form asks whether applicants have reliable access to a personal vehicle and someone at home who can receive packages. Those questions point to package handling, not remote assistant work. A recruitment page promises fully remote work paying up to $5,000 a month Why Amazon makes such good bait People expect Amazon to be hiring. A hiring announcement can make an “Amazon is hiring” message seem plausible. But the remote assistant jobs on these sites are separate from Amazon’s announced seasonal roles. “Working with Amazon” can sound believable. Businesses can provide services to Amazon sellers without being part of Amazon. The sites use names that resemble those of logistics or seller-support businesses, which can make the connection harder to judge at a glance. The pitch targets people looking for flexible work. “Work from home” and a few hours a day can appeal to parents, students, and people looking for a second job. The tactic has been used before. Amazon says it saw more reports of scammers posing as recruiters in September and October 2025. In June, we warned about Amazon job texts offering $250 to $500 a day for 60 to 90 minutes of work. The sites we found add a careers site, a company website, and a polished application form to make the offer look more convincing. Several names, apparent links We found multiple recruitment and application sites using Amazon-like branding: amzssapplication[.]com and jobsamzss[.]com , two careers pages for the “Remote Assistant” job applyamazonsp[.]com , an application form for the same job, under the name “Amazon Seller Pro LLC” The sites use byte-identical site icons. Their domains were registered through the same registrar between July 23 and October 26. These similarities suggest a connection, although they do not establish who operates each site. The same remote assistant pitch appears on another domain The recruitment pages list “HR” email addresses on three additional domains: amzncrew[.]com, joinamzn[.]com, and workatamzn[.]com. These addresses do not establish an affiliation with Amazon. To verify a job with Amazon itself, check its official job boards at amazon.jobs or hiring.amazon.com . Independent businesses serving Amazon sellers hire separately, so verify their offers by contacting the business through contact details you find independently. The recruitment pages link to amzshippings[.]com, a website advertising preparation and shipping services for Amazon sellers. That’s a newly registered domain with hidden ownership details. A remote job that asks about your car and doorstep Although the careers pages on these sites describe the role as fully remote, the application asks: “Do you have reliable access to a personal vehicle?” If not, it asks applicants to explain how they would transport packages. “If you’re not home, is there a person to receive parcels?” A remote assistant wouldn’t normally need to receive or transport packages. These questions are warning signs of reshipping , also known as parcel-mule fraud . The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says that a job asking you to receive shipments, repackage them, and send them elsewhere is a reshipping scam. The goods may have been bought with stolen payment details, and people recruited this way can be left handling packages connected to fraud. The form collects personal information The application form asks applicants for personal information The form collects your name, phone, email, home address including apartment number, felony history, education and employment history. It promises “Your data is secure” and sends submissions through Formspree, a third-party form service. We could not establish who receives the information. The page also tells search engines not to index it. No resume is needed. Instead, the careers page says: “ Our HR team calls you directly … Keep your phone on — we don’t schedule in advance. “ In the page code, that note sits below a leftover template comment: “ PASTE YOUR TEXT HERE. ” The recruitment page’s footer states: “Amazon Shipping Services is not affiliated with or endorsed by Amazon.com, Inc.” What could happen if you apply? Sharing your details could expose you to identity theft . If you take the job, you could also be asked to move packages or money tied to fraud. Identity theft: Your name, contact details, and home address can be useful to criminals . Be especially cautious if anyone later asks for your Social Security number, bank details, or ID. Being drawn into fraud: If you receive or forward packages bought with stolen payment details, your address may be linked to their movement. Losing money: A fake employer might later send a check and ask you to return some of the money or use it to buy supplies. The FTC warns that fake checks can bounce after the money has been sent on. How to stay safe Find Amazon jobs on amazon.jobs. Amazon says genuine job opportunities are listed on its official job board. Check the domain, not the logo. Anyone can copy Amazon’s colors and branding. Be wary of high pay for little work , especially when there’s no résumé or scheduled interview. Don’t receive or forward packages for an employer you haven’t verified. Don’t send ID photos, your Social Security number, or money before verifying the employer. If you already applied, don’t give an unscheduled caller your bank details, ID, or money. If you shared sensitive information, follow the steps at IdentityTheft.gov and consider placing a credit freeze. How Malwarebytes helps Malwarebytes Browser Guard blocks scam pages like these. And if you’re not sure whether a job offer is real, give the link or put a screenshot of the offer into Malwarebytes Scam Guard before you reply. It will assess whether it’s a scam and give you advice on what to do next. Recruitment and application sites observed amzssapplication[.]com applicationsamz[.]com apply.amzapplicationra[.]com applyamazonsp[.]com hiringamazonsp[.]com hiringamzss[.]com jobsamazonsp[.]com jobsamzss[.]com joinamazonsp[.]com onlineapplicationamz[.]com ra.amzncrew[.]com ra.applicationsamz[.]com ra.onlineapplicationamz[.]com workatamazonsp[.]com www.jobsamzss[.]com www.onlineapplicationamz[.]com Something feel off? Check it before you click. Malwarebytes Scam Guard helps you analyze suspicious links, texts, and screenshots instantly.   • Don’t receive or forward packages for an employer you haven’t verified.
  • Don’t send ID photos, your Social Security number, or money before verifying the employer.

items.title: FBI Warns Hackers Abuse Google Search to Spread Gootloader Malware and Launch Ransomware Attacks
items.summary: The FBI has warned that cybercriminals are using poisoned search results and compromised WordPress websites to spread Gootloader malware, giving ransomware operators an entry point into business networks. The attacks turn searches for legal documents, contracts, and business information into opportunities to trick users into downloading malicious JavaScript files. In a November 16, 2026, FLASH advisory, the bureau said it had identified more than 1,000 infected WordPress websites and 216 domains controlled by the Gootloader administrator as of October. The FBI linked this infrastructure to more than $28 million in ransomware payments, showing how document searches can lead to costly network compromises. Analysts behind the FBI warning published through IC3.gov’s Gootloader advisory identified the malware as an initial access framework rather than a ransomware encryptor. It establishes the foothold attackers need to deliver additional tools, steal credentials, move between systems, and prepare follow-on attacks against organizations across multiple sectors. FBI Warns Hackers Abuse Google Search The campaign relies on search engine optimization poisoning, which pushes attacker-controlled content alongside legitimate resources. Between 2020 and 2026, operators targeted search phrases with limited competition, including jurisdiction-specific contract clauses. Earlier reporting on Gootloader’s blackhat SEO techniques documented how fake forum discussions and hidden keywords helped malicious pages match users’ document searches. Legal professionals remain a major target. The FBI described searches aimed at practicing attorneys, in-house counsel, law firm partners, privacy teams, and legal technology decision-makers. Compromised WordPress websites serve different roles, acting as lure pages, redirectors, traffic filters, or relay infrastructure. Hidden keyword links and arranged backlinks increase their visibility in search results. A traffic distribution system checks details such as a visitor’s country, referring page, cookies, and IP address before deciding which content to display. This filtering means visitors can receive different content from the same compromised site. The operation’s recent evolution includes WordPress comment-path abuse, geographic filtering, and a stronger focus on U.S. legal professionals. Once a victim opens the downloaded JavaScript, the infection can progress beyond the browser. The FBI traced earlier versions through ZIP-delivered scripts and Windows Script Host execution, followed by PowerShell, scheduled tasks, and registry-resident payloads. Previous research into Gootloader’s fileless ransomware delivery explains how later-stage components can run from memory after being stored in the registry. The advisory also maps activity involving defense evasion, credential theft, and lateral movement, including process injection, AMSI impairment, remote services, and pass-the-hash authentication. These capabilities explain why a single script execution deserves urgent investigation: deleting the original download does not remove every payload or restore trust in the affected computer. Detection, Containment, and WordPress Protection Defenders should connect browser downloads with script execution, PowerShell activity, persistence changes, and unusual network connections. Earlier reporting on Gootloader’s lateral movement activity described attackers progressing from a poisoned search result toward domain infrastructure. The FBI recommends collecting process trees, scheduled tasks, browser history, DNS records, proxy logs, and endpoint memory where appropriate. If an archive was downloaded but not opened, users should avoid extracting or previewing it and submit it through their organization’s security process. If JavaScript executed, disconnect network access and follow incident-response procedures. Change exposed credentials from a clean device after investigators assess the damage, and reimage systems when persistence, credential theft, or additional malware is confirmed. Prevention includes restricting Windows Script Host where unnecessary, controlling scripts with WDAC or AppLocker, and blocking unauthorized execution from user-writable folders. WordPress owners should patch software, remove unused components, enforce strong administrator authentication, and monitor file integrity. Recent coverage of Gootloader infrastructure disruption efforts also underscores why website cleanup and credential resets remain necessary after takedowns. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Source-listed artifact Investigative relevance easinvoker.exe Copied executable associated with DLL sideloading C:\Windows with a trailing space Mock trusted directory used for masquerading AmsiScanBuffer Function targeted for defense impairment bashupload.com Alternate upload destination mentioned for exfiltration Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . items.title: Reducing Microsoft Sentinel Costs Without Compromising Detection – Part 3: The DNS Quest
items.summary: In our previous blog, Reducing Microsoft Sentinel Costs Without Compromising Detection – Part 2: The Firewall Quest , we described the application of Summary rules to Firewall events. In this part of our blog series, we focus on another expensive log source, DNS. We will explore DNS events and how Summary Rules can be leveraged in this high-volume log source to effectively reduce Sentinel costs while maintaining detection capabilities. DNS is one of the crucial log sources in terms of security monitoring. In an environment, DNS events offer detailed visibility of queries and responses originating from workstations and servers. From a security perspective, this telemetry is highly valuable for threat monitoring, as DNS activity frequently reveals early or post-infection indicators of compromise. During incident response, DNS logs help reconstruct attacker activity, identify affected hosts and establish timelines with greater precision. In practice, maintaining this level of logging strengthens detection capabilities, improves investigative depth, and supports faster, evidence-based containment and remediation decisions. Detect Threats through DNS Events Detection Types DNS telemetry supports a range of detection and threat-hunting scenarios, including DNS tunneling, command-and-control beaconing 1 , malicious domain lookups identified through threat intelligence, DNS-based data exfiltration, and communications with newly observed or otherwise suspicious domains. In DNS events there are specific fields that contain interesting information for our detections. Fields like Dns Query content , Dns Query Type , Dns Response code can be leveraged for numerous detection use cases. Summary-Based DNS Threat Detections In the previous blog, we presented a way to use firewall events for detecting network scan attacks based on the aggregated information that is being generated by the summary rules. This was done by aggregating events which have similar characteristics on fields like Source IP , Destination IP , Destination Port and Protocol . For the DNS approach, we will propose and analyze a different approach. We will use Summary Rules to filter DNS events ingested into an Auxiliary/Data Lake 2 table to identify patterns that indicate a suspicious or malicious DNS query, or a different behavioral anomaly in the DNS events that are generated by our servers. Based on a detection logic, an event of the suspicious traffic will be generated by the Summary Rule and stored in the newly generated Analytic Tier table that is used by the Summary Rule. Finally, we will use this event in this table to generate an alert using an Analytic Rule. To demonstrate our Summary based DNS threat detection, we will focus on a common technique used by adversaries, DNS Tunneling. What is DNS Tunneling ? DNS Tunneling 3 attack is a technique used by adversaries for command & control of infected devices, exfiltration by transferring data out of the network DNS tunneling attack is a technique that abuses the Domain Name System (DNS) to secretly transfer and exfiltrate data or communicate with a compromised device for command & control purposes, and even bypassing firewall or proxy restrictions by a covert channel of communication. To shortly describe this technique, an attacker starts by compromising a device inside an organization. The malware that has been deployed on the device, encodes information gathered from the host (credentials, files, or even just host or network information) into subdomain request. The device then sends DNS queries to a domain controlled by the attacker, enabling the attacker to collect and decode the information while also using the same channel to send commands to the compromised host. An example of encoding for DNS tunneling is the usage base32 4 to encode a message which is then used as the subdomain of the request. Sliver C2 5 is an example of an offensive tool that uses base32 for its DNS C2 activities. Lab Infrastructure Setup As we mentioned in the First and Second blog of this series , we have presented the split transformation rules. These rules are used to redirect a part of the ingestion stream to the Data Lake. However, for DNS events, we will go one step further, by ingesting all Microsoft DNS Analytical events to Data Lake. For this showcase we will focus on Microsoft DNS Analytical 6 events. This option can also be applied to telemetry from other DNS products, provided the queries described in the following section are adapted to the relevant field names and schemas. The examples in this document are specifically tailored to Microsoft DNS analytical events. We will keep the example simple and are not going to describe all DNS infrastructure and event telemetry that happens under the hood. For this example we will focus on simple request and response activities from the DNS servers. We will also consider a fully configured internal DNS server that has DNS Analytic events enabled. In the following demonstration, we will use sample request and response events from DNS Analytics events. Each event contains the following interesting information that we would like to filter. DNS Tunneling Testing In order to test one of the DNS Tunneling attack variations, base32 encoding in FQDN, we will use the following small Powershell script to generate DNS events that emulate this attack pattern. This script calculates a base32 encoded payload for the subdomain part, constructs the subdomain and a domain of our choice and performs the DNS requests. The domain we use is a test domain that does not exist, thus we will receive only NXDOMAIN 7 responses for these requests. $Domain = "total-legitimate-domain.domain" $Iterations = 25 function New-Base32String { param([int]$Length = 45) # 63 = DNS label max $base32Chars = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567".ToCharArray() -join (1..$Length | ForEach-Object { $base32Chars | Get-Random }) } for ($i = 1; $i -le $Iterations; $i++) { $subdomain = New-Base32String -Length 45 $fqdn = "$subdomain.$Domain" Write-Host "[$i] Querying TXT record for $fqdn..." try { (Resolve-DnsName -Name $fqdn -Type TXT).Strings } catch { Write-Warning "Query failed for $fqdn : $_" } Start-Sleep -Seconds 0 # optional delay between queries } $Domain = "total-legitimate-domain.domain" $Iterations = 25 function New-Base32String { param ([ int ] $Length = 45 ) # 63 = DNS label max $base32Chars = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567" .ToCharArray() -join ( 1 .. $Length | ForEach-Object { $base32Chars | Get-Random }) } for ( $i = 1 ; $i -le $Iterations ; $i ++) { $subdomain = New-Base32String -Length 45 $fqdn = " $subdomain . $Domain " Write-Host "[ $i ] Querying TXT record for $fqdn ..." try { ( Resolve-DnsName -Name $fqdn -Type TXT).Strings } catch { Write-Warning "Query failed for $fqdn : $_ " } Start-Sleep -Seconds 0 # optional delay between queries } This script will simulate the base32 subdomain creation based on the set of characters that are used in base32 and perform batched DNS requests for the domain provided as parameter. The results observed during execution is the following: DNS Simulation script results Summary Rule Development Unlike the previous blog of our series for Firewall log sources, as we mentioned earlier, we will propose a different approach on the Summary Rule creation. In this case, the Summary Rule will not just be used to aggregate records and store them in a new analytics table, it will be used to detect the suspicious activity in question and store the interesting information to an analytics table. After the new record is added to the analytic table, an Analytic Rule will trigger and generate the necessary alert. The following KQL query uses regex to match the base32 payload in the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) field of the event. Moreover, in the query we parse Top-Level and Second-Level parts of the domain to be able to use them later in aggregation. Then, by using the summarize operator 8 , we group the records based on the SourceIP and Second-Level part of domain that has performed these dns queries. Finally, we are checking the two threshold variables for the number of requests and the number of subdomains, since we intend to identify multiple DNS communication attempts to the same domain with different subdomains, an indicator of possible command and control communication with a specific domain. We add the columns Alert Title , Alert Description , Alert Severity , Alert Notification to enhance the title, description and severity of the future alert that will be generated by the Analytic Rule. // Potential DNS Tunnel with Base32 in Queries // Supported Vendor and Product: Microsoft - DNS Server // Thresholds: let RequestThreshold = 50; let SubdomainThreshold = 10; ASimDnsActivityLogs | where EventProduct =~ 'DNS Server' | where EventSubType in("request", "response") | where ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr) | extend TLD = tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[-1]) | extend SLD_part = tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[-2]) | where SLD_part != "" | extend SLD = strcat(SLD_part, ".", TLD) | where DnsQuery matches regex @"(?:^|\.)(?:[a-z2-7]{24,}|[A-Z2-7]{24,})(?:\.[A-Za-z0-9\-]+){2,}$" //Match base32 characters with high length in subdomain (at least 24 chars) | summarize minTimeGenerated = min(TimeGenerated), maxTimeGenerated = max(TimeGenerated), make_set(DnsQueryTypeName, 8), DnsQuery = make_set(DnsQuery, 50), SubdomainCount = dcount(DnsQuery), EventCount = sum(EventCount), Count = count() by SrcIpAddr, SLD, EventSubType, EventVendor, EventProduct | where Count >= RequestThreshold | where SubdomainCount >= SubdomainThreshold | summarize minTimeGenerated = min(minTimeGenerated), maxTimeGenerated = max(maxTimeGenerated), DnsQuery = make_set(DnsQuery, 50), EventSubType = make_set(EventSubType, 5), make_set(set_DnsQueryTypeName), EventCount = sum(EventCount), Count = sum(Count) by SrcIpAddr, SLD, EventVendor, EventProduct | extend alert_title = 'Potential DNS Tunnel with Base32 in Queries', alert_description = 'DNS Tunneling is a technique used to encode data or encapsulate another communication protocol within the DNS protocol for the purpose of exfiltrating information, establishing and concealing C2 traffic, downloading tooling in compromised systems and bypassing local network security controls within the environment. A common implementation technique in DNS tunneling for passing information through DNS requests is to use a base32 encoding in the subdomains of the requested domain. Typical DNS tunneling traffic in that case will consist of multiple requests for the same domain with base32 encoded subdomains. For further information check https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cyberpedia/what-is-dns-tunneling', alert_severity = 'Medium', alert_notification = "dns_sr_alert" // Potential DNS Tunnel with Base32 in Queries // Supported Vendor and Product: Microsoft - DNS Server // Thresholds: let RequestThreshold = 50 ; let SubdomainThreshold = 10 ; ASimDnsActivityLogs | where EventProduct =~ 'DNS Server' | where EventSubType in ( "request" , "response" ) | where ipv4_is_private (SrcIpAddr) | extend TLD = tostring ( split (DnsQuery, "." )[- 1 ]) | extend SLD_part = tostring ( split (DnsQuery, "." )[- 2 ]) | where SLD_part != "" | extend SLD = strcat (SLD_part, "." , TLD) | where DnsQuery matches regex @"(?:^|\.)(?:[a-z2-7]{24,}|[A-Z2-7]{24,})(?:\.[A-Za-z0-9\-]+){2,}$" //Match base32 characters with high length in subdomain (at least 24 chars) | summarize minTimeGenerated = min (TimeGenerated), maxTimeGenerated = max (TimeGenerated), make_set (DnsQueryTypeName, 8 ), DnsQuery = make_set (DnsQuery, 50 ), SubdomainCount = dcount (DnsQuery), EventCount = sum (EventCount), Count = count() by SrcIpAddr, SLD, EventSubType, EventVendor, EventProduct | where Count >= RequestThreshold | where SubdomainCount >= SubdomainThreshold | summarize minTimeGenerated = min (minTimeGenerated), maxTimeGenerated = max (maxTimeGenerated), DnsQuery = make_set (DnsQuery, 50 ), EventSubType = make_set (EventSubType, 5 ), make_set (set_DnsQueryTypeName), EventCount = sum (EventCount), Count = sum (Count) by SrcIpAddr, SLD, EventVendor, EventProduct | extend alert_title = 'Potential DNS Tunnel with Base32 in Queries' , alert_description = 'DNS Tunneling is a technique used to encode data or encapsulate another communication protocol within the DNS protocol for the purpose of exfiltrating information, establishing and concealing C2 traffic, downloading tooling in compromised systems and bypassing local network security controls within the environment. A common implementation technique in DNS tunneling for passing information through DNS requests is to use a base32 encoding in the subdomains of the requested domain. Typical DNS tunneling traffic in that case will consist of multiple requests for the same domain with base32 encoded subdomains. For further information check https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cyberpedia/what-is-dns-tunneling' , alert_severity = 'Medium' , alert_notification = "dns_sr_alert" This query returns the following results. We can observe the sequence of requests and responses between our “compromised” host with IP Address 192.168.20.105 and the Internal DNS Server with IP Address 192.168.20.101 : Query Results We proceed and create the Summary Rule in Microsoft Sentinel by specifying the name, description and query of the rule, the destination table that will include the results and the frequency that the rule will run. Regarding the frequency, we recommend a 1-hour interval for this rule to run. Unlike the Firewall example we provided on the previous blog, in this case, since we create the actual detection rule, which is a threshold rule, we will need a decent amount of time to gather records for the detection to run. In many cases of Command & Control, a 1-hour interval can give us enough records to hit the threshold we need. Of course, since each environment is different, these thresholds can be set lower accordingly, and as a result, making the rule more sensitive.This requires a baseline configuration for each organization. Summary Rule creation wizard Summary Rule configuration Analytic Rule Development Now that we have the newly created Summary Rule in place, we need to be able to trigger an alert each time a new record is populated. To do this, we will create an Analytic Rule that will handle the results of the Summary Rule. In this Analytic Rule’s query we check the records from the table dns_sr_alerts_CL and the field alert_notification . If there is a match, an alert will trigger that has the Alert Title , Alert Description and Alert Severity preset by the Summary Rule’s query. Using this we are able to create multiple Summary Rules and a singly Analytic Rule that handles the results based on the field’s information. dns_sr_alerts_CL | where isnotempty(alert_title) | where alert_notification == "dns_sr_alert" | project-reorder alert_* dns_sr_alerts_CL | where isnotempty (alert_title) | where alert_notification == "dns_sr_alert" | project-reorder alert_* Analytic Rule creation wizard Analytic Rule creation wizard The screenshot below demonstrates the incidents generated by the Analytic Rule we created. Analytic Rule Incident triggered Cost Comparison Based on the presented solution and our internal assessments across multiple clients’ environments, this approach can reduce the cost of ingesting DNS events by roughly 95% compared to the original ingestion cost. In some cases, the cost reduction is even higher. The cost reduction is greater than outlined in our previous blog post because the detection logic is applied to the Summary Rule. As a result, the analytics table stores only the records generated for alerting through the Analytic Rule, rather than the actual DNS records. In addition to ingestion costs, each execution of the Summary Rule incurs a query cost based on its configured interval for the data that are scanned. However, according to our internal assessments, the average cost per execution remains relatively low. As we mentioned on the previous blog, to better estimate projected costs for your specific environment, use Microsoft’s Sentinel Cost Estimator app 9 or calculate based on Microsoft’s Sentinel pricing listings 10 . Wrapping Up In the third part of this blog series, we demonstrated an alternative way to use Microsoft Sentinel Summary Rules on Microsoft DNS Analytic events to reduce ingestion costs while preserving the critical visibility required for effective threat detection and incident response. The demonstrated approach is applied to Microsoft DNS Analytic events but can be extended to additional DNS products based on each environment’s requirements. References Extrahop, “What is C2 Beaconing? Definition & Prevention”. Available: https://www.extrahop.com/resources/attacks/c-c-beaconing ︎ Microsoft, “What is Microsoft Sentinel data lake?”. Available: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/datalake/sentinel-lake-overview ︎ Palo Alto Networks, “What Is DNS Tunneling?”. Available: https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cyberpedia/what-is-dns-tunneling ︎ Wikipedia, “Base32 Encoding”. Available: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base32 ︎ Github, “Sliver C2 Framework”. Available: https://github.com/bishopfox/sliver ︎ Microsoft, “DNS Analytical Event Logging”. Available: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/networking/dns/dns-logging-and-diagnostics ︎ Cloudns, “What is NXDOMAIN?”. Available: https://www.cloudns.net/blog/what-is-nxdomain/ ︎ Microsoft, “summarize operator”. Available: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/kusto/query/summarize-operator ︎ Microsoft, “Microsoft Sentinel cost estimator”. Available: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/pricing/microsoft-sentinel/cost-estimator ︎ Microsoft, “Microsoft Sentinel pricing”. for ($i = 1; $i -le $Iterations; $i++) {
    $subdomain = New-Base32String -Length 45
    $fqdn = "$subdomain.$Domain"

    Write-Host "[$i] Querying TXT record for $fqdn..."

    try {
        (Resolve-DnsName -Name $fqdn -Type TXT).Strings
    }
    catch {
        Write-Warning "Query failed for $fqdn : $_"
    }

    Start-Sleep -Seconds 0   # optional delay between queries
}
$Domain = "total-legitimate-domain.domain"
$Iterations = 25

function New-Base32String {
    param([int]$Length = 45)   # 63 = DNS label max
    $base32Chars = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567".ToCharArray()
    -join (1..$Length | ForEach-Object { $base32Chars | Get-Random })

for ($i = 1; $i -le $Iterations; $i++) {

This script will simulate the base32 subdomain creation based on the set of characters that are used in base32 and perform batched DNS requests for the domain provided as parameter. The results observed during execution is the following:

DNS Simulation script results
Summary Rule Development

Unlike the previous blog of our series for Firewall log sources, as we mentioned earlier, we will propose a different approach on the Summary Rule creation. In this case, the Summary Rule will not just be used to aggregate records and store them in a new analytics table, it will be used to detect the suspicious activity in question and store the interesting information to an analytics table. After the new record is added to the analytic table, an Analytic Rule will trigger and generate the necessary alert.

The following KQL query uses regex to match the base32 payload in the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) field of the event. Moreover, in the query we parse Top-Level and Second-Level parts of the domain to be able to use them later in aggregation. Then, by using the summarize operator8, we group the records based on the SourceIP and Second-Level part of domain that has performed these dns queries. Finally, we are checking the two threshold variables for the number of requests and the number of subdomains, since we intend to identify multiple DNS communication attempts to the same domain with different subdomains, an indicator of possible command and control communication with a specific domain. We add the columns Alert Title, Alert Description, Alert Severity, Alert Notification to enhance the title, description and severity of the future alert that will be generated by the Analytic Rule.

// Potential DNS Tunnel with Base32 in Queries
// Supported Vendor and Product: Microsoft - DNS Server
// Thresholds:
let RequestThreshold = 50;
let SubdomainThreshold = 10;
ASimDnsActivityLogs
| where EventProduct =~ 'DNS Server'
| where EventSubType in("request", "response")
| where ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)
| extend TLD = tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[-1])
| extend SLD_part = tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[-2])
| where SLD_part != ""
| extend SLD = strcat(SLD_part, ".", TLD)
| where DnsQuery matches regex @"(?:^|\.)(?:[a-z2-7]{24,}|[A-Z2-7]{24,})(?:\.[A-Za-z0-9\-]+){2,}$" //Match base32 characters with high length in subdomain (at least 24 chars)
| summarize
    minTimeGenerated = min(TimeGenerated),
    maxTimeGenerated = max(TimeGenerated),
    make_set(DnsQueryTypeName, 8),
    DnsQuery = make_set(DnsQuery, 50),
    SubdomainCount = dcount(DnsQuery),
    EventCount = sum(EventCount),
    Count = count()
    by SrcIpAddr, SLD, EventSubType, EventVendor, EventProduct
| where Count >= RequestThreshold
| where SubdomainCount >= SubdomainThreshold
| summarize
    minTimeGenerated = min(minTimeGenerated),
    maxTimeGenerated = max(maxTimeGenerated),
    DnsQuery = make_set(DnsQuery, 50),
    EventSubType = make_set(EventSubType, 5),
    make_set(set_DnsQueryTypeName),
    EventCount = sum(EventCount),
    Count = sum(Count)
    by SrcIpAddr, SLD, EventVendor, EventProduct
| extend
    alert_title = 'Potential DNS Tunnel with Base32 in Queries',
    alert_description = 'DNS Tunneling is a technique used to encode data or encapsulate another communication protocol within the DNS protocol for the purpose of exfiltrating information, establishing and concealing C2 traffic, downloading tooling in compromised systems and bypassing local network security controls within the environment. A common implementation technique in DNS tunneling for passing information through DNS requests is to use a base32 encoding in the subdomains of the requested domain. Typical DNS tunneling traffic in that case will consist of multiple requests for the same domain with base32 encoded subdomains. For further information check https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cyberpedia/what-is-dns-tunneling',
    alert_severity = 'Medium',
    alert_notification = "dns_sr_alert"
// Potential DNS Tunnel with Base32 in Queries
// Supported Vendor and Product: Microsoft - DNS Server
// Thresholds:
let RequestThreshold = 50;
let SubdomainThreshold = 10;
ASimDnsActivityLogs
| where EventProduct =~ 'DNS Server'
| where EventSubType in("request", "response")
| where ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)
| extend TLD = tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[-1])
| extend SLD_part = tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[-2])
| where SLD_part != ""
| extend SLD = strcat(SLD_part, ".", TLD)
| where DnsQuery matches regex @"(?:^|\.)(?:[a-z2-7]{24,}|[A-Z2-7]{24,})(?:\.[A-Za-z0-9\-]+){2,}$" //Match base32 characters with high length in subdomain (at least 24 chars)
| summarize
    minTimeGenerated = min(TimeGenerated),
    maxTimeGenerated = max(TimeGenerated),
    make_set(DnsQueryTypeName, 8),
    DnsQuery = make_set(DnsQuery, 50),
    SubdomainCount = dcount(DnsQuery),
    EventCount = sum(EventCount),
    Count = count()
    by SrcIpAddr, SLD, EventSubType, EventVendor, EventProduct
| where Count >= RequestThreshold
| where SubdomainCount >= SubdomainThreshold
| summarize
    minTimeGenerated = min(minTimeGenerated),
    maxTimeGenerated = max(maxTimeGenerated),
    DnsQuery = make_set(DnsQuery, 50),
    EventSubType = make_set(EventSubType, 5),
    make_set(set_DnsQueryTypeName),
    EventCount = sum(EventCount),
    Count = sum(Count)
    by SrcIpAddr, SLD, EventVendor, EventProduct
| extend
    alert_title = 'Potential DNS Tunnel with Base32 in Queries',
    alert_description = 'DNS Tunneling is a technique used to encode data or encapsulate another communication protocol within the DNS protocol for the purpose of exfiltrating information, establishing and concealing C2 traffic, downloading tooling in compromised systems and bypassing local network security controls within the environment. A common implementation technique in DNS tunneling for passing information through DNS requests is to use a base32 encoding in the subdomains of the requested domain. Typical DNS tunneling traffic in that case will consist of multiple requests for the same domain with base32 encoded subdomains. For further information check https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cyberpedia/what-is-dns-tunneling',
    alert_severity = 'Medium',
    alert_notification = "dns_sr_alert"

This query returns the following results. We can observe the sequence of requests and responses between our “compromised” host with IP Address 192.168.20.105 and the Internal DNS Server with IP Address 192.168.20.101 :

Query Results

We proceed and create the Summary Rule in Microsoft Sentinel by specifying the name, description and query of the rule, the destination table that will include the results and the frequency that the rule will run. Regarding the frequency, we recommend a 1-hour interval for this rule to run. Unlike the Firewall example we provided on the previous blog, in this case, since we create the actual detection rule, which is a threshold rule, we will need a decent amount of time to gather records for the detection to run. In many cases of Command & Control, a 1-hour interval can give us enough records to hit the threshold we need. Of course, since each environment is different, these thresholds can be set lower accordingly, and as a result, making the rule more sensitive.This requires a baseline configuration for each organization.

Summary Rule creation wizard
Summary Rule configuration
Analytic Rule Development

Now that we have the newly created Summary Rule in place, we need to be able to trigger an alert each time a new record is populated. To do this, we will create an Analytic Rule that will handle the results of the Summary Rule. In this Analytic Rule’s query we check the records from the table dns_sr_alerts_CL and the field alert_notification. If there is a match, an alert will trigger that has the Alert Title, Alert Description and Alert Severity preset by the Summary Rule’s query. Using this we are able to create multiple Summary Rules and a singly Analytic Rule that handles the results based on the field’s information.

dns_sr_alerts_CL
| where isnotempty(alert_title)
| where alert_notification == "dns_sr_alert"
| project-reorder alert_*
dns_sr_alerts_CL
| where isnotempty(alert_title)
| where alert_notification == "dns_sr_alert"
| project-reorder alert_*

Analytic Rule creation wizard
Analytic Rule creation wizard

The screenshot below demonstrates the incidents generated by the Analytic Rule we created.

Analytic Rule Incident triggered
Cost Comparison

Based on the presented solution and our internal assessments across multiple clients’ environments, this approach can reduce the cost of ingesting DNS events by roughly 95% compared to the original ingestion cost. In some cases, the cost reduction is even higher. The cost reduction is greater than outlined in our previous blog post because the detection logic is applied to the Summary Rule. As a result, the analytics table stores only the records generated for alerting through the Analytic Rule, rather than the actual DNS records. In addition to ingestion costs, each execution of the Summary Rule incurs a query cost based on its configured interval for the data that are scanned. However, according to our internal assessments, the average cost per execution remains relatively low. As we mentioned on the previous blog, to better estimate projected costs for your specific environment, use Microsoft’s Sentinel Cost Estimator app9 or calculate based on Microsoft’s Sentinel pricing listings10.

Wrapping Up

In the third part of this blog series, we demonstrated an alternative way to use Microsoft Sentinel Summary Rules on Microsoft DNS Analytic events to reduce ingestion costs while preserving the critical visibility required for effective threat detection and incident response. The demonstrated approach is applied to Microsoft DNS Analytic events but can be extended to additional DNS products based on each environment’s requirements.

items.title: Hackers Exploit Exposed AI Vendor Key to Breach 10 Barracuda Cloud Accounts in 44 Hours
items.summary: Hackers used a cloud access key exposed through an AI vendor to reach approximately 10 Barracuda cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours. The intrusion moved through stored secrets, development systems, and Kubernetes clusters, showing how one forgotten credential can open a path across several connected platforms. Barracuda recorded the activity between November 1 and November 2, 2026. The key had been provided to a third-party AI company for an earlier project but remained active after that work ended. According to Barracuda, the vendor’s development environment was compromised in October, apparently exposing the credential. The company acknowledged that failing to retire the key left an unnecessary entry point into its cloud environment. Barracuda researchers identified activity matching ARTEX, an open-source AI-driven penetration-testing framework, rather than naming a standalone malware family. Hackers Exploit Exposed AI Vendor Key In its technical incident report , the company linked the intrusion to automated credential searches and machine-style resource labels. Separately, the Fireworks AI data breach illustrates related vendor exposure risks, although Barracuda did not name its AI supplier. The first recorded API call occurred at 04:33 UTC on November 1. Within minutes, the attacker began checking which resources the key could access. It then read stored secrets, including AWS access keys and Azure service principal secrets, using each discovery to expand access rather than relying on a single compromised account. Over the following 24 hours, the attacker moved from cloud accounts into a data analytics system, obtained a source-code access token, and reached Kubernetes clusters. It also decrypted infrastructure-as-code state files and collected credentials from server metadata services and Kubernetes service accounts. Each exposed secret became another route through the environment. Early on November 2, the attacker pushed temporary branches into several repositories. These triggered build workflows designed to print build-system secrets into job logs. Encoding the secrets prevented normal log-masking controls from hiding them. The repository activity took less than four hours, and the final recorded attacker activity occurred at 23:31 UTC that day. Barracuda said ARTEX uses a planner agent to choose actions while worker agents execute tools and share findings. Its findings complement reporting on ARTEX AI agent attacks involving rapid privilege escalation. However, the framework’s use does not identify the attacker: multiple criminal and state-aligned groups have reportedly adopted it. Credential Theft, Persistence, and Customer Response The attacker searched for cryptocurrency material, including wallet-related environment variables, Ethereum keystores, private keys, seed phrase files, and Kubernetes secrets. Barracuda said no wallet material existed on the searched systems. AI-service credentials were also within reach, but their theft or resale was not established. The observed behavior was consistent with financial motives. Inside a Kubernetes cluster, the attacker deployed a container that mounted the underlying server’s filesystem. Although access was read-only, it allowed credential harvesting. An attempt to create a new administrative cloud identity was blocked. Barracuda removed the container on November 4, Pacific time, then rotated credentials across the affected systems. The incident surfaced when an engineer reported unusual account activity on November 4. The vendor shared information about its own compromise that same day. The chain echoes the Cursor vendor key breach , where exposed credentials enabled further access, but the disclosures do not establish a common attacker. By discovery, Barracuda’s recorded intrusion had already ended. One reached system stored credentials used by Barracuda XDR to collect customer telemetry. Investigators found no direct evidence that those credentials were accessed, but incomplete logging prevented them from ruling it out. Barracuda therefore treated reachable secrets as potentially compromised and asked affected customers to revoke and recreate relevant integration credentials. Barracuda said customers not contacted did not need to act. Its broader recommendations included replacing long-lived keys with short-lived, narrowly scoped access, limiting movement between systems, and preparing rapid secret rotation. The incident highlights a basic problem: automated attackers can finish exploiting connected credentials before a human investigation begins. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Source-listed clue Context i followed by digits Machine-style resource labels WALLET , MNEMONIC , SEED , PRIV Environment variables searched Ethereum keystores, extended private keys, seed phrase files Cryptocurrency targets Wallet-related Kubernetes secrets Cryptocurrency searches Encoded secrets in build logs Credential exposure technique Container mounting the host filesystem read-only Credential-harvesting behavior Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . The intrusion moved through stored secrets, development systems, and Kubernetes clusters, showing how one forgotten credential can open a path across several connected platforms. Barracuda recorded the activity between November 1 and November 2, 2026.

The key had been provided to a third-party AI company for an earlier project but remained active after that work ended.

According to Barracuda, the vendor’s development environment was compromised in October, apparently exposing the credential. The company acknowledged that failing to retire the key left an unnecessary entry point into its cloud environment.

Barracuda researchers identified activity matching ARTEX, an open-source AI-driven penetration-testing framework, rather than naming a standalone malware family.

Hackers Exploit Exposed AI Vendor Key

In its technical incident report, the company linked the intrusion to automated credential searches and machine-style resource labels.

Separately, the Fireworks AI data breach illustrates related vendor exposure risks, although Barracuda did not name its AI supplier.

The first recorded API call occurred at 04:33 UTC on November 1. Within minutes, the attacker began checking which resources the key could access.

It then read stored secrets, including AWS access keys and Azure service principal secrets, using each discovery to expand access rather than relying on a single compromised account.

Over the following 24 hours, the attacker moved from cloud accounts into a data analytics system, obtained a source-code access token, and reached Kubernetes clusters.

It also decrypted infrastructure-as-code state files and collected credentials from server metadata services and Kubernetes service accounts. Each exposed secret became another route through the environment.

Early on November 2, the attacker pushed temporary branches into several repositories. These triggered build workflows designed to print build-system secrets into job logs.

Encoding the secrets prevented normal log-masking controls from hiding them. The repository activity took less than four hours, and the final recorded attacker activity occurred at 23:31 UTC that day.

Barracuda said ARTEX uses a planner agent to choose actions while worker agents execute tools and share findings.

Its findings complement reporting on ARTEX AI agent attacks involving rapid privilege escalation. However, the framework’s use does not identify the attacker: multiple criminal and state-aligned groups have reportedly adopted it.

Credential Theft, Persistence, and Customer Response

The attacker searched for cryptocurrency material, including wallet-related environment variables, Ethereum keystores, private keys, seed phrase files, and Kubernetes secrets.

Barracuda said no wallet material existed on the searched systems. AI-service credentials were also within reach, but their theft or resale was not established. The observed behavior was consistent with financial motives.

Inside a Kubernetes cluster, the attacker deployed a container that mounted the underlying server’s filesystem. Although access was read-only, it allowed credential harvesting.

Barracuda therefore treated reachable secrets as potentially compromised and asked affected customers to revoke and recreate relevant integration credentials.

Barracuda said customers not contacted did not need to act. Its broader recommendations included replacing long-lived keys with short-lived, narrowly scoped access, limiting movement between systems, and preparing rapid secret rotation.
