items.title: Pluralistic: Remembrance of proteins past (17 Nov 2026)
items.summary: Today's links Remembrance of proteins past : People like what they like. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : BBC's bullshit DRM story; Radical hotel-room coffee independence; Foreclosure map predicts Trump vote; Pinkest pink v Anish Kapoor; Bruce Sterling on the Trump election; Keep the hope machine running; "Messy"; Jam To-Day; Billy Bragg x file-sharing; Second Life v copying; Best Buy claims copyright over prices; All cab conversations in Oxford must be recorded; The end of "software objectivity"; "Pirate Utopia"; Mamdani's photocopier-kicker; Biden does(n't) like SOPA; "The Freedom Maze"; Obama's weapons in Trump's hands; Gilmore/Barlow audio; MPAA v video iPods; RIP SF's neon Yahoo sign; NYC deputy mayor says no filming cops; Bannon wants to deport Indian CEOs; Academic economists charge $1k/h to defend giga-mergers; Iphones secretly spy on your calls; Office Depot fakes malware infections; Live Nation murdered at Astroworld; Games industry's self-induced brain injury. Upcoming appearances : Folkestone, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. Remembrance of proteins past ( permalink ) Without a doubt, the best piece of media from the 2026 midterms was Scott Colom's "Pick another senator instead" ad from his triumphant Mississippi senate campaign against GOP incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith: https://youtu.be/zpUnm09lTUk?si=3ApbHida5_VpQCLB&t=2219 Some background: Colom is the first Black Mississippi senator elected since Reconstruction gave way to Jim Crow. He's also the first Democratic Mississippi senator since 1982. Colom's campaign shifted the statewide vote leftward by 19 points, and he won a quarter of the state's white votes. Colom ran a great campaign and promoted great policies, but also: he ran one of the great political ads of all time. That ad skewered Hyde-Smith's "let them eat whey powder" remark to WLOX Biloxi host Hugh Keeton, who asked her about the cost of living crisis and the high price of beef, to which she replied that people "have so many proteins to choose from": https://www.mississippifreepress.org/americans-who-cant-afford-beef-have-so-many-proteins-to-choose-from-says-us-sen-cindy-hyde-smith/ Colom's ad plays a montage of Mississippians expressing disgust with Hyde-Smith's response, saying "I'd rather choose another senator instead." Colom was quick to credit content creator Ryan Sayles, who joined the campaign after doing some freelance work for them, as the ad's mastermind: https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/12/ryan-sayles-scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-01163508 Much has been said about the ad's style, especially the viral "s-h-e-e-e-i-t" voiced by US Army vet Russ Hudson, who stepped in to do the ad when his father declined to curse on camera: https://edition.cnn.com/2026/11/15/politics/scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-mississippi-senate But the most important analysis on the ad is of its substance , specifically how it repudiates one of the key doctrines of neoliberal, austerity economics, as David Dayen writes for The American Prospect : https://prospect.org/2026/11/16/how-the-mississippi-senate-win-exposed-austerity-logic/ Neoliberalism is the signature achievement of the "law and economics" movement that came out of the University of Chicago. The central conceit of law and econ is that economics is a "hard science" (not a social science) and that its domain is a deterministic, quantifiable physics of human behavior. Economists went so far as to create a fake "Nobel Prize" in economics in a bid to elevate their work out of the social sciences: https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics This "science" claims it can replace squishy, qualitative questions with mathematical models that can output the objectively correct answer to every thorny political question, thereby substituting an obscure form of mathematics for political deliberation: https://pluralistic.net/2023/04/03/all-models-are-wrong/#some-are-useful This is a remarkably cheap and transparent stunt. To produce this "mathematics of human behavior," you must first quantize all the qualitative questions so that they can be plugged into variables in econ equations. But here's the problem: assigning a numeric value to a qualitative factor is a qualitative exercise! When an economist decides that the pain you'll experience as a result of their policy prescriptions is worth "7" while the benefit is worth "8," they are not doing objective work, they're just declaring their own judgments (and biases) to be empirical observations, while demoting your judgments to mere "feelings" (and biases): https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics Economism doesn't just eliminate qualitative questions from policymaking: it incinerates all of those qualitative factors so that economists can perform mathematics on whatever dubious quantitative residue remains in the crucible: https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-qualia/ This is where Scott Colom's brilliant campaign ad comes in. As Dayen points out, when Hyde-Smith made her "many other proteins to choose from," gaffe, she was referencing a key piece of economic theory that has been thoroughly weaponized by the neoliberals: "substitution." On its face, substitution is just the commonsense proposition that when prices for one good or service go up, some consumers will substitute another. When gas prices go up, more people ride the bus. When Instagram increases its ad-load, more people switch to Mastodon or Bluesky. When your ISP jacks up your price, you might switch to another carrier. So far, so good. Indeed, one of the best things about digital products and services is how low digital "switching costs" (the cost you bear when switching from one service to another) can be. The lower the switching costs are, the easier it is to substitute one thing for another. This means that, in a state of nature, tech bosses have to be careful about enshittifying their products, lest their users defect to a rival. This is why tech bosses have spent decades doing everything they can to jack up those "switching costs." They want to convert all their users into hostages: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2021/08/facebooks-secret-war-switching-costs Substitution is real and it makes sense. The problem comes when neoliberal economists use this idea in policy . In the early 2010s, Barack Obama proposed applying substitution to the American welfare system through something called "Chained CPI." "CPI" stands for the "Consumer Price Index": this is a measurement of the cost of a "basket of goods" (a bunch of supposedly representative household items) that is used to make inflationary adjustments to a variety of payments. When the CPI goes up, so do social security, welfare and disability payments. Otherwise, inflation would continually reduce the living standards of everyone who receives these entitlements. "Chained CPI" takes the CPI and applies substitution to it. Rather than asking whether hamburger just got more expensive, the economists who calculate CPI ask whether the cheapest protein at the grocery store got more expensive (because hamburger can be swapped out for another protein). Chained CPI's intent and effect is to reduce payments to retirees, disabled people, and poor people. Chained CPI is always going to be lower than CPI, because chained CPI only rises when the cheapest "substitute" for one of the items in CPI's "basket of goods" gets more expensive. In effect, the "basket of goods" becomes a transdimensional basket, one that contains every substitute good that might have gone into the basket in all possible parallel universes. Economists get to universe-shop for the dimension where that basket has the lowest cost, and then we all have to live in their chosen universe. Obama tried to adopt it 2013 as part of a "grand bargain" to reduce the deficit, but was thwarted by the Tea Party Caucus, who refused the grand bargain on the grounds that it contained an infinitesimal tax rise for the richest Americans: https://abcnews.com/blogs/politics/2013/04/obamas-chained-cpi-throws-off-pols-and-heres-how-it-works/ But chained CPI is one of the most cherished ideas of neoliberal thinktanks, so it came back in 2017 for Trump's tax giveaway to the super-rich, whose costs were partially offset by using chained CPI to calculate tax brackets, the standard deduction, and the Earned Income Tax Credit: https://newrepublic.com/article/145688/biggest-trojan-horse-republican-tax-plan As Dayen writes, "[This created] a regressive tax increase by eroding deductions and credits and pushing people into higher tax brackets. The wealthy were unaffected by this since they were already in the highest tax bracket and itemized rather than using the standard deduction." Which brings me back to Cindy Hyde-Smith's foot-in-mouth remarks about "so many proteins." Whether or not Hyde-Smith knew it, she was referencing this substitution/chained CPI doctrine when she told people that beef inflation didn't matter because other proteins were available. In doing so, she was performing economism's cheapest trick: pretending that her opinions are objective facts, while other people's opinions are just feelings . As Dayen writes, "[W]ho decides whether the cheaper product they switch to is 'similar' to the one that’s become so expensive that the consumer must give it up?…The logic is, approximately: You're not doing as badly as you think, so pick another protein and quit your whining." People do substitute one thing for another as a matter of economic necessity. But the idea that a "substitute" is an "equivalent" can only be accepted if you first buy into the economist's conceit that all qualitative matters can be safely incinerated, leaving the expert to do math on the quantitative ash. In this conceit, if you can't afford hamburgers and end up substituting chicken or fish, then you've found a new protein and have lost no "welfare." If you think otherwise, then you are expressing an irrational preference (unlike economists, whose preference for having a Nobel prize of their own is so empirically correct that it could be detected by a Martian peering at Earth through a telescope). It's not only Cindy Hyde-Smith who unconsciously metabolized the idea of substitution as "rationality"; it's the voters, too, who recognized in Hyde-Smith's remarks the arrogance of policy elites who've spent decades discounting their views as "feelings" while declaring their own views to be experimental validated facts. Not only do voters recognize this move: they hate it. They know that elites are perfectly capable of expressing strong views about qualitative matters and moving heaven and Earth to achieve a life that fits with their aesthetics. They know that the same Ivy League economists who dismiss their preferences as "irrational" will revel for 4,000 pages' worth of Marcel Proust expounding on the spiritual, intangible reasons for choosing his favorite baked goods. Economics is the study of why people do things, but somewhere along the way it became a club used to force people to do the things that powerful people prefer. The (alleged) "rationalism" of economism has worn out its welcome. You don't need an economics degree to understand why that "rationalism" is a cheap trick: after 50 years of neoliberalism, a Martian with a telescope could spot it. Remembrance of proteins past (permalink)

Without a doubt, the best piece of media from the 2026 midterms was Scott Colom's "Pick another senator instead" ad from his triumphant Mississippi senate campaign against GOP incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith:

https://youtu.be/zpUnm09lTUk?si=3ApbHida5_VpQCLB&t=2219

Some background: Colom is the first Black Mississippi senator elected since Reconstruction gave way to Jim Crow. He's also the first Democratic Mississippi senator since 1982. Colom's campaign shifted the statewide vote leftward by 19 points, and he won a quarter of the state's white votes.

Colom ran a great campaign and promoted great policies, but also: he ran one of the great political ads of all time. That ad skewered Hyde-Smith's "let them eat whey powder" remark to WLOX Biloxi host Hugh Keeton, who asked her about the cost of living crisis and the high price of beef, to which she replied that people "have so many proteins to choose from":

https://www.mississippifreepress.org/americans-who-cant-afford-beef-have-so-many-proteins-to-choose-from-says-us-sen-cindy-hyde-smith/

Colom's ad plays a montage of Mississippians expressing disgust with Hyde-Smith's response, saying "I'd rather choose another senator instead." Colom was quick to credit content creator Ryan Sayles, who joined the campaign after doing some freelance work for them, as the ad's mastermind:

https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/12/ryan-sayles-scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-01163508

Much has been said about the ad's style, especially the viral "s-h-e-e-e-i-t" voiced by US Army vet Russ Hudson, who stepped in to do the ad when his father declined to curse on camera:

https://edition.cnn.com/2026/11/15/politics/scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-mississippi-senate

But the most important analysis on the ad is of its substance, specifically how it repudiates one of the key doctrines of neoliberal, austerity economics, as David Dayen writes for The American Prospect:

https://prospect.org/2026/11/16/how-the-mississippi-senate-win-exposed-austerity-logic/

Neoliberalism is the signature achievement of the "law and economics" movement that came out of the University of Chicago. The central conceit of law and econ is that economics is a "hard science" (not a social science) and that its domain is a deterministic, quantifiable physics of human behavior. Economists went so far as to create a fake "Nobel Prize" in economics in a bid to elevate their work out of the social sciences:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics

This "science" claims it can replace squishy, qualitative questions with mathematical models that can output the objectively correct answer to every thorny political question, thereby substituting an obscure form of mathematics for political deliberation:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/04/03/all-models-are-wrong/#some-are-useful

This is a remarkably cheap and transparent stunt. To produce this "mathematics of human behavior," you must first quantize all the qualitative questions so that they can be plugged into variables in econ equations. But here's the problem: assigning a numeric value to a qualitative factor is a qualitative exercise!

When an economist decides that the pain you'll experience as a result of their policy prescriptions is worth "7" while the benefit is worth "8," they are not doing objective work, they're just declaring their own judgments (and biases) to be empirical observations, while demoting your judgments to mere "feelings" (and biases):

https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics

Economism doesn't just eliminate qualitative questions from policymaking: it incinerates all of those qualitative factors so that economists can perform mathematics on whatever dubious quantitative residue remains in the crucible:

https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-qualia/

This is where Scott Colom's brilliant campaign ad comes in. As Dayen points out, when Hyde-Smith made her "many other proteins to choose from," gaffe, she was referencing a key piece of economic theory that has been thoroughly weaponized by the neoliberals: "substitution."

On its face, substitution is just the commonsense proposition that when prices for one good or service go up, some consumers will substitute another. When gas prices go up, more people ride the bus. When Instagram increases its ad-load, more people switch to Mastodon or Bluesky. When your ISP jacks up your price, you might switch to another carrier.

So far, so good. Indeed, one of the best things about digital products and services is how low digital "switching costs" (the cost you bear when switching from one service to another) can be. The lower the switching costs are, the easier it is to substitute one thing for another.

This means that, in a state of nature, tech bosses have to be careful about enshittifying their products, lest their users defect to a rival. This is why tech bosses have spent decades doing everything they can to jack up those "switching costs." They want to convert all their users into hostages:

https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2021/08/facebooks-secret-war-switching-costs

Substitution is real and it makes sense. The problem comes when neoliberal economists use this idea in policy. In the early 2010s, Barack Obama proposed applying substitution to the American welfare system through something called "Chained CPI."

"CPI" stands for the "Consumer Price Index": this is a measurement of the cost of a "basket of goods" (a bunch of supposedly representative household items) that is used to make inflationary adjustments to a variety of payments. When the CPI goes up, so do social security, welfare and disability payments. Otherwise, inflation would continually reduce the living standards of everyone who receives these entitlements.

"Chained CPI" takes the CPI and applies substitution to it. Rather than asking whether hamburger just got more expensive, the economists who calculate CPI ask whether the cheapest protein at the grocery store got more expensive (because hamburger can be swapped out for another protein).

Chained CPI's intent and effect is to reduce payments to retirees, disabled people, and poor people. Chained CPI is always going to be lower than CPI, because chained CPI only rises when the cheapest "substitute" for one of the items in CPI's "basket of goods" gets more expensive. In effect, the "basket of goods" becomes a transdimensional basket, one that contains every substitute good that might have gone into the basket in all possible parallel universes. Economists get to universe-shop for the dimension where that basket has the lowest cost, and then we all have to live in their chosen universe.

Obama tried to adopt it 2013 as part of a "grand bargain" to reduce the deficit, but was thwarted by the Tea Party Caucus, who refused the grand bargain on the grounds that it contained an infinitesimal tax rise for the richest Americans:

https://abcnews.com/blogs/politics/2013/04/obamas-chained-cpi-throws-off-pols-and-heres-how-it-works/

But chained CPI is one of the most cherished ideas of neoliberal thinktanks, so it came back in 2017 for Trump's tax giveaway to the super-rich, whose costs were partially offset by using chained CPI to calculate tax brackets, the standard deduction, and the Earned Income Tax Credit:

https://newrepublic.com/article/145688/biggest-trojan-horse-republican-tax-plan

As Dayen writes, "[This created] a regressive tax increase by eroding deductions and credits and pushing people into higher tax brackets. The wealthy were unaffected by this since they were already in the highest tax bracket and itemized rather than using the standard deduction."

Which brings me back to Cindy Hyde-Smith's foot-in-mouth remarks about "so many proteins." Whether or not Hyde-Smith knew it, she was referencing this substitution/chained CPI doctrine when she told people that beef inflation didn't matter because other proteins were available. In doing so, she was performing economism's cheapest trick: pretending that her opinions are objective facts, while other people's opinions are just feelings.

As Dayen writes, "[W]ho decides whether the cheaper product they switch to is 'similar' to the one that’s become so expensive that the consumer must give it up?…The logic is, approximately: You're not doing as badly as you think, so pick another protein and quit your whining."

People do substitute one thing for another as a matter of economic necessity. But the idea that a "substitute" is an "equivalent" can only be accepted if you first buy into the economist's conceit that all qualitative matters can be safely incinerated, leaving the expert to do math on the quantitative ash.

In this conceit, if you can't afford hamburgers and end up substituting chicken or fish, then you've found a new protein and have lost no "welfare." If you think otherwise, then you are expressing an irrational preference (unlike economists, whose preference for having a Nobel prize of their own is so empirically correct that it could be detected by a Martian peering at Earth through a telescope).

It's not only Cindy Hyde-Smith who unconsciously metabolized the idea of substitution as "rationality"; it's the voters, too, who recognized in Hyde-Smith's remarks the arrogance of policy elites who've spent decades discounting their views as "feelings" while declaring their own views to be experimental validated facts. Not only do voters recognize this move: they hate it.

They know that elites are perfectly capable of expressing strong views about qualitative matters and moving heaven and Earth to achieve a life that fits with their aesthetics. They know that the same Ivy League economists who dismiss their preferences as "irrational" will revel for 4,000 pages' worth of Marcel Proust expounding on the spiritual, intangible reasons for choosing his favorite baked goods.

Economics is the study of why people do things, but somewhere along the way it became a club used to force people to do the things that powerful people prefer. The (alleged) "rationalism" of economism has worn out its welcome. You don't need an economics degree to understand why that "rationalism" is a cheap trick: after 50 years of neoliberalism, a Martian with a telescope could spot it.

items.title: Proton gives Lumo AI access to files, email and workplace tools – with permissions set action by action
items.summary: Proton has launched Lumo Desktop, a Windows, macOS and Linux app that turns its privacy-focused AI assistant into something closer to an agent. The update introduces three features – Connectors, Schedules and Skills – that allow Lumo to reach into a user’s files, inbox and business tools, run tasks on a timer and remember how its owner likes things done. Giving an AI assistant that kind of reach raises obvious security questions, and Proton is pitching granular control as the answer. For every connector, users can choose which actions Lumo may carry out automatically, which require approval and which are blocked entirely. Proton’s own example: Lumo can be allowed to search an inbox, made to ask before sending an email, and prevented from deleting messages at all. What Lumo can now reach Connectors cover a broad attack surface, which makes those permissions matter. Supported integrations include: Local tools: filesystem access, shell execution and browser content fetching. Proton Mail: via Proton Mail Bridge. Third-party services: Dropbox for personal files, plus Jira and Confluence for workplace use. MCP: custom local or remote Model Context Protocol servers. Connected tools are switched on in conversations by default; users can disable individual connectors from each conversation’s Tools menu. Security teams will want to note both the default and the inclusion of shell execution when assessing the app for managed endpoints. Schedules apply the same model to unattended work. Each scheduled task, such as a weekly inbox summary or a monthly spending review, carries its own permission set, and tasks can be edited, paused or deleted at any time. Source code published Proton is also publishing the source code for Lumo Desktop so the public can inspect the tools. The company describes this as the first step in a wider commitment to transparency about how it uses AI, including sharing tools it builds for internal use. “As AI assistants become more capable, people should be able to benefit from that progress without giving up control over their personal data,” said Eamonn Maguire, Director of Engineering for AI at Proton. Data handling Proton says conversations and data from connected apps and files are never used to train AI models or to serve personalised ads. Chat history is protected by zero-access encryption, meaning only the user can read it – not Proton – and Lumo keeps no server-side logs. The limited data Lumo stores is covered by Swiss privacy law and hosted on European infrastructure, which Proton says places it outside the scope of the US CLOUD Act. Lumo Desktop is available now for Windows, macOS and Linux. Existing Custom Lumos will be migrated automatically to the new Skills format.
items.summary_html:
Proton has launched Lumo Desktop, a Windows, macOS and Linux app that turns its privacy-focused AI assistant into something closer to an agent. The update introduces three features – Connectors, Schedules and Skills – that allow Lumo to reach into a user’s files, inbox and business tools, run tasks on a timer and remember how its owner likes things done.

Giving an AI assistant that kind of reach raises obvious security questions, and Proton is pitching granular control as the answer. For every connector, users can choose which actions Lumo may carry out automatically, which require approval and which are blocked entirely. Proton’s own example: Lumo can be allowed to search an inbox, made to ask before sending an email, and prevented from deleting messages at all.

What Lumo can now reach

Connectors cover a broad attack surface, which makes those permissions matter. Supported integrations include:

  • Local tools: filesystem access, shell execution and browser content fetching.
  • Proton Mail: via Proton Mail Bridge.
  • Third-party services: Dropbox for personal files, plus Jira and Confluence for workplace use.
  • MCP: custom local or remote Model Context Protocol servers.

Connected tools are switched on in conversations by default; users can disable individual connectors from each conversation’s Tools menu. Security teams will want to note both the default and the inclusion of shell execution when assessing the app for managed endpoints.

Schedules apply the same model to unattended work. Each scheduled task, such as a weekly inbox summary or a monthly spending review, carries its own permission set, and tasks can be edited, paused or deleted at any time.

Source code published

Proton is also publishing the source code for Lumo Desktop so the public can inspect the tools. The company describes this as the first step in a wider commitment to transparency about how it uses AI, including sharing tools it builds for internal use.

“As AI assistants become more capable, people should be able to benefit from that progress without giving up control over their personal data,” said Eamonn Maguire, Director of Engineering for AI at Proton.

Data handling

Proton says conversations and data from connected apps and files are never used to train AI models or to serve personalised ads. Chat history is protected by zero-access encryption, meaning only the user can read it – not Proton – and Lumo keeps no server-side logs. The limited data Lumo stores is covered by Swiss privacy law and hosted on European infrastructure, which Proton says places it outside the scope of the US CLOUD Act.

Lumo Desktop is available now for Windows, macOS and Linux. Existing Custom Lumos will be migrated automatically to the new Skills format.

items.title: CNN, BBC, Zoom, and other sites served malicious code in supply-chain attack
items.summary: .kadence-column490141_ece28d-44 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column490141_ece28d-44 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column490141_ece28d-44 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column490141_ece28d-44 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column490141_ece28d-44 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column490141_ece28d-44 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column490141_ece28d-44{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column490141_ece28d-44 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column490141_ece28d-44 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article Attackers used Optimizely to spread code targeting visitors’ payments and devices Researchers found affected files linked to 178 organizations, including CNN, BBC, and Zoom If you visited an affected site on November 16, check your payments and update your devices Visiting a familiar website should not mean exposing your payment details to criminals. But attackers found a way to put malicious code on websites belonging to some of the world’s best-known organizations by compromising a service those sites trusted. On November 16, security researcher Scott Helme and his team at Report URI identified malicious JavaScript in Optimizely files associated with 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, Salesforce, and GitLab. The code could redirect cryptocurrency payments, skim payment card details, and deliver exploit kits targeting vulnerable iPhones and iPads. Check Report URI’s full list to see which websites were affected. Optimizely provides software that helps businesses test and personalize their websites. To accomplish this, a website adds a small piece of JavaScript called a snippet. This loads Optimizely’s code into visitors’ browsers, where it can change their experience and measure the results. In this incident, it also provided a way for unauthorized changes to reach visitors through an otherwise legitimate website. Optimizely is widely used. Website technology tracker BuiltWith currently reports detecting it on roughly 190,000 live websites . That is its overall usage, not the number affected by this incident. This qualifies as a supply-chain attack because, instead of breaking into every website separately, criminals abused a shared service those websites relied on. The BBC provides a prominent example of how the attack unfolded. Report URI’s timeline records a clean capture of its Optimizely snippet at 02:21 UTC on November 16, followed by an injected version at 04:21 UTC. By 08:28 UTC, the researchers observed the main malicious payload being loaded on bbc.com. This does not establish that the BBC’s own servers were breached, or that every BBC visitor was infected. It shows how a third-party script used by a trusted website can become the route through which malicious code reaches a visitor’s browser. Optimizely confirmed the incident and says it fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. Report URI also said all the infected Optimizely files it was monitoring were clean by 23:11 UTC on November 16 and had remained clean since. How to stay safe Visitors cannot reasonably be expected to inspect every script a website loads, and disabling JavaScript can make many websites unusable. The most useful steps are to keep devices updated and check any potentially affected transactions. Update your iPhone or iPad. Install the latest iOS or iPadOS version available for your device. This is particularly important if you visited an affected website on November 16, because the attack included exploit delivery aimed at older, vulnerable versions. Use an up-to-date real-time anti-malware solution . This can help detect and block malware on your devices. Review cryptocurrency transfers made during the incident. Check the actual destination address against the intended recipient’s address, confirming it directly with the recipient through a trusted channel. The attack was specifically designed to change payment destinations. Check payment card activity. If you entered card details on an affected page on November 16, monitor your account and contact your card issuer promptly about suspicious transactions. Enable transaction alerts where available. You could also consider identity theft protection with credit monitoring to help spot signs of identity misuse, such as new credit accounts opened in your name. Watch for unusual account activity. Investigate unexpected account changes or unfamiliar sessions, particularly for services you were using on affected pages. The code could steal some cookies, which can contain information used to keep you signed in. The main responsibility rests with the organizations delivering code to visitors. The incident shows why website operators also need to monitor what third-party scripts do and restrict the other scripts and data connections they can introduce. Consumers shouldn’t have to audit a website’s software supply chain before reading the news or making a purchase. Stop threats before they can do any harm.   • Researchers found affected files linked to 178 organizations, including CNN, BBC, and Zoom

Visiting a familiar website should not mean exposing your payment details to criminals. But attackers found a way to put malicious code on websites belonging to some of the world’s best-known organizations by compromising a service those sites trusted.

On November 16, security researcher Scott Helme and his team at Report URI identified malicious JavaScript in Optimizely files associated with 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, Salesforce, and GitLab. The code could redirect cryptocurrency payments, skim payment card details, and deliver exploit kits targeting vulnerable iPhones and iPads. Check Report URI’s full list to see which websites were affected.

Optimizely provides software that helps businesses test and personalize their websites. To accomplish this, a website adds a small piece of JavaScript called a snippet. This loads Optimizely’s code into visitors’ browsers, where it can change their experience and measure the results. In this incident, it also provided a way for unauthorized changes to reach visitors through an otherwise legitimate website.

Optimizely is widely used. Website technology tracker BuiltWith currently reports detecting it on roughly 190,000 live websites. That is its overall usage, not the number affected by this incident. This qualifies as a supply-chain attack because, instead of breaking into every website separately, criminals abused a shared service those websites relied on.

Report URI’s timeline records a clean capture of its Optimizely snippet at 02:21 UTC on November 16, followed by an injected version at 04:21 UTC. This does not establish that the BBC’s own servers were breached, or that every BBC visitor was infected. It shows how a third-party script used by a trusted website can become the route through which malicious code reaches a visitor’s browser.

Optimizely confirmed the incident and says it fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. Report URI also said all the infected Optimizely files it was monitoring were clean by 23:11 UTC on November 16 and had remained clean since.

How to stay safe

Visitors cannot reasonably be expected to inspect every script a website loads, and disabling JavaScript can make many websites unusable. The most useful steps are to keep devices updated and check any potentially affected transactions.

Enable transaction alerts where available. You could also consider identity theft protection with credit monitoring to help spot signs of identity misuse, such as new credit accounts opened in your name.
  • Watch for unusual account activity. Investigate unexpected account changes or unfamiliar sessions, particularly for services you were using on affected pages. The code could steal some cookies, which can contain information used to keep you signed in.

The main responsibility rests with the organizations delivering code to visitors. The incident shows why website operators also need to monitor what third-party scripts do and restrict the other scripts and data connections they can introduce. items.title: Hackers Exploit Critical ScreenConnect Flaw to Silently Run Malware on MSP Technicians’ Computers
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting a critical ScreenConnect vulnerability to run malicious files on managed service provider technicians’ computers without showing a confirmation prompt. The attack turns a routine remote support connection into an infection route, putting workstations with access to customer systems, management tools, and saved credentials at risk. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-84869, carries a CVSS score of 9.9. ConnectWise disclosed it on September 8, 2026, and CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog three days later. The earlier CISA ScreenConnect exploitation warning highlighted unauthorized file transfers and execution during active sessions. Researchers from Huntress identified confirmed exploitation, including a November 12 incident where an attacker installed a rogue remote access client on a technician’s workstation in about nine seconds. Their published technical investigation also documented widespread delivery attempts and earlier efforts to reach technicians through customer support sessions. Hackers Exploit Critical ScreenConnect Flaw The flaw affects how ScreenConnect host clients handle guest file transfers in Support and Access sessions. A malicious guest can send a file and trigger its execution without the technician’s approval, potentially with elevated rights. The technician only needs to join the session; the attacker can control the guest machine or enter a legitimate customer session as an additional guest. In the November 12 compromise, the technician joined an unnamed Access session. Their client immediately launched a guest-supplied batch script from its temporary folder. The script restarted itself with a hidden window through PowerShell, decoded Telegram connection details, and notified the attacker that another machine had been reached. Next, it checked the Windows version, tested administrative access, and downloaded an installer. Windows Installer unpacked the package as an administrative image rather than performing a normal installation, leaving no standard installation record. Hackers Exploit Critical ScreenConnect Flaw to Silently Run Malware on MSP Technicians’ Computers The payload then started a rebranded ScreenConnect client disguised as a Windows Update component and connected to the attacker’s relay. Between October 20 and November 16, Huntress recorded at least 688,000 guest requests to run batch files across 42 MSP ScreenConnect servers, originating from 29 IP addresses. These were delivery attempts, not 688,000 successful infections. Attackers repeatedly sent requests while waiting for technicians to connect. Earlier worm-like ScreenConnect malware activity demonstrated how altered remote access clients could misuse file transfers to reach connected machines. On November 13, a second technician’s client opened an attacker-supplied text file, apparently testing whether execution worked. October activity also included attempts to place a script in technicians’ Windows Startup folders. Huntress did not confirm that every attempted delivery executed or established persistence. Patching Technician Clients and Investigating Exposure MSPs should update every technician’s ScreenConnect host client to 26.6.5 or later, alongside affected Access agents. Updating the server alone does not repair vulnerable software on technicians’ computers. Where immediate patching is impossible, Huntress relays ConnectWise’s recommendation to remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups. Investigators should examine guest-originated file execution and transfer events, then establish whether a technician was connected at the same time. On workstations, unexpected scripts launched by ScreenConnect, hidden PowerShell activity, unfamiliar Startup entries, and connections to unrecognized relays deserve attention. The separate SCKit remote access campaign involved suspected third-party extension abuse; Huntress distinguishes that entry route from direct exploitation of this client vulnerability. Confirmed compromise calls for workstation isolation, removal of unauthorized clients, and rotation of reachable management, vault, and customer administrator credentials. items.title: Is your OpenTelemetry pipeline becoming a performance bottleneck?
items.summary: At Cloud Native Days Austria 2026, I presented a talk called How to Defeat OTel’s Silent Killer: The Performance Overhead , exploring a problem that is easy to overlook when building observability pipelines: the cost of collecting telemetry itself. OpenTelemetry has become a cornerstone of cloud-native observability, providing standardized APIs, SDKs, and tooling for generating, collecting, processing, and exporting metrics, logs, and traces. However, instrumentation and telemetry processing are not free. Every span created, attribute attached, and batch exported consumes resources. As applications scale, poorly configured telemetry pipelines can introduce significant CPU usage, memory pressure, network traffic, and storage costs. In some cases, the infrastructure responsible for observing a system can become a performance problem of its own. The good news is that much of this overhead can be understood, measured, and reduced without sacrificing the visibility engineers depend on. Where does OpenTelemetry overhead come from? When discussing OpenTelemetry performance, we often focus on the application SDK. However, the cost extends beyond instrumentation. The entire telemetry pipeline contributes to resource consumption, from generating spans and collecting metrics to processing, exporting, and storing data. Instrumentation overhead is also workload-dependent. Two applications using the same instrumentation libraries can experience very different results depending on request throughput, attribute volume, runtime behavior, and the number of spans generated per request. This is why relying on a single overhead percentage can be misleading. Instead, we should examine CPU consumption, memory usage, application latency, telemetry volume, and the behavior of the Collector under load. There is also an important trade-off between application safety and telemetry completeness. When a pipeline becomes overloaded, backpressure and memory safeguards can protect the application and OpenTelemetry Collector, but they may also lead to rejected or dropped telemetry. The objective is not simply to minimize resource consumption. It is to maintain useful observability while keeping its operational cost predictable. Investigating the Collector: five common configuration problems For my demonstration, I used Telemetrygen , an OpenTelemetry utility that generates synthetic telemetry, to investigate how Collector configuration affects resource consumption. The investigation focused on five common sources of unnecessary overhead. 1. Inefficient batching Exporting small amounts of telemetry frequently can increase serialization work, export requests, and network overhead. The OpenTelemetry Collector groups telemetry inside the exporter’s sending queue before transmitting it downstream, helping amortize this work across larger payloads. (Note: Historically, this was handled by a standalone batch processor, which is now deprecated in favor of built-in exporter batching). However, batching parameters should reflect the actual workload. Larger batches are not automatically better: they can increase buffering requirements and affect export latency. exporters: otlp_grpc: endpoint: "otel-backend:4317" sending_queue: enabled: true sizer: items queue_size: 100000 batch: enabled: true min_size: 8192 flush_timeout: 200ms Configuring batch inside an exporter’s sending_queue groups spans, metrics, or logs before forwarding them downstream, improving compression efficiency and durability while reducing export overhead. Batches are sent when a configured size threshold is reached or a timeout expires. In this example, min_size: 8192 triggers an export when the batch reaches 8,192 items, while flush_timeout: 200ms triggers an export regardless of batch size. Once batching is enabled, these values are the Collector’s documented defaults, not universal performance recommendations. (Note: Because unbatched requests enter the queue first in this architecture, this example switches sizer from the default requests to items with a queue_size of 100000 to prevent smaller, unbatched bursts from overflowing the queue). The important point is to measure how batching affects resource consumption and throughput rather than relying on example configurations. 2. Unnecessary resource attributes Resource attributes provide valuable context about the systems producing telemetry. But collecting and forwarding attributes that nobody uses can increase payload sizes and downstream processing costs. For example, an application might need host.name, host.arch , and os.type for troubleshooting, but not detailed hardware information such as host.cpu.model.name or host.cpu.cache.l2.size . The OpenTelemetry Collector’s resource detection processor allows engineers to configure which system attributes are collected. Disabling unnecessary attributes can reduce telemetry volume and processing overhead, although the impact on storage and cardinality depends on the backend. A practical example: Keep the hostname and operating system type, but disable CPU model and cache metadata when those details are not needed for troubleshooting. 3. Aggressive receiver polling Infrastructure receivers collect metrics at configured intervals, often independently of application traffic. Polling host metrics , container statistics, databases, and network services every few seconds creates continuous work even when applications are relatively idle. Increasing collection intervals from 10 to 30 seconds, where operational requirements permit, can reduce collection frequency and associated overhead. This introduces a trade-off: lower polling frequency means less temporal resolution. The appropriate interval depends on how quickly a metric changes and how it is used for troubleshooting or alerting. 4. Exporting every trace Not every successful request needs to produce a trace that is retained. Exporting all traces can consume significant bandwidth, Collector resources, and backend capacity, particularly in high-throughput applications. Sampling provides a way to control this volume. Head-based sampling makes decisions early, reducing downstream work. Tail-based sampling makes decisions after observing more of a trace, enabling policies that retain errors or other diagnostically interesting requests. These policies retain traces with an error status and probabilistically sample 5% of traces, including potentially some additional error traces. However, tail sampling is not free. It requires buffering trace data until a decision can be made, introducing additional memory and processing overhead. Choosing a sampling strategy means balancing cost, diagnostic value, and the resources needed to make sampling decisions. 5. Memory safeguards applied too late The OpenTelemetry Collector includes a memory_limiter processor to help manage memory pressure. Processor ordering matters. When enrichment and transformation processors run before memory limiting, the Collector may perform additional work on telemetry that is subsequently refused under memory pressure. Memory limiting is a protective mechanism rather than a performance optimization in itself. Its purpose is to improve stability under pressure, not necessarily to reduce CPU consumption during normal operation. Placing the memory limiter early in the pipeline helps apply safeguards before more expensive processing. It is important to understand that the memory limiter is not a substitute for appropriate resource limits or capacity planning. It can refuse incoming data when memory pressure becomes excessive, and receivers must handle this behavior correctly to avoid unnecessary telemetry loss. From local experiments to production architecture Optimizing a single Collector is only part of the solution. In Kubernetes, telemetry workloads can fluctuate significantly as applications scale, deployments change, and traffic increases. A Collector configuration that performs well under synthetic load may behave differently in production. Here are some architectural practices that can help address these challenges. Separate collection from centralized processing. A two-tier architecture can use lightweight edge Collectors for local collection and gateway Collectors for more expensive processing. This allows different parts of the pipeline to scale according to their workloads. Control telemetry volume early. Filtering unnecessary attributes, removing unneeded data, and avoiding excessive cardinality can reduce the amount of information processed and transferred downstream. These decisions should preserve the context required for debugging and correlation. Plan for memory pressure and backend outages. Kubernetes memory limits, Collector memory safeguards, bounded queues, and retry mechanisms serve different purposes. Persistent queues can improve resilience during temporary backend failures, but they still require capacity planning and cannot guarantee delivery under every failure scenario. Scale with signal-specific requirements in mind. Horizontal scaling can increase throughput, but stateful processing requires additional consideration. Tail sampling, for example, generally requires spans belonging to the same trace to reach the same processing instance. These architectural decisions are just as important as tuning individual processors. Don’t forget the instrumentation One of the most effective optimizations happens before telemetry reaches the Collector. Instrumentation should answer meaningful operational questions rather than collect everything simply because it is possible. Excessive spans, high-cardinality attributes, and unnecessary instrumentation can increase resource consumption throughout the entire pipeline. For metrics, attributes containing unbounded values such as unique request IDs can create large numbers of distinct time series. For traces and logs, excessive attributes and events increase payload sizes and may affect backend processing or indexing costs. Why I chose Telemetrygen for my demo When preparing my performance investigation, I initially considered using the official OpenTelemetry Astronomy Shop . While it is an excellent environment for exploring instrumentation across microservices, its multiple applications, databases, and supporting services introduce additional CPU and memory consumption. For this experiment, I wanted to isolate the Collector’s performance overhead without the background noise of a complete application environment. Instead, I chose Telemetrygen , a lightweight utility for generating synthetic traces, metrics, and logs at controlled rates. In my OpenTelemetry performance overhead demo , I used synthetic telemetry to investigate how Collector configuration affects resource consumption. The demonstration walks through common inefficiencies, including missing batching, unnecessary resource attributes, aggressive receiver polling, excessive trace export, and memory limiter placement, showing how targeted configuration changes can improve pipeline efficiency. This approach helped isolate Collector behavior, but it is only one part of the performance picture. For understanding instrumentation overhead inside real applications, a complete environment such as Astronomy Shop remains valuable. Exploring instrumentation further Reducing overhead starts with understanding what telemetry an application generates and why. The official OpenTelemetry instrumentation documentation introduces automatic and manual instrumentation, while the sampling documentation explains how to control trace volume. These are useful starting points for reviewing instrumentation decisions before optimizing the Collector itself. For engineers interested in investigating performance further, the OpenTelemetry Collector documentation covers pipeline configuration and processing. The OpenTelemetry community is also a good place to discuss performance challenges. The Collector SIG focuses on Collector architecture, performance, and configuration, with discussions taking place in the #otel-collector channel on CNCF Slack. For questions about instrumentation overhead in a specific programming language, the corresponding language SIG is a better starting point. The OpenTelemetry community page provides information about SIGs, public meetings, and how to get involved. Making performance part of observability design OpenTelemetry overhead is not a single problem with a single configuration fix. It is the combined effect of instrumentation decisions, data volume, processor configuration, export behavior, and infrastructure architecture. The most useful lesson from this investigation is that observability pipelines should be measured and optimized like any other production system . Start with controlled benchmarks. Understand where resources are consumed. Introduce configuration changes individually, and evaluate their impact on CPU, memory, latency, throughput, and telemetry loss. Most importantly, treat example configurations as starting points rather than production-ready defaults. OpenTelemetry gives us the tools to understand complex distributed systems. With thoughtful instrumentation, careful pipeline configuration, and appropriate scaling strategies, we can ensure that collecting this information does not become an unnecessary burden on the systems we are trying to observe.

  3. Plan for memory pressure and backend outages. Kubernetes memory limits, Collector memory safeguards, bounded queues, and retry mechanisms serve different purposes. Persistent queues can improve resilience during temporary backend failures, but they still require capacity planning and cannot guarantee delivery under every failure scenario.
  4. Scale with signal-specific requirements in mind. Horizontal scaling can increase throughput, but stateful processing requires additional consideration. Tail sampling, for example, generally requires spans belonging to the same trace to reach the same processing instance.

These architectural decisions are just as important as tuning individual processors.

Don’t forget the instrumentation

One of the most effective optimizations happens before telemetry reaches the Collector.

Instrumentation should answer meaningful operational questions rather than collect everything simply because it is possible. Excessive spans, high-cardinality attributes, and unnecessary instrumentation can increase resource consumption throughout the entire pipeline.

For metrics, attributes containing unbounded values such as unique request IDs can create large numbers of distinct time series. For traces and logs, excessive attributes and events increase payload sizes and may affect backend processing or indexing costs.

Why I chose Telemetrygen for my demo

When preparing my performance investigation, I initially considered using the official OpenTelemetry Astronomy Shop. While it is an excellent environment for exploring instrumentation across microservices, its multiple applications, databases, and supporting services introduce additional CPU and memory consumption.

For this experiment, I wanted to isolate the Collector’s performance overhead without the background noise of a complete application environment.

Instead, I chose Telemetrygen, a lightweight utility for generating synthetic traces, metrics, and logs at controlled rates.

In my OpenTelemetry performance overhead demo, I used synthetic telemetry to investigate how Collector configuration affects resource consumption. The demonstration walks through common inefficiencies, including missing batching, unnecessary resource attributes, aggressive receiver polling, excessive trace export, and memory limiter placement, showing how targeted configuration changes can improve pipeline efficiency.

This approach helped isolate Collector behavior, but it is only one part of the performance picture. For understanding instrumentation overhead inside real applications, a complete environment such as Astronomy Shop remains valuable.

Exploring instrumentation further

Reducing overhead starts with understanding what telemetry an application generates and why. The official OpenTelemetry instrumentation documentation introduces automatic and manual instrumentation, while the sampling documentation explains how to control trace volume. These are useful starting points for reviewing instrumentation decisions before optimizing the Collector itself.

For engineers interested in investigating performance further, the OpenTelemetry Collector documentation covers pipeline configuration and processing. The OpenTelemetry community is also a good place to discuss performance challenges. The Collector SIG focuses on Collector architecture, performance, and configuration, with discussions taking place in the #otel-collector channel on CNCF Slack.

For questions about instrumentation overhead in a specific programming language, the corresponding language SIG is a better starting point. The OpenTelemetry community page provides information about SIGs, public meetings, and how to get involved.

Making performance part of observability design

OpenTelemetry overhead is not a single problem with a single configuration fix.

It is the combined effect of instrumentation decisions, data volume, processor configuration, export behavior, and infrastructure architecture.

The most useful lesson from this investigation is that observability pipelines should be measured and optimized like any other production system.

Start with controlled benchmarks. Understand where resources are consumed. Introduce configuration changes individually, and evaluate their impact on CPU, memory, latency, throughput, and telemetry loss.

Most importantly, treat example configurations as starting points rather than production-ready defaults.

OpenTelemetry gives us the tools to understand complex distributed systems. With thoughtful instrumentation, careful pipeline configuration, and appropriate scaling strategies, we can ensure that collecting this information does not become an unnecessary burden on the systems we are trying to observe.

items.title: Formal Verification of the Signal Protocol Using AI
items.summary: This seems like a good thing: Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees­a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. […] The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work. Alternate link . Details : First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human ­ just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Technical paper .

Details:

First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. Check your photo permissions if you want to limit that access. Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million) for accessing Android users’ entire camera rolls without specific consent or adequate disclosure. The regulator says the violation remains ongoing for some users, despite changes Meta has made. The decision concerns Facebook’s “Get camera roll suggestions when you’re browsing Facebook” feature. Launched in 2023, the idea is to use your photos and videos to suggest potential social media posts. You might be surprised to hear that Facebook can access every photo or video in your gallery if you’ve granted full photo access. That includes pictures of your kids, restaurant receipts, and that Wi-Fi password label you photographed awkwardly on the router behind the TV. But you might have granted that access without realizing it also enabled photo suggestions. That’s the problem, said the regulator. Facebook’s app requested access to the camera roll through a single permission that applies across the entire app, covering multiple features with different requirements. The Garante said: “The permission is preceded by a non-specific notice (’enable other features’) which does not make it clear to the user that they are also authorising suggestions from the camera roll.” One permission, lots of features Asking permission for lots of things via one request violated Article 122 of the Italian Data Protection Code, according to the regulator. That code is Italy’s privacy law, and its Article 122 implements the EU’s ePrivacy Directive, which protects data stored on devices such as smartphones. The Garante said access for this feature required free and informed consent. Facebook also failed to adequately explain its use of the photo gallery, and the suggestions feature was on by default. Granting full photo access could give the app ongoing access to the entire library, the regulator said, without users being able to verify which information was actually being used. The regulator’s investigation started in July 2025 after consumer organization Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti submitted a report. That prompted the Garante to conduct its own technical analysis. Meta had asked for Ireland to handle the case. Like many other technology companies, Meta’s main EU presence is in Ireland, whose regulator handles many cross-border privacy cases. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules at issue do not use that system. Meta disagrees Meta told Reuters that users must grant device permission before the feature can operate and can change that permission in their settings. The social media company also called the fine, which amounts to less than 0.5% of global revenues, “disproportionate.” It will appeal, it told reporters . The Garante attributed the amount of the fine to the high number of people affected (around 20 million Android users in Italy) along with the duration of the incident, which it referred to as a breach. It also called Meta out for its “poor level of cooperation.” Changes that the company made to its app were introduced late and only applied to users who update the app, it added. Aside from the financial penalty, the regulator has ordered Meta to request consent separately for the camera roll suggestions feature. It must get that consent after explaining to users what it will use the data for and how to disable it. The company must turn it off by default even for those who previously gave the blanket permission, it said, and if it doesn’t comply by the 60-day deadline then it must not enable the feature for users who haven’t given consent. The regulator is preparing for a potential follow-up. It has left the door open to address the possible use of content to train AI , which Meta has denied. The Garante also “reserves the right” to assess a new feature that allows the content of the camera roll to be processed in the cloud. Meta announced an opt-in photo suggestions feature for the US and Canada in October 2025. It analyzes media to find memorable moments and suggests creative edits. Meta says suggestions remain private unless users choose to share them, and the feature can be turned off in Facebook’s camera roll settings. What Facebook users can do The Italian order does not automatically change permissions for users elsewhere, but you can review your own settings. On Android, go to Settings > Apps > Facebook > Permissions > Photos and videos , then select Don’t allow to revoke gallery access. Depending on your Android version and the app, you may also have an option to allow access only to selected photos and videos. Menu names can vary by device. While Italy’s decision didn’t target iPhone users, they can also review Facebook’s photo access under Settings > Privacy & Security > Photos . items.title: Holiday shopping in a world of fakes: How AI is changing the game
items.summary: It’s the most wonderful time of the year, especially for scammers. The holiday shopping season is packed with tempting one-day-only deals, gift guides, and retailers promising the perfect present at the perfect price. And wherever shoppers go, scammers aren’t far behind. Cybercriminals have always taken advantage of the holiday rush. Now AI makes it easier to create fake storefronts, products, reviews, and promotions that look and sound legitimate. For consumers, knowing what—and who—to trust is getting harder. Shoppers are worried. According to Malwarebytes research, 77% of consumers are concerned about being scammed by a retailer using a fake AI website, or using AI to misrepresent products or reviews. That concern is grounded in experience: More than one in four consumers (28%) have experienced an AI-related shopping scam in the past year Some were misled by AI-generated product photos or reviews. Others described ordering products that never arrived, sometimes from legitimate-looking websites that turned out to be fake. With the holiday shopping season upon us, we’re looking at how AI is changing the shopping experience, where consumers see risks and benefits, and how to shop more safely. When a great looking product isn’t what it seems Realistic product images, glowing reviews, and professional-looking websites can make unfamiliar retailers seem trustworthy. AI makes it easier to create all three in one polished package, which is convincing enough to deceive even careful shoppers. For some, these convincing fakes have made buying online feel unsettling. One survey respondent commented: “It seems as though when I’m shopping online, I notice the models are AI-generated or even the products themselves and that scares me. I can’t tell what’s real or not anymore. I don’t even know if what I’m looking to buy is real! I don’t know if what is being advertised is the actual product. AI is going too far.” Survey respondents shared real-life experiences that help explain those fears. One described receiving products that looked nothing like the photos: “I buy fewer items that I don’t already know from real life because I fell for manipulated images and the delivered items barely resembled the edited pictures in the shop!” This aligns with what we’re seeing too. As an example, earlier this year we found cat face flower seeds being sold online. But manipulated images don’t have to look this extreme, or this obvious. As AI improves, telling what’s genuine from what’s fake is getting much more difficult. Some of our survey respondents described seeing convincing fake storefronts that took their money without delivering anything: “It was a fake website promoting shoes. I bought them and it turned out to be an AI website. Now I’ll be more wary of these websites and what they look like.” These experiences are especially common among younger shoppers. 42% of Gen Z say they’ve experienced an AI-related shopping scam, compared with 30% of Millennials, 22% of Gen X, and just 9% of Boomers and older. The impact goes beyond lost money or a missing package. Respondents described feeling embarrassed, angry and unsettled by how convincing the deception was. For many, that experience left a lasting distrust of online retailers. How AI brings scams directly to shoppers Scammers don’t have to wait for shoppers to stumble across a fake website. With the help of AI, they can send convincing, personalized messages that appear to come from familiar brands, bringing scams directly to consumers. It’s no wonder that global mega-retailer Amazon is the most impersonated brand that we see in our threat intelligence data, followed by Walmart, Temu, Costco, and Steam. *Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026 Scammers are getting personal Nearly one in four consumers (24%) say they’ve received a scam message that felt highly personalised, sometimes including their name or other personal details. Among Gen Z, that figure rises to almost one in three (32%). We came across a scam that linked a person’s phone number and name with a fake Facebook Marketplace listing to act as a conversation lure and get them to respond. Answering a message is often the first step in what can become a very costly scam. Even when shoppers spot the warning signs, a personalised scam can leave them feeling uneasy. One respondent explained: “I received an email that was clearly directed to me personally, yet it seemed “off” which was an alarm for me. I investigated it before clicking on anything and knew then that it was a scam. It made me feel like nothing is safe out there anymore and you have to be hyper-alert at every moment when online.” Spotting scams among the shopping noise Delivery companies are an obvious choice for scammers to impersonate at this time of year. With more purchases being made, it can be hard to keep track of which retailer is using which delivery service, and on which date it will arrive. *Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026 Common delivery scam lures we’ve seen include: A delayed parcel notification, paired with a request to pay a small fee through a link A failed-delivery claim demanding address confirmation or rescheduling. Short deadlines or “final notice” language to create a sense of urgency. Lookalike delivery company domains and off-brand links. In this example, scammers use a fake missed delivery, the USPS brand, and a sense of urgency (48 hours) in order to get their target to click. The broader research shows just how challenging this environment has become: 85% agree that sophisticated scams can be hard to distinguish from the real thing 85% believe AI makes it easier for scammers and criminals to target people Even the most routine messages about purchases and deliveries warrant a closer look, and that’s one more thing for consumers to worry about during an already busy time of year. Where shoppers accept AI Despite their concerns, many consumers accept some uses of AI in retail. In the survey, 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% accept AI-generated salespeople. Including neutral responses, those figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively. There’s also growing acceptance of AI on the retailer side. 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% are okay with AI-generated salespeople. Including those who feel neutral about these practices, the figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively. That shows how willing consumers are to let AI into the shopping process, despite their concerns. That acceptance extends to product images: 60% say using AI to enhance them is no different from existing advertising practices. Product photos have long been staged, edited and polished to make merchandise look its best; AI can do the same. Shoppers’ responses show that concern about AI and acceptance of its use can coexist. In the holiday rush, distinguishing a useful shopping aid from a convincing deception can be difficult. Shoppers are taking precautions, but the burden is growing Some shoppers are responding in practical ways, starting with where they choose to buy: 36% have limited purchases from unfamiliar online retailers. 26% have limited purchases from social media accounts As one respondent explained: “I am more wary of purchasing something from an ad I see on social media. I tend to search for the item online myself and find a legit website to order from.” Others are checking information more carefully: One respondent described checking reviews on another website after watching a convincing product video on social media, only to uncover signs of a scam. Another now deliberately seeks out negative or neutral reviews and real customer photos. Others describe comparing information across multiple sources rather than taking any online content at face value. One respondent summed up the need for extra caution: “I tell my children not everything that glitters is gold. Always be careful and check everything yourself. With AI today you can make everything look beautiful but beautiful doesn’t mean true, correct or authentic. Fact checking is the order of the day.” Beyond checking information for themselves, consumers also value having another person to turn to when they need help. Nearly seven in ten (69%) say they’d spend extra time or pay more for human customer service, while 43% say they’ve tried to talk to a real person rather than an AI customer service system. AI may make shopping more convenient for some, but that doesn’t mean consumers want to rely on it for every interaction. How to spot AI-powered shopping scams this holiday season AI can make fake stores, product photos, and reviews look extremely convincing. Here are four ways to protect yourself: Slow down. Scammers use urgency to rush you. During the holidays, limited-time deals and delivery alerts can be especially persuasive. Don’t let a countdown or unexpected message stop you from checking first. Guard your information. Be wary of unexpected requests from sellers or delivery services for passwords, payment details, or other personal information. A message can use your name or mention a recent purchase and still be fake. You can check which data Verify the source. Check independent reviews and compare product photos and details across websites. Go to the retailer’s official site directly instead of following links in messages.
